## M & I Bank v. Elsea

399 S.W.3d 834 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Also captioned UMB Bank, N.A. v. Landmark National Bank

Holding: A disposition of collateral is commercially reasonable if it is conducted in good faith and in accordance with standard commercial practices. The adequacy of the price is a factor but is not the sole determinant of whether the sale complied with UCC requirements. This case addressed whether the sale of collateral after a default was conducted in a 'commercially reasonable' manner. Following the debtor's default on a loan, M & I Bank repossessed and sold the collateral. The debtor challenged the bank's action, arguing that the sale price was significantly below market value and that the bank failed to market the collateral appropriately. The UCC requires that every aspect of the disposition of collateral, including method, manner, time, and place, must be commercially reasonable. The trial court found in favor of the bank, noting that while the price was low, the bank had taken steps to advertise and find buyers. The debtor appealed, claiming the bank ignored higher potential offers. The appellate court reviewed the standards for commercial reasonableness, noting that it is not merely about achieving the highest possible price but about the process being fair and in line with standard commercial practices in the relevant industry. The court ultimately affirmed the judgment, finding that the bank's actions satisfied the UCC requirements for a commercially reasonable disposition of collateral.

Second stored summary Holding: A termination statement filed by the authorized secured party is effective, and subsequent creditors may rely on the public record as it appears. Unauthorized or mistaken filings create significant liability for the filer, but the public record must remain reliable. This case dealt with the conversion of collateral and the priority of competing security interests in inventory. UMB Bank and Landmark National Bank both claimed security interests in the same inventory of the debtor. The issue was whether one bank's security interest had been 'terminated' or if it remained in effect. The court analyzed the effectiveness of a UCC-3 termination statement that had been filed. Landmark argued that the termination statement was filed in error or without authorization, but UMB Bank argued it was entitled to rely on the public record. The court examined the requirements for the effective termination of a financing statement under UCC Section 9-513. The court held that because the termination statement was filed by the authorized party, it was effective, and subsequent creditors were entitled to rely upon the state of the public record. This case emphasizes the reliance interest that third parties have in the accuracy of the UCC filings and the legal consequences of filing termination statements.

## M.A. Mortenson Co. v. Saunders Concrete Co.

676 S.W.2d 194 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Kansas City · 1984 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an integrated written purchase order constitutes the complete agreement between the parties. Extrinsic evidence cannot be used to contradict or modify the written terms of the purchase order. In this construction dispute, a concrete supplier sued a general contractor for the unpaid balance on materials delivered for a project. The contractor defended by arguing that the concrete was defective and caused delays, for which it sought damages. The case centered on the interpretation of the purchase order and whether it contained the entire agreement between the parties. The court analyzed whether the purchase order was an integrated contract, which would bar the introduction of prior or contemporaneous oral agreements. The appellate court found that the purchase order was intended to be the final expression of the parties' agreement. The court rejected the contractor's attempt to use extrinsic evidence to modify the terms of the contract regarding the concrete's specifications. The holding reaffirmed the strength of the parol evidence rule in commercial transactions, emphasizing that parties must ensure all important specifications and terms are included in the final written contract to be enforceable.

## M.A.B. v. Nicely

909 S.W.2d 669 · Mo. banc · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an 'as-is' clause does not insulate a seller from liability under the MPA if there is a deliberate omission of a material fact. The court reversed the trial court's judgment and remanded for further findings on the seller's intent. The plaintiff initiated a lawsuit against a seller regarding a contract for a used vehicle, alleging that the seller failed to disclose that the vehicle had been in a major accident and was salvaged. The plaintiff asserted that the seller's failure to disclose the vehicle's history constituted a violation of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA) and fraud. The seller defended the action by stating that the sale was 'as-is' and that the plaintiff had the opportunity to inspect the vehicle prior to purchase. The trial court ruled in favor of the defendant, finding that the 'as-is' clause effectively waived any claims for non-disclosure. On appeal, the Missouri Supreme Court analyzed the enforceability of 'as-is' clauses when there is an affirmative duty to disclose material facts under the MPA. The court addressed whether the MPA creates an exception to the traditional caveat emptor rule in the sale of goods by individuals and small businesses, particularly when the seller possesses superior knowledge about the hidden defects of the product being sold to a consumer.

## M.A.B. v. Nicely

545 S.W.3d 383 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the summary judgment, holding that the plaintiff's expert did not establish a specific breach of the standard of care. The expert's testimony was found to be conclusory and speculative. This medical malpractice action stemmed from the delivery of a child who suffered a brachial plexus injury. The parents alleged that the obstetrician applied excessive force during the delivery, resulting in permanent nerve damage to the child's shoulder and arm. The trial court granted summary judgment for the defendant based on a lack of admissible expert testimony demonstrating a breach of the standard of care. The appellate court examined the admissibility of the plaintiff's expert testimony, specifically evaluating whether the expert possessed the required knowledge and experience to provide a qualified opinion on obstetric procedures. The discussion highlighted the strict requirements for qualifying experts in medical malpractice litigation and the necessity of linking the alleged breach directly to the resulting injury. The case serves as an example of the procedural hurdles plaintiffs must overcome to survive summary judgment in cases where the primary evidence relies on complex medical causation testimony.

## M.E.R. v. J.A.R.

495 S.W.3d 186 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court's decision to permit the relocation was within its sound discretion after weighing the benefits to the mother against the impact on the children. The appellate court emphasized that trial courts are given wide latitude in these determinations. The father appealed an order modifying child custody, which granted the mother the right to move the children to a different state. The father argued that the trial court failed to conduct a proper analysis under Section 452.377, specifically regarding whether the relocation was in the children's best interests. He provided testimony that the children had a strong social network and were performing well in their current school. The mother argued that the relocation was necessary due to her own job prospects and that the children would be supported by family in the new state. The trial court acknowledged the difficulty of the decision but concluded that the mother's proposed plan was realistic and that the children would continue to have a strong relationship with the father through extended visitation periods. On appeal, the court looked at whether the trial court had balanced the potential disruption to the children's lives against the benefits of the mother's career move. The appellate court assessed if the trial court abused its discretion in its interpretation of the statutory factors for determining whether relocation is in the child's best interests.

## M.G. v. City of St. Louis

467 S.W.3d 351 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the city was not liable for the breach because the contract was subject to annual appropriation and no funds had been appropriated for the services in question. The court ruled that the contractor assumed the risk of non-payment by entering into a contract dependent on future city budgets. This case involved a breach of contract claim brought by a private security company against the City of St. Louis regarding a contract for services. The company alleged that the City failed to pay for services rendered during specific events and unilaterally reduced the contract value. The City defended by arguing that the contract was subject to annual appropriation and that since the budget was not passed to cover these services, it had no contractual obligation to pay. The court analyzed the constitutional and statutory limitations on municipal contracts, particularly the principle that a city cannot be bound by a contract that exceeds its current budget appropriations. This decision is crucial for understanding the limitations of municipal contracting authority and the inherent risks that private contractors face when dealing with entities that are dependent on annual appropriations. The case reinforces the requirement that contractors verify the availability of funds and the legal authority for municipal entities to enter into multi-year commitments.

## M.G. v. St. Luke's Health System, Inc.

676 S.W.3d 524 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2023 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the statute of limitations was not tolled because the plaintiff failed to show the injury was inherently undiscoverable within the statutory period. It affirmed the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the defendant. The plaintiff brought a claim against the health system alleging professional negligence related to the failure to diagnose an underlying condition during a hospital stay. The core of the dispute involved the application of the statute of limitations to a medical malpractice claim where the injury manifested after the date of the alleged negligence. The defendant argued that the statute of repose barred the claim because the action was not filed within the period prescribed by state law for medical negligence. The plaintiff contended that the discovery rule should toll the statute of limitations, arguing that the patient could not have known about the malpractice until a later date. The litigation focused on whether the specific circumstances of the case qualified for an exception to the strict statutory deadlines. The appellate court reviewed the lower court's ruling on summary judgment, analyzing the interplay between discovery-based tolling and the absolute bars set by the legislature regarding medical claims.

## M.J.H. v. K.L.H.

658 S.W.3d 210 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2023 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the denial of the motion to modify custody. The court held that the trial court's findings were sufficient and that no abuse of discretion occurred in maintaining the existing arrangement. In this custody modification action, the father appealed the trial court's decision to deny his request for joint physical custody. The father alleged that there had been a change in circumstances regarding the children's schedules and the mother's ability to facilitate a co-parenting relationship. The trial court, after conducting an evidentiary hearing, found that while the parents had disagreements, the mother remained the primary caregiver and that a change to joint physical custody would not serve the children's best interests. The appellate court scrutinized the trial court's analysis of the Section 452.375 factors. The appellate court observed that the trial court had specifically addressed the children's needs for stability and the ongoing conflict between the parents, which was a significant factor in denying the modification. The court reiterated that the child's interest in a stable environment frequently outweighs the parents' interest in an equal division of time, especially in high-conflict cases. The appellate court found no abuse of discretion in the trial court's refusal to modify the custody arrangement, noting that the trial court appropriately prioritized the children's emotional and academic stability.

## M.L. v. SSM Health Care St. Louis

533 S.W.3d 726 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the statutory cap on noneconomic damages in medical malpractice cases is unconstitutional as it violates the right to a trial by jury. The jury's role in assessing damages cannot be superseded by fixed legislative caps. This case involved a birth injury medical malpractice claim. The parents of an infant who suffered hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy sued the hospital and the attending obstetrician. They alleged that the medical team failed to react appropriately to signs of fetal distress. The appeal focused on the applicability of the cap on noneconomic damages in medical malpractice cases as established by Missouri statutes. The plaintiffs argued that the statutory cap was unconstitutional as it violated the right to a jury trial. The Supreme Court of Missouri reviewed the history of medical malpractice damage caps and their impact on the constitutional rights of plaintiffs seeking redress for catastrophic injuries. The court conducted a thorough constitutional analysis, examining whether the legislative intervention in civil damage awards infringed upon the judicial branch's authority or the jury's role in determining damages. This case is a landmark decision regarding the limits of legislative power in restricting the recovery of damages in medical malpractice actions in Missouri, having significant implications for both plaintiffs and insurance defendants.

## M.L.G. v. J.A.G.

290 S.W.3d 109 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court did not err in denying the modification request. The moving party failed to meet the high burden of proving a substantial and continuing change in circumstances. The parents entered into a settlement agreement regarding custody and child support, which was later incorporated into the divorce decree. Less than two years later, the father moved for modification, claiming the child's academic performance had declined and the mother's residence was unsuitable. The trial court denied the motion, noting that the father failed to demonstrate a substantial change in circumstances as required by statute. The father appealed, arguing that the trial court ignored the child's needs. The appellate court reviewed the requirements for modification under Section 452.410 RSMo, which requires a change in circumstances that makes the original order unreasonable. The court found that the father's evidence regarding academic performance was insufficient to prove that the current living situation was detrimental to the child. The court emphasized that finality in custody decrees is important and that modification should not be granted simply because a parent is dissatisfied with the existing arrangement. The judgment was affirmed, with the court noting that the trial court's discretion in determining whether circumstances have changed significantly must be respected absent clear error.

## M.L.H. v. W.H.

290 S.W.3d 725 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the restriction of visitation was justified by the evidence presented. It affirmed the trial court's decision as essential to ensure the child's safety and well-being. The parents were involved in a custody dispute where the father was accused of physical abuse against the child. The trial court restricted the father's visitation to supervised visits only. The father appealed, claiming the evidence of abuse was speculative and that

Second stored summary the trial court's decision unfairly limited his parental rights. The appellate court examined the standard for restricting parental rights, noting that clear and convincing evidence of potential harm is required to justify limitations on visitation. The court reviewed the trial court's findings based on the testimony of the child's therapist and school officials. The appellate court concluded that the trial court's decision was well-grounded in the evidence provided and was necessary to protect the child. The court reaffirmed that while parents have fundamental rights to associate with their children, these rights are not absolute and must yield when there is a substantiated risk of physical or emotional harm to the child.

## M.M. v. S.D.

363 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: Landlords are generally not liable for the criminal acts of third parties. A duty may arise only if the landlord has actual knowledge of a specific, imminent risk or has undertaken to provide security and did so negligently. A tenant sued their landlord after being the victim of a crime committed by a third party on the apartment premises. The tenant alleged that the landlord was negligent in failing to provide adequate security, specifically citing the lack of functional locks on building entrance doors. The trial court dismissed the complaint, ruling that there was no duty for a landlord to protect a tenant from the criminal acts of third parties. The tenant appealed, arguing that the landlord's previous knowledge of other criminal incidents in the area created a foreseeable risk of future crime, thereby establishing a duty to provide reasonable security. The appellate court examined the standard for landlord liability concerning third-party criminal activity. The court reiterated that as a general rule, a landlord has no duty to protect tenants from the criminal acts of third persons. However, the court acknowledged a 'special relationship' exception where the landlord assumes a duty by taking specific safety measures or where the landlord had actual knowledge of a specific, imminent risk of harm. The court found that the tenant failed to allege sufficient facts demonstrating that the landlord knew of a specific threat to the plaintiff. Consequently, the court affirmed the dismissal, holding that the allegations did not meet the high threshold required to impose liability on a landlord for third-party criminal conduct.

## M.M. v. S.R.

721 S.W.2d 125 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1986 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an integration clause in a written lease agreement generally precludes the admission of evidence concerning prior or contemporaneous oral agreements. The tenant's labor cannot be substituted for the rent required by the clear, unambiguous terms of the written contract. The landlord initiated an action to evict a tenant, claiming the tenant had failed to pay the agreed-upon rent for three consecutive months. The tenant defended by stating they had performed extensive landscaping and property maintenance work in lieu of cash rent, as agreed to in an oral side-letter. The trial court ruled for the landlord, finding that the written lease, which contained an integration clause, clearly required cash payments and did not provide for services as a form of rent. The tenant appealed, arguing that the integration clause was not absolute and that their labor constituted valid consideration that should be recognized. The appellate court examined the parol evidence rule and the effect of integration clauses in residential leases. The court considered whether the evidence of the side-agreement was admissible to vary the terms of the written lease and whether the landlord's prior acceptance of the labor as payment created a waiver of the cash-only requirement. The analysis focused on the clarity of the lease terms and the importance of written agreements in preventing disputes over compensation methods.

## M.M. v. Steyer

339 S.W.3d 591 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the manager committed a material breach of the property management contract. It remanded the case for recalculation of damages consistent with the liability limitations in the written agreement. This case involved a dispute arising from a property management agreement where the plaintiff sought damages for alleged breaches of fiduciary duty and contract violations. The underlying agreement contained specific clauses regarding the maintenance of residential properties and the remittance of rental income. The dispute focused on whether the property manager had failed to perform necessary repairs and mismanaged funds collected from tenants. The defendant argued that the contract provided for limited liability and that the plaintiff's failure to provide notice of the alleged breaches precluded recovery under the express terms of the agreement. The trial court initially found in favor of the property owner, determining that the manager had materially breached the contract by failing to account for expenses and neglecting property standards. Upon appeal, the defendant challenged the trial court's calculation of damages and the interpretation of the notice provision. The Court of Appeals reviewed the record to determine if the trial court properly applied the principles of contract law regarding material breach and the duty to mitigate damages. The court found that while the breach was established, the damages awarded needed to be strictly linked to the contractual limitations defined in the agreement.

## M.P. v. Farmers Insurance Exchange

644 S.W.3d 522 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the insurer failed to make a meaningful offer of UM coverage as required by statute. Consequently, the court ordered the policy to be reformed to include higher UM coverage limits. This case involved a dispute over the 'uninsured motorist' coverage limits in an automobile insurance policy. The insured was involved in an accident with an uninsured driver and claimed that the insurer had failed to provide adequate notice regarding the coverage options, specifically the ability to stack uninsured motorist (UM) benefits. The insured argued that the insurer violated the Missouri Insurance Code requirements for disclosure of UM coverage options. The insurer maintained that it had complied with all statutory disclosure requirements and that the policy's anti-stacking provision was valid and enforceable. The case required the court to examine the insurer's disclosure documents to determine if they met the statutory 'meaningful offer' requirement. The court looked at the policy application and the disclosure forms to evaluate whether the insured was fully informed of the implications of their coverage choices. The decision centered on the interpretation of the statutory requirements for UM coverage offers and whether the insurer's failure to adequately inform the insured entitled the insured to higher coverage limits through judicial reformation of the contract.

## M.P. v. Progressive Therapy Services, Inc.

557 S.W.3d 465 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the claims asserted were for professional negligence because they required technical or scientific knowledge to establish the standard of care. Consequently, the plaintiff was required to comply with the statutory affidavit of merit requirement. This case involves a claim of negligence against a healthcare service provider. The plaintiff alleged that the provider's employees failed to monitor a patient properly, leading to an injury. The case turned on whether the alleged actions constituted 'professional negligence' under Missouri's medical malpractice statutes or 'ordinary negligence.' This distinction is critical because it determines whether the plaintiff must comply with the procedural requirements of Section 538.225, such as filing an affidavit of merit, and whether the case is subject to the caps on non-economic damages provided in Chapter 538. The court examined the definition of 'health care services' and whether the specific conduct at issue fell within the scope of the statutory definition of medical malpractice. The decision provides clarity on the boundary between administrative/ordinary negligence and professional medical malpractice in a healthcare setting, which significantly impacts how such cases are pleaded and defended in trial courts.

## M.R. v. Schmidt

849 S.W.2d 699 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1993 · Missouri

Holding: A landlord may be held liable under constructive notice if a dangerous condition in a common area exists for a sufficient duration that a reasonable inspection would have uncovered it. Regular inspections are a component of the landlord's duty. In this case, a tenant brought a claim against their landlord for injuries caused by a broken stair in a shared stairwell. The landlord argued that they had no knowledge of the broken stair and that the tenant had failed to inform them of the condition, despite having been aware of it for several weeks. The trial court found in favor of the landlord. The tenant appealed, arguing that the landlord had a duty to conduct periodic inspections of the common areas, which would have revealed the defect even without specific notice. The appellate court examined the obligation of landlords to inspect common areas. The court determined that a landlord must exercise reasonable care to discover and repair dangerous conditions in areas over which they retain control. The court held that if a condition has existed long enough that a reasonable inspection would have uncovered it, the landlord can be held liable under a theory of constructive notice. Finding that the evidence supported the conclusion that the stair was broken for a significant period, the appellate court reversed and remanded, holding that the trial court must determine if the landlord failed in their duty to reasonably inspect the premises.

## M.R. v. V.R.

452 S.W.3d 687 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: A landlord's unauthorized entry into a leased property constitutes a breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment. However, recovery of damages requires proof of actual loss rather than mere technical breach. This case involved a conflict between a residential tenant and a landlord regarding the privacy rights of the tenant and the landlord's right of entry. The landlord repeatedly entered the property without providing the required notice under the lease and without the tenant's consent. The tenant filed suit alleging trespass and breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment. The trial court found that the landlord's actions constituted a breach of the lease, but it awarded nominal damages because the tenant failed to prove actual financial loss. The appellate court held that while the landlord's entry was a technical breach, the tenant's claim for significant monetary damages was not supported by the evidence of actual harm. The court reaffirmed that tenants have a legal right to quiet enjoyment, which includes a

Second stored summary reasonable expectation of privacy, but that damages for a breach of this covenant must be grounded in documented financial loss or specific, measurable distress. The case provides guidance on the threshold for recovery in claims alleging landlord intrusion upon a tenant's privacy.

## M.S. v. C.S.

402 S.W.3d 596 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the property division. The court held that the trial court's determination that the home was marital property was supported by sufficient evidence and was not an abuse of discretion. In this dissolution matter, the parties contested the division of property, specifically real estate and personal property purchased during the marriage. The husband argued that the trial court inequitably distributed the property, failing to account for his separate contributions toward the down payment on the marital home. The wife argued that the property was acquired as a gift to both parties. The appellate court examined the principles of separate and marital property as defined by Missouri law and the evidentiary standards for rebutting the presumption that property acquired during marriage is marital. The opinion explains how courts differentiate between individual gifts and marital assets. The court also reviewed the trial court's findings regarding the conduct of the parties during the marriage as a factor in the property division, ensuring that the final judgment was consistent with the statutory goals of achieving a just and equitable distribution.

## M.T. v. J.T.

408 S.W.3d 194 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's denial of the mother's relocation request and the subsequent modification of child custody to the father. The court found these decisions to be in the children's best interests. This appeal concerned a modification of child custody and visitation. The mother, who had primary physical custody, sought to relocate with the children out of state. The father objected to the relocation and requested a change in custody. The trial court denied the mother's request to relocate and modified the custody arrangement, awarding primary physical custody to the father. The mother appealed, arguing the trial court erred by denying her relocation request and by changing custody without sufficient evidence of a material change in circumstances. The appellate court considered the statutory factors for relocation and the evidence regarding the children's best interests. The court also reviewed the evidence of the parents' fitness and the father's demonstrated ability to meet the children's needs. The court found that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying the relocation request and in modifying custody.

## M.W. v. D.W.

598 S.W.3d 172 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The judgment was affirmed. The appellate court held that the trial court did not abuse its discretion, as the evidence showed that the father failed to demonstrate a substantial and continuing change in circumstances necessitating a modification. The central issue in this appeal was the modification of a parenting plan due to a significant change in the children's school schedule and the parents' work hours. The father sought to increase his parenting time, asserting that the existing schedule was no longer practical or beneficial. The mother opposed the modification, arguing that the existing arrangement was working well for the children and that the father's requests were inconsistent with the children's best interests. The appellate court reviewed whether the trial court abused its discretion in refusing to modify the parenting plan. The opinion explores the 'substantial and continuing change' requirement for modification under Missouri law and discusses the trial court's role in evaluating the credibility of the parties. The court highlighted the importance of stability for children in custody arrangements and the necessity of showing that a requested change will genuinely improve the children's welfare rather than just favoring one parent's convenience or scheduling preferences.

## M.W. v. L.W.

632 S.W.3d 411 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The trial court's custody determination was affirmed as it was based on substantial evidence and prioritized the child's best interests. The court properly weighed the statutory factors provided in the Missouri statutes. In this matter, the trial court entered a judgment granting primary physical custody to the father. The mother appealed, arguing that the court failed to adequately consider the statutory factors under Section 452.375, specifically regarding the need for frequent and meaningful contact with both parents. The mother contended that the distance between the parents' homes made the trial court's custody plan unworkable and detrimental to the child. The appellate court reviewed the record to determine if the trial court's findings were supported by substantial evidence. It was noted that the trial court conducted a thorough review of the parents' relative abilities to provide for the child and their willingness to facilitate contact. The appellate court found that the trial court's decision to award primary physical custody to the father was justified given the mother's history of instability. The court affirmed the judgment, reiterating that the primary focus of the appellate review in custody matters is to ensure that the judgment is in the child's best interests and supported by the record as a whole.

## M.W. v. S.C.

981 S.W.2d 581 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the alleged oral contract was too vague to be enforceable. It further ruled that the plaintiff failed to provide sufficient evidence of an agreement to overcome the Statute of Frauds. This case involved a dispute over an oral contract for the transfer of personal property and services between two individuals. One party alleged that the other party failed to perform agreed-upon services in exchange for a set compensation. The defending party argued that there was no meeting of the minds and that the alleged agreement was barred by the Statute of Frauds, as it was not in writing and was intended to last for a duration of more than one year. The appellate court evaluated the elements of an oral contract, emphasizing the requirement for clear, definite terms and consideration. The court looked at the conduct of the parties to determine if partial performance existed, which could potentially bypass the Statute of Frauds. The case explores the evidentiary challenges associated with enforcing oral contracts and the strict requirement that plaintiffs must prove the existence and terms of the agreement with a high degree of certainty.

## Maasen v. Shaw

133 S.W.3d 514 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a prescriptive easement was established. The defendants failed to overcome the presumption of adversity, and the use was found to be open and continuous. This dispute concerned a prescriptive easement over a logging road. The plaintiffs, who owned a timber tract, had used the road for decades. The defendants, new owners of the land the road crossed, installed locked gates and prohibited entry. The defendants argued that the plaintiffs' use was merely 'neighborly accommodation.' The court explained that to defeat a prescriptive claim, a defendant must show that the use was permitted by the owner at the outset. The evidence showed that the road was used by multiple individuals over several decades without any evidence of permission being sought or granted. The appellate court affirmed the trial court's finding that the plaintiffs' use was continuous, open, and adverse. The ruling emphasizes that in the absence of evidence of a permit or license, long-term use of a road by a party not owning the land is presumed to be adverse. The decision provides a clear application of the presumption of adversity in Missouri prescriptive easement law, placing the burden of proving permissive use squarely on the party asserting it.

## MacFarlane v. City of St. Louis

544 S.W.3d 282 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Also captioned State ex rel. R.W. v. City of St. Louis

Holding: The court held that while the Sunshine Law mandates broad access to public records, it does not abrogate the attorney-client privilege. Public bodies must specifically identify which records are privileged and demonstrate their exempt status to avoid violating transparency mandates. This case addressed the intersection of the Sunshine Law and the City of St. Louis's document retention and production processes. The plaintiff requested emails and documents from the City's legal department, which the City refused to produce, citing attorney-client privilege and the work-product doctrine. The court examined whether the Sunshine Law's mandate for public access is superseded by common law privileges and the rules of civil procedure. The dispute centered on whether the City's internal legal correspondence remained 'public records' even if they were characterized as 'internal work product.' The court looked at the legislative history of Section 610.021, which allows for the closure of records related to legal actions, causes of action, or litigation. The appellate court emphasized that the Sunshine Law must be interpreted in a way that does not destroy essential privileges, yet prevents public bodies from using 'privilege' as a blanket excuse to hide administrative or operational records. The opinion highlights the importance of the City establishing a clear record regarding why specific documents qualify for exemption. The court ultimately determined that the lower court needed to conduct an in-camera review to properly balance the statutory obligations of the Sunshine Law against the recognized privileges of a public entity acting as a client.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that civilian oversight boards are public governmental bodies and are therefore subject to the Sunshine Law. It ruled that such bodies must disclose their records unless they can meet the high burden of proving a specific statutory exemption. This case analyzed whether records of a civilian oversight board tasked with monitoring police activity were public records subject to disclosure under the Sunshine Law. The City of St. Louis argued that these records were sensitive because they contained personal information and details of complaints that could lead to litigation. The court looked at the exemption for records related to 'legal actions' and 'personnel records.' The appellate court conducted an exhaustive review of whether the Sunshine Law applies to independent oversight boards that are created by the city. The court affirmed that if such a body functions on behalf of the city or uses public funds to fulfill its mandate, it is a 'public governmental body' within the meaning of the law. The court also examined the balance between the

Second stored summary public's right to monitor the police and the need to protect the privacy of those involved in the oversight process. The decision underscores that oversight mechanisms are meant to function in the public eye to build trust, and thus, their records should be accessible to the greatest extent possible under the law, unless clearly excluded by specific statutory provisions.

## MacNeil v. City of Kan. City

104 S.W.3d 775 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that cities must strictly adhere to notice requirements for public meetings. It also held that the real estate exemption cannot be used as a broad excuse for avoiding public deliberation on major municipal projects.

Second stored summary The plaintiffs sued the city, claiming that the city council violated the Sunshine Law by holding private meetings regarding the development of a professional sports stadium. The city claimed the meetings were necessary for confidential negotiations. The plaintiffs argued that the council failed to provide the required notice of these meetings and that the subject matter did not fit within the real estate exemption of the Sunshine Law. The court examined whether the city had followed the notice requirements, which stipulate that notice must be given at least 24 hours in advance, except in emergencies. The court also scrutinized whether the negotiations mentioned by the city were real or just a pretext for avoiding public scrutiny. This case serves as a precedent for the requirements of public notice and the necessity of linking closed sessions to specific, authorized statutory exemptions. The court rejected the city's claim that the sensitive nature of the development exempted the meetings from the general mandate of transparency.

## Macon v. City of Independence

635 S.W.3d 596 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the award, holding that psychological injuries arising from workplace harassment can constitute a compensable injury. The court emphasized that the injury must still be linked to the work as the prevailing factor. The claimant, a municipal employee, filed for benefits related to psychological injuries arising from workplace harassment and stressful conditions. The employer argued that the injury was not an 'accident' under the Missouri Workers' Compensation Law because it did not arise from a single, identifiable event but rather a long-term accumulation of stress. The Commission awarded benefits, finding that the cumulative effect of the harassment reached the level of a compensable occupational disease or injury. The City appealed, contending that the statute requires a sudden, violent, or external event to qualify as an accident, and that psychological claims require higher standards of proof. The appellate court evaluated the statutory definitions of 'accident' and 'occupational disease.' The court highlighted the legal distinction between physical and mental injuries, noting that psychological claims are subject to heightened scrutiny. However, the court found that the Commission's factual findings regarding the constant, unusual stress caused by the harassment provided a basis for the award. The decision reinforces that while psychological injuries are complex, they are compensable when linked to specific, stressful employment circumstances that exceed ordinary day-to-day work stress.

## Madden v. C & K Properties

747 S.W.2d 705 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1988 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the landlord had a duty to maintain the common areas in a reasonably safe condition. It found that the issue of the tenant's comparative negligence was a question for the jury to decide. The plaintiff filed suit after suffering injuries from a fall in an apartment complex parking lot, alleging that the landlord failed to maintain safe premises and failed to provide adequate lighting. The landlord contended that the plaintiff was contributorily negligent and that the hazard was known to the plaintiff prior to the fall. The litigation focused on the landlord's duty of care regarding common areas in multi-unit housing developments. The appellate court considered whether the landlord's knowledge of the defect was superior to that of the tenant and whether the landlord had taken reasonable precautions to prevent foreseeable harm to tenants and visitors. The summary highlights the analysis of duty, breach, and causation in the context of residential property management, emphasizing the requirement that landlords exercise ordinary care to keep common areas in a reasonably safe condition for the protection of their tenants.

## Madden v. C & K Props.

747 S.W.2d 707 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1988 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a landlord may be liable if they retain control over the portion of the premises where the injury occurs. It reversed the lower court's dismissal, allowing the case to proceed to discovery on the control issue. The plaintiff was injured while working at a commercial facility and brought suit against the property owner for failing to maintain safe conditions in a loading dock area. The legal issue centered on whether the plaintiff, as an employee of a tenant, could maintain a premises liability action against the landlord. The defendant argued that the control of the premises had been fully surrendered to the tenant under the lease agreement. The court examined the 'retention of control' exception, which permits liability if the landlord continues to oversee the specific area where the injury occurred. The case provides significant insight into the contractual allocation of responsibility between commercial landlords and tenants in Missouri, specifically addressing the scope of the landlord's immunity once possession is transferred to the business tenant.

## Madden v. C & K Props., LLC

347 S.W.3d 536 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a landlord has a non-delegable duty to maintain common areas in a reasonably safe condition for tenants. Tenant knowledge of a defect does not automatically absolve the landlord of liability for injuries resulting from that defect. Madden was injured while walking on an exterior staircase at an apartment complex owned by the defendant. The staircase had loose handrails and uneven treads. Madden sued for negligence, alleging the landlord failed to repair known defects. The trial court entered judgment for the landlord based on the theory that the tenant knew of the defects and thus the landlord owed no duty. The appellate court reversed, clarifying the duty of a landlord to maintain common areas under their control. The court explained that a landlord has a non-delegable duty to keep common areas safe for tenants and invitees. Even if a tenant is aware of a defect, the landlord is not necessarily shielded from liability if the condition presents an unreasonable risk of harm. The court found that the landlord had sufficient

Second stored summary notice of the deterioration of the staircase and failed to take corrective action, thus constituting a breach of duty. This decision reinforced the protective standards for residential tenants regarding common area maintenance.

## Madden v. C & K Props., LLC

528 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: Whether a condition is open and obvious is generally a factual determination for the jury. Summary judgment is inappropriate when there is conflicting evidence regarding whether a hazard could have been perceived by a reasonable person. The plaintiff, a patron of a shopping center, was injured when they tripped over an uneven curb in the parking lot. The plaintiff claimed the premises were in a dangerous condition. The defendant moved for summary judgment, arguing that the curb was open and obvious. The trial court granted the motion. The plaintiff appealed, asserting that the height variation in the curb was a 'hidden' defect rather than an open and obvious condition. The appellate court examined the principles of premises liability, specifically focusing on the expectation of safety for invitees. The court determined that whether a condition is open and obvious is a question of fact, not law, unless the evidence is undisputed. Because the plaintiff presented expert evidence that the curb did not meet safety codes and was obscured by lighting, the appellate court reversed the trial court's grant of summary judgment, holding that the question of whether the defendant breached their duty of care was for a jury to decide.

## Madden v. C & K Props., LLC

632 S.W.3d 378 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: To establish premises liability, an invitee must prove that the possessor of land knew or should have known of the dangerous condition. Constructive notice requires showing the condition existed for a sufficient length of time for the owner to discover and remediate it. The plaintiff, a delivery driver, was injured while making a delivery to a commercial building owned by the defendant. The plaintiff slipped on an accumulation of mud and debris on a loading dock, which he alleged was a dangerous condition that the owner failed to remedy or warn against. The defendant argued that as a business owner, they were not liable because the condition was transitory and not created by them. The trial court granted summary judgment for the defendant, finding no evidence that the defendant had actual or constructive notice of the debris. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that the defendant had constructive notice because the debris had been present for a sufficient period for the defendant to have discovered and removed it. The appellate court examined the duty of a business owner toward an invitee. The court held that while the owner has a duty to maintain the premises, the plaintiff must show that the owner knew or should have known of the specific dangerous condition to prevail on a premises liability claim.

## Mader v. City of Springfield

892 S.W.2d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that public notice for a closed meeting must be specific enough to inform the public of the nature of the business to be transacted. It ruled that vague or generalized notices fail to comply with the Sunshine Law. Proper notice is a prerequisite for a valid closed session. In this case, citizens alleged that the city council violated the Sunshine Law by holding a closed session that did not conform to the legal notice requirements. The core issue was whether the city council's agenda correctly notified the public of the reasons for the proposed closed session, as required by law. The city contended that their general notice was sufficient under the circumstances. The court examined the requirements for public notice under Chapter 610, emphasizing that the public must be provided with enough information to understand the general subject matter being discussed, even if specific sensitive details are redacted. The appellate court found that the city's generic, vague notice failed to inform the public of the nature of the business to be conducted in private. The decision underscores that the notice requirement is a substantive, not merely technical, component of the Sunshine Law, intended to prevent surprise closures and ensure that the public can challenge the legality of meeting closures before they occur.

## Mader v. City of St. Louis

417 S.W.3d 289 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the employee had a protected property interest in his employment based on city regulations. It affirmed that the lack of due process violated Section 1983. The plaintiff, a former city employee, alleged that the city violated his Fourteenth Amendment rights by terminating him without adequate procedural due process, leading to a Section 1983 claim. The city argued that the employee was at-will and therefore did not possess a protected property interest in his employment that required a pre-termination hearing. The court examined the relevant city charter and civil service regulations to determine if they created a legitimate claim of entitlement to continued employment. Finding that the regulations specifically limited the city's power to terminate to only 'for cause' reasons, the court concluded that the employee held a property interest. Consequently, the lack of notice and an opportunity to be heard constituted a violation of procedural due process. This case clarifies the intersection of municipal employment law and constitutional protections, serving as a reminder that local regulations

Second stored summary can create property interests that trigger federal due process obligations when the municipality seeks to terminate employment.

## Mader v. J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, N.A.

686 F.3d 896 · United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (applying Missouri Law) · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the plaintiff fell under the administrative exemption, as her duties required the exercise of independent judgment on significant business matters. It affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the employer. The ruling clarified the boundaries of the administrative exemption as applied to financial sector employees under Missouri law. While a federal court case, this decision provides significant insight into Missouri's approach to wage and hour claims related to overtime exemptions. The plaintiff, a bank employee, claimed that she was misclassified as an exempt administrative employee and was therefore entitled to overtime pay under Missouri law. The bank contended that her duties satisfied the criteria for the administrative exemption under both federal and state wage laws. The appellate court performed a detailed 'duties test' analysis, examining whether the employee's role involved the exercise of independent judgment and discretion regarding matters of significance. The litigation revolved around the specific job responsibilities of a bank analyst and whether those responsibilities rose to the level of management or executive functions. The parties argued extensively over the interpretation of the Missouri administrative rules that mirror the federal FLSA exemptions. The outcome relied heavily on the factual nuances of the employee's authority and the degree of supervision she received during her tenure at the bank.

## Magee v. Blue Ridge Professional Building Co.

821 S.W.2d 839 · Missouri Supreme Court · 1991 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that the statute of limitations on a wage claim is not tolled unless the employee proves affirmative acts of concealment by the employer. The discovery rule cannot be used to extend the filing period absent clear evidence that the employer prevented the discovery of the wage underpayment. In Magee, the plaintiff brought a claim for unpaid wages, alleging that her employer had miscalculated the amounts owed based on an oral agreement. The primary legal issue was whether the statute of limitations for a wage claim was tolled due to the employer's alleged fraudulent concealment of the true hours worked and payments made. The defendant argued that the action was time-barred because the plaintiff failed to bring the suit within the statutory period provided by Missouri law for wage and labor claims. The court examined the standards for tolling the statute of limitations, specifically the requirement of 'active concealment' by the defendant. The decision explored the balance between the policy of encouraging timely litigation and the fairness of allowing claims where an employer has actively misled an employee about their compensation. The Supreme Court provided guidance on the evidentiary threshold required to invoke the discovery rule in employment cases, setting a precedent for how Missouri courts handle claims where the lack of documentation, combined with potential bad faith by the employer, obscures the factual basis for a wage claim.

## Manning v. Missouri Department of Transportation

Holding: The Court held that the Commission's determination of notice and medical causation was supported by the evidence. The employer denied the claim, asserting that the claimant did not report the injury promptly and that the injury was not work-related. The matter was heard by the Labor and Industrial Relations Commission, which determined that the claimant had established a compensable injury. On appeal, the Missouri Department of Transportation argued that the Commission erred in its interpretation of the notice requirements under Missouri law. The appellate court scrutinized the evidence regarding the timeline of the reporting and the medical nexus between the work activities and the shoulder condition. The court found that the Commission properly weighed the medical evidence and the credibility of the witnesses. The court affirmed that as long as the Commission's decision is based on competent and substantial evidence, the appellate court will not disturb the findings, even if it might have reached a different conclusion upon an initial review of the medical records and testimony.

565 U.S. 266 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2012 · Federal

Holding: Attorney abandonment constitutes 'cause' to excuse a procedural default in a federal habeas case. When an attorney entirely fails to communicate with or represent the client, the resulting procedural failures cannot be imputed to the client, thereby allowing the client to overcome a procedural bar. Corey Ray Maples was sentenced to death in Alabama. During his state post-conviction proceedings, his pro bono attorneys left their law firm without notifying the court or the petitioner, leading to missed filing deadlines and the dismissal of his state appeal. Because the appeal was missed, the petitioner's federal habeas claims were procedurally defaulted. Maples argued that the abandonment by his attorneys constituted 'cause' to excuse the default. The Supreme Court agreed. Distinguishing between standard attorney error, which is attributed to the client, and attorney abandonment, the Court held that the attorneys' conduct severed the agency relationship between them and the petitioner. Because the petitioner had no knowledge of the abandonment and was effectively left without legal representation, his failure to comply with the state's procedural rules was excused. This case created a critical distinction in habeas law: while a client is responsible for their lawyer's mistakes, a client is not responsible for a lawyer's complete abandonment of the case. It provided a necessary mechanism for relief in cases of egregious professional neglect.

## Mapp v. Ohio

367 U.S. 643 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1961 · Federal

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The exclusionary rule, which prevents the use of evidence obtained through illegal searches and seizures, applies to all states under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible. Dolree Mapp was convicted of possessing obscene materials after an illegal police search of her home. The police had entered her house without a valid warrant, claiming they were searching for a bombing suspect. During the search, they found no suspect, but discovered prohibited books. Mapp appealed her conviction, arguing that the evidence was obtained through an unreasonable search and seizure and should not have been admissible in court. The Supreme Court faced the issue of whether the exclusionary rule, which had previously only applied to federal courts, should be incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment and applied to state court proceedings. This landmark case addressed the fundamental protection against state infringement on the right to be secure in one's home and papers.

## Martin v. City of Washington

848 S.W.2d 487 · Missouri Supreme Court · 1993 · Missouri

Holding: Sovereign immunity is waived for public entities when they fail to maintain public property in a safe condition. A city is liable for injuries caused by a dangerous roadway condition if it had notice and failed to take remedial measures. Martin sued the City of Washington for negligence regarding the design and maintenance of a municipal roadway where a vehicular accident occurred. The plaintiff alleged that the city's failure to provide adequate signage and road curvature correction constituted a breach of their duty to maintain public streets in a safe condition. The city invoked the doctrine of sovereign immunity. The Supreme Court of Missouri analyzed the waiver of sovereign immunity under Missouri law, specifically for cases involving the dangerous condition of public property. The court determined that the waiver applies when the dangerous condition creates a direct, foreseeable risk of harm and the entity had notice of that condition. The court found in favor of the plaintiff, establishing that cities can be held liable for negligent design or maintenance of public roads when those conditions are not naturally occurring and are caused by the public entity's own actions or failure to act as expected.

## Martin v. Missouri Department of Labor

342 S.W.3d 390 · Mo. Ct. App. W.D. · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the state employee was entitled to overtime pay because the executive exemption did not apply to the specific training duties. The ruling underscored that state agencies must follow the same wage protections they enforce. This dispute arose from the Department of Labor's own personnel classification policies. An employee challenged the state's failure to pay overtime for time spent during mandatory state-wide training sessions that occurred after regular hours. The Department argued that the employee was an executive-exempt manager and that the training was a requirement of her professional standing, not a 'work' requirement subject to overtime pay. The appellate court examined the state personnel manual alongside the MMWL. The court found that the state's attempt to use internal policy as a defense against mandatory state wage laws was ineffective. The decision highlights that even governmental entities are held to the strict requirements of wage statutes when they fail to align their internal personnel policies with the broader state legislative intent regarding employee compensation.

## Martinez v. California

444 U.S. 277 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1980 · Federal

Holding: State parole officials are not constitutionally liable for the criminal acts of a released prisoner. The decision to grant parole is generally too remote to constitute a violation of a victim's due process rights. The plaintiffs were the survivors of a girl murdered by a parolee, Thomas Humbert. They sued state parole officials under Section 1983, alleging that the decision to parole Humbert, who had a history of violent crimes, violated their daughter's right to life under the Fourteenth Amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the parole board's action was the proximate cause of the girl's death. The Supreme Court addressed whether the state officials' decision to release the prisoner made them liable for the harm caused by his subsequent actions. The Court ruled that the parole board's decision did not deprive the victim of life without due process of law. The Court reasoned that the parole board's decision was too remote a consequence of the victim's death to hold the state actors liable for a constitutional violation. While the Court did not rule out the possibility that the state might be liable in more extreme circumstances involving a special relationship, here the victim was not a member of the public in a way that created a direct, proximate link to the parole board's administrative decision.

## Martinez v. Ryan

566 U.S. 1 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2012 · Federal

Holding: A prisoner may establish cause for a procedural default of an ineffective-assistance-of-trial-counsel claim if they demonstrate that they had no counsel or ineffective counsel in the initial-review collateral proceeding. This narrow exception applies specifically to states that require trial-level ineffective assistance claims to be brought during post-conviction collateral review. Luis Martinez was convicted of sexual assault in Arizona state court. He sought post-conviction relief, alleging ineffective assistance of trial counsel. Under Arizona law, claims of ineffective assistance of trial counsel must be brought in initial-review collateral proceedings rather than on direct appeal. Martinez's appointed post-conviction counsel failed to raise the trial counsel's ineffective performance, resulting in the procedural default of that claim in federal court. Martinez argued that this default should be excused because he had no counsel during the initial collateral proceeding to raise the claim. The Supreme Court addressed whether a procedural default of an ineffective-assistance-of-trial-counsel claim can be excused by the ineffective assistance of initial-review collateral counsel. The Court established a narrow equitable exception to the procedural default rule. It held that where a state requires that claims of ineffective assistance of trial counsel be raised in an initial-review collateral proceeding, a procedural default will not bar a federal habeas court from hearing a substantial claim of ineffective assistance at trial if, in the initial-review collateral proceeding, there was no counsel or counsel in that proceeding was ineffective. This decision provided a critical pathway for petitioners to bypass procedural bars for meritorious Sixth Amendment claims.

## Massaro v. United States

538 U.S. 500 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2003 · Federal

Holding: Ineffective assistance of counsel claims are not procedurally defaulted if they are not raised on direct appeal. These claims are properly brought in a collateral proceeding under 28 U.S.C. 2255 because such proceedings allow for the development of the necessary factual record to evaluate attorney performance. Joseph Massaro was convicted of federal racketeering charges and subsequently filed a motion under 28 U.S.C. 2255 to vacate his sentence, claiming ineffective assistance of trial counsel. The trial court and the Second Circuit refused to hear the claim on direct appeal because it had not been raised at trial, asserting a procedural bar. The Second Circuit maintained that claims of ineffective assistance not raised at trial were procedurally defaulted and could not be considered on collateral review unless they were raised on direct appeal. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the conflict regarding the timing of ineffective assistance claims. The Court held that an ineffective assistance of counsel claim need not be raised on direct appeal, whether or not there was new counsel and whether or not the basis for the claim was apparent from the trial record. The Court reasoned that claims of ineffective assistance are better suited for collateral proceedings because the trial record is often incomplete regarding counsel's reasoning, and post-conviction hearings provide a necessary vehicle for developing the factual record required to evaluate such claims. This ruling established a clear federal rule favoring collateral review for Sixth Amendment claims.

## Matal v. Tam

582 U.S. 218 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2017 · Federal

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court struck down the disparagement clause. It held that the First Amendment prevents the government from denying trademark protection based on the disparaging nature of the mark. Simon Tam and his band, 'The Slants,' sought federal trademark registration for their band name, but the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office refused, citing the Lanham Act's 'disparagement clause,' which prohibits the registration of trademarks that may disparage persons, institutions, or beliefs. Tam challenged the denial, arguing that the clause violated the First Amendment. The Supreme Court examined whether the disparagement clause was a form of unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. The Court held that the clause was indeed unconstitutional, noting that trademarks are private speech, not government speech, and that the government cannot deny registration simply because it finds the message of the mark to be offensive or disparaging. The decision reinforced the principle that the First Amendment protects even controversial or offensive speech from government-imposed conditions on the granting of benefits like trademark protection.

## Matal v. Tam

137 S. Ct. 1744 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2017 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the Disparagement Clause of the Lanham Act violates the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment. It concluded that trademarks are private speech, not government speech, and that the government cannot ban speech simply because it is disparaging to others. The case arose when the Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) denied registration of the trademark 'THE SLANTS,' a name chosen by an Asian-American rock band. The PTO argued that the name violated the Disparagement Clause of the Lanham Act, which prohibits trademarks that may disparage persons or institutions. Simon Tam, the band's frontman, appealed the denial, arguing that the statute violated the First Amendment. The Federal Circuit Court of Appeals initially ruled in favor of Tam, concluding that the Disparagement

Second stored summary Clause was unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. The government appealed to the Supreme Court. The core issue was whether trademarks constitute government speech or private speech and whether the regulation of 'disparaging' content constitutes an unconstitutional restraint on speech. The government contended that trademarks are a form of government-registered, commercial speech subject to more lenient standards. The petitioner argued that the government was attempting to suppress offensive speech, which is a hallmark of viewpoint discrimination prohibited by the First Amendment. The Court analyzed the history of the Disparagement Clause and its application, ultimately finding it to be a broad, ill-defined prohibition that allowed the government to censor speech simply because it found the message offensive to certain groups.

## Mathews v. Eldridge

424 U.S. 319 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1976 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require an evidentiary hearing prior to the termination of Social Security disability benefits. It established a balancing test that weighs individual interests against government efficiency and the risk of error. The respondent, George Eldridge, had his Social Security disability benefits terminated by the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare without a prior evidentiary hearing. Eldridge argued that the procedures violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The district court and the court of appeals held that an evidentiary hearing was required before the termination of benefits. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to determine whether the administrative procedures, which provided for a pre-termination notice and an opportunity to submit written evidence followed by a full post-termination hearing, satisfied constitutional requirements. The Court established a three-part balancing test to evaluate procedural due process claims: the private interest affected by the official action, the risk of erroneous deprivation through existing procedures compared to the probable value of additional safeguards, and the government's interest, including the fiscal and administrative burdens of providing additional procedures. The Court determined that the existing process for disability termination was sufficient, emphasizing that disability benefits are not based on demonstrated financial need like welfare payments, and that medical determinations are uniquely suitable for written submission rather than oral testimony.

## Mathews v. Lucas

427 U.S. 495 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1976 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that the evidentiary requirements for illegitimate children to receive Social Security benefits do not violate the Due Process Clause. The classification is rationally related to the government's interest in verifying actual dependency. The Supreme Court considered whether the Social Security Act's requirements for illegitimate children to prove dependency on a deceased wage earner in order to receive survivor's benefits violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. Unlike legitimate children, who were automatically presumed dependent, illegitimate children had to satisfy specific evidence burdens. The claimants argued that this distinction created an unconstitutional classification based on illegitimacy, effectively denying them due process and equal protection. The Court analyzed the issue under a 'rational basis' standard rather than strict scrutiny. The Court held that the requirement for illegitimate children to provide some evidence of dependency did not violate the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause. It concluded that the legislation was reasonably related to the legitimate governmental interest of ensuring that benefits were directed only to those children who were actually dependent on the deceased, and that the evidentiary requirements were not an insurmountable barrier to receiving the benefits to which they were otherwise entitled under the act.

## Mathews v. United States

485 U.S. 58 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1988 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a federal criminal defendant is entitled to an entrapment instruction if there is sufficient evidence, even if they deny the elements of the crime. This ensures the defendant's right to present a full and fair defense. This case involved a defendant who was indicted for accepting a bribe while working as a federal employee. He sought to raise an entrapment defense, but the trial court refused to allow it because he would not admit to all the elements of the crime. The Supreme Court addressed whether a defendant can argue entrapment while simultaneously denying that they committed the offense. The Court held that even if a defendant denies one or more elements of the crime, they are still entitled to an entrapment instruction whenever there is sufficient evidence from which a reasonable jury could find entrapment. The Court emphasized that procedural fairness requires that a defendant be permitted to present a defense, and the government's argument that the defendant's position was logically inconsistent did not justify barring the defense. This decision safeguards the defendant's Fifth Amendment right to a fair trial by ensuring they are not forced to choose between the right to present a full defense and the right to maintain their innocence. The ruling underscores the broad scope of procedural fairness within federal criminal proceedings.

## Matrixx Initiatives, Inc. v. Siracusano

563 U.S. 27 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2011 · Federal

6 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that materiality is not dependent on statistical significance. Rather, information is material if it would have been viewed by a reasonable investor as having significantly altered the total mix of available information. This case tested the definition of materiality in the context of adverse health events. Matrixx manufactured a cold remedy and faced allegations that it suppressed information about reports that the product caused a loss of smell in users. The company argued that these reports were not 'material' because they were not statistically significant enough to establish a causal link to the product. The Supreme Court rejected the notion that statistical significance is a prerequisite for materiality. The Court held that the 'total mix' of information standard remains the test, and that a company must consider whether a reasonable investor would view the reported side effects as significantly altering the perception of the company's product risks and prospects. Even in the absence of a confirmed scientific study, a

Second stored summary series of reports regarding a serious issue can be material. The ruling is crucial for pharmaceutical companies and consumer product manufacturers, as it underscores their obligation to disclose emerging risks, regardless of the lack of exhaustive scientific verification.

## Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp.

475 U.S. 574 · U.S. Supreme Court · 1986 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that antitrust plaintiffs must show that their claims make economic sense to survive summary judgment. Speculative claims of conspiracy in predatory pricing cases are insufficient without strong evidence. This complex antitrust case involved claims by American television manufacturers that Japanese rivals had engaged in a decades-long conspiracy to price their products below cost in the U.S. market to drive domestic competitors out of business. The defendants moved for summary judgment, arguing the plaintiffs failed to provide evidence of a plausible predatory pricing scheme. The Supreme Court held that for summary judgment in an antitrust case, the plaintiff's claim must make economic sense. The Court found that predatory pricing schemes are inherently difficult to maintain because the predator must bear significant losses and face the risk that prices will rebound before it can recoup its investment. Because the evidence presented by the domestic manufacturers was as consistent with permissible competition (low prices) as it was with an illegal conspiracy, the Court ruled that the plaintiffs had failed to demonstrate a genuine issue of material fact, making it significantly harder for plaintiffs to survive early dismissals in complex predatory pricing cases.

## Matter of Estate of Hagnauer

644 S.W.3d 603 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the evidence was insufficient to overcome the presumption of validity afforded to a properly executed deed. The finding that the decedent possessed the capacity to convey the property was supported by substantial evidence. The transfer was upheld as a valid exercise of the decedent's rights. This matter involved a dispute over the title and ownership of real property following the death of the owner, which triggered a contest regarding the validity of a property transfer deed. The heirs argued that the deed was executed under undue influence and lacked the requisite mental capacity, rendering the transfer invalid. The respondent argued that the transfer was part of a legitimate estate planning strategy and that the decedent possessed the legal capacity to convey the interest. The proceedings involved extensive discovery into the decedent's medical records and financial history leading up to the transaction. The trial court examined the legal standards for setting aside a deed based on fiduciary relationships and the presumption of undue influence that arises when a grantee in a confidential relationship receives a significant benefit. The case required the court to determine whether the presumption of undue influence was adequately rebutted by the evidence presented. Furthermore, the court looked at the chain of title and the formal requirements for the recording of the deed. The appellate review focused on whether the trial court's factual findings were supported by substantial evidence and whether it applied the correct legal principles concerning the burden of proof in deed contest cases involving alleged undue influence, which is a common area of litigation in Missouri probate and property law.
