## Mund v. English

936 S.W.2d 860 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: Under the doctrine of practical location, where parties have for many years recognized and acquiesced in a boundary line, that line will be treated as the true boundary regardless of subsequent surveys. This doctrine serves to provide stability in land ownership and protect long-standing expectations against modern measurement adjustments. The parties in this action were owners of adjacent lots in a rural subdivision. The plaintiffs sought to establish the boundary line as being consistent with an old survey and a fence that had existed since the subdivision's creation. The defendants, however, commissioned a new survey that contradicted the old markers, claiming an additional portion of the land as their own. The dispute was complicated by the fact that the original survey markers were lost or destroyed over time. The trial court focused on the 'doctrine of practical location,' under which long-standing boundaries accepted by successive owners are treated as the true boundary. The appellate court analyzed the history of how the property had been taxed, fenced, and utilized. It determined that both parties and their predecessors had historically recognized the old fence as the property line for over forty years, and that the new survey, while perhaps technically accurate according to modern measurements, could not override the well-established practical boundary. The court ruled that the historical boundary line should stand, as it had been relied upon by all parties for decades, and any other result would cause inequitable disruption to property expectations.

## Mund v. English

959 S.W.2d 474 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: Long-term acquiescence in a boundary line, as evidenced by consistent fence lines or historical markers, will override a conflicting modern survey. Courts prioritize the established, historical treatment of property lines over technical measurements to ensure stability in land ownership. This boundary dispute between neighboring rural landowners centered on the interpretation of a 1920 deed that included a vague reference to a 'large oak tree' as a corner marker. The trial court used a forensic survey to locate where the tree likely stood, but the plaintiffs argued that the survey ignored the actual usage of the land by the families involved for over seventy years. The appellate court considered whether the trial court correctly prioritized the survey evidence over the long-standing occupation. It held that while surveys are important, they are not always the final word when historical evidence of a line exists. The court examined the doctrine of 'acquiescence,' which holds that where owners have recognized a boundary line through conduct, that line becomes the legal boundary. The court ruled that the families' long-term adherence to the line marked by the remnants of the old tree row was sufficient to establish the boundary as a matter of law, regardless of what the new survey indicated. The court's decision reaffirmed that long-term, established boundaries in rural settings are to be protected for the sake of stability.

## Mund v. Norfolk & Western Railway Co.

734 S.W.2d 875 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 1987 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the insurer had a duty to defend because the petition filed by the employee alleged facts that potentially fell within the coverage of the policy. The court emphasized that the duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify and is triggered by the potential for coverage as pled. This matter involved a complex dispute between an employer's liability insurer and a third party regarding the duty to defend and indemnify. A railroad employee was injured on the job, and the railroad was subsequently sued by the employee for negligence. The railroad's insurer denied coverage, asserting that the specific type of loss fell under a policy exclusion relating to workers' compensation and employer's liability. The dispute required the court to interpret the language of a commercial general liability (CGL) policy and reconcile it with the statutory requirements for railway liability. The appellate court examined whether the insurer had an 'implied' duty to defend even when it believed the ultimate loss might not be covered, emphasizing the broad nature of the duty to defend versus the narrower duty to indemnify. The case underscores the significance of carefully drafted exclusionary clauses in commercial policies and the procedural requirements for an insurer to withdraw from a defense under Missouri law.

## Munday v. Capitol Indemnity Corp.

783 S.W.2d 468 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1990 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an 'assault and battery' exclusion in a liability policy applies to all claims arising from such events, even when labeled as negligent supervision. The 'arising out of' language effectively excludes the entire incident. The insured, a security guard company, was sued for negligence after one of its guards shot a patron. The company's general liability insurer denied coverage, citing an exclusion for 'assault and battery' claims. The insured argued that the claim was based on negligent supervision, not on the assault and battery itself, and therefore, the exclusion should not apply. The trial court granted summary judgment for the insurer. The appellate court examined the policy language, which explicitly stated that the exclusion applied to claims 'arising out of' assault and battery, regardless of the theory of liability. The court found that because the injury would not have occurred 'but for' the assault, the 'arising out of' language captured the negligence claims as well. The court concluded that the language was broad and intended to exclude any liability stemming from such incidents, regardless of the legal label attached to the lawsuit. The denial of coverage was upheld as consistent with the clear language of the insurance contract.

## Munday v. P & L Partners, LLC

594 S.W.3d 257 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a party seeking to enforce a provision of a contract, such as a capital call, must strictly adhere to the notice and procedural requirements set forth in the agreement. Failure to follow these steps precludes a claim that the other party breached the contract. A real estate investor sued a property developer for breach of a joint venture agreement, claiming the developer sold the project to a third party without informing the investor and without distributing the profits as required by their contract. The developer argued that the joint venture agreement had expired due to the investor's failure to contribute additional capital when requested. The trial court found that the capital call made by the developer was not in accordance with the contract's notice provisions and that the agreement remained in effect when the property was sold. The developer appealed, arguing that the trial court erred in its interpretation of the notice requirement for capital calls. The appellate court upheld the trial court's ruling, finding that the contract clearly defined the procedures for requesting additional capital and that the developer failed to follow them. Therefore, the developer could not terminate the investor's interest in the venture, and the failure to distribute profits constituted a breach of the agreement.

## Munday v. Walker

999 S.W.2d 317 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1999 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that adverse possession does not require a conscious intent to steal land; a mistaken belief regarding boundary lines does not negate the element of hostile possession if the claimant exercised exclusive control over the property. The plaintiffs brought a quiet title action to establish a boundary line, claiming that a strip of land between their property and the defendants' property belonged to them through adverse possession. The defendants relied on the legal descriptions in their deed to claim ownership of the strip. The trial court found in favor of the plaintiffs, determining that they had adversely possessed the land by maintaining, mowing, and landscaping the disputed strip for more than ten years. The defendants appealed, asserting that the plaintiffs'

Second stored summary use was not 'hostile' because they had mistaken the location of the boundary. The appellate court addressed the 'mistaken belief' defense to adverse possession in Missouri. It clarified that the subjective intent of the possessor is not the determining factor for the hostility element; rather, the focus is on whether the claimant occupied the land as their own and exercised exclusive control over it in a manner that notified the true owner of the adverse claim. Since the plaintiffs treated the disputed strip as their own for the statutory period without permission, the court affirmed the adverse possession claim, ruling that even a good-faith mistake regarding boundary lines does not preclude the acquisition of title through adverse possession.

## Murphy v. Stonewall Kitchen, LLC

503 S.W.3d 308 · Mo. App. E.D. · 2016 · Missouri

4 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that the plaintiff failed to show an ascertainable loss because the labels contained the ingredient list which provided the truth to any consumer who read it. The court affirmed the dismissal of the MPA claim. A consumer filed a class action lawsuit against a manufacturer of food products, alleging violations of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA). The plaintiff claimed that the labels on the company's products were misleading because they indicated the products were 'all natural' while containing synthetic ingredients. The defendant argued that the label complied with FDA regulations and that any inconsistency with the consumer's expectations was not a deceptive act. The trial court dismissed the complaint, ruling that the plaintiff had not pleaded the 'ascertainable loss' requirement with sufficient specificity. The appellate court examined the pleading requirements for an MPA claim in the context of food labeling. The court addressed the 'reasonable consumer' standard, specifically whether a consumer is entitled to rely on the 'all natural' claim when the ingredients list--which is required by law--actually discloses the presence of synthetic substances. The case explored the tension between regulatory compliance and the state's interest in preventing deceptive marketing, weighing whether the label as a whole prevents a consumer from being misled.

## N.A.P. Consumer Electronics Corp. v. Gen. Elec. Capital Corp.

320 S.W.3d 233 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District, reversed the trial court's judgment regarding damages, finding that the calculation was flawed. However, the court affirmed the finding that NAP had breached the lease agreement by failing to make payments. The court remanded the case for a recalculation of damages based on the correct contractual terms.

Second stored summary This case involved a dispute over a lease agreement for electronic equipment. N.A.P. Consumer Electronics Corp. (NAP) leased equipment from General Electric Capital Corp. (GECC). NAP claimed that GECC breached the lease agreement by failing to provide certain services and by overcharging for equipment. GECC counterclaimed, alleging that NAP breached the agreement by failing to make timely payments. The trial court found in favor of GECC on its counterclaim and awarded damages. NAP appealed, arguing that the trial court erred in its interpretation of the lease terms, the admission of evidence, and the calculation of damages. The appellate court examined the specific provisions of the lease agreement, the conduct of both parties, and the evidence presented at trial to determine whether a breach occurred and if the damages awarded were appropriate.

## N.A.S.S. v. Allied Property & Casualty Insurance Co.

595 S.W.3d 520 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the exclusion for continuous or repeated seepage and leakage was unambiguous and applied to the facts of the case. The court affirmed the summary judgment for the insurer, finding that the damage did not qualify as a sudden and accidental event. This case involved a coverage dispute regarding damage to property resulting from a series of water leaks. The insured filed a claim for property damage, but the insurer denied the claim, citing a long-term seepage and leakage exclusion. The policy provided coverage for 'sudden and accidental' water damage but specifically excluded damage caused by leaks that occurred over an extended period. The insured argued that the leak was a single, discrete event that occurred during the policy period. The court was tasked with interpreting the term 'sudden' within the context of the insurance policy. The insurer provided evidence of mold growth and structural decay indicative of a long-standing moisture issue, which it argued supported its denial based on the policy's clear exclusions. The insured offered conflicting expert testimony regarding the timeline of the water infiltration. The court analyzed whether there was any ambiguity in the policy's language regarding the temporal definition of 'sudden'. The court reviewed the trial court's decision, which granted summary judgment for the insurer based on the finding that the damage was excluded under the plain language of the contract.

## N.E. v. Am. Family Mut. Ins. Co.

644 S.W.3d 603 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's ruling, holding that the policy's water damage exclusion was unambiguous. It ruled that the insurer had no duty to defend or indemnify for the sewer backup loss. The insured plaintiffs sought coverage under a homeowners policy for damages resulting from a basement sewage backup. American Family Mutual Insurance Company denied coverage based on a policy exclusion for water damage, specifically relating to water that backs up through sewers or drains. The plaintiffs argued that the language of the exclusion was ambiguous and that it should be construed in favor of coverage because the cause of the backup was external to the home's plumbing system. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the insurer, concluding that the unambiguous language of the policy clearly excluded coverage for the damage claimed. On appeal, the plaintiffs challenged the interpretation of the 'sewer backup' exclusion, asserting that it conflicted with other sections of the policy. The Court of Appeals analyzed the plain language of the policy provisions, noting that the exclusion was broad and clearly intended to limit the insurer's liability for such specific hazards unless an endorsement was purchased. The court found that the trial court's application of the plain meaning rule was correct and that there was no ambiguity in the exclusion clause.

## N.E. v. HCR Manorcare, LLC

632 S.W.3d 403 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the duty to defend is triggered when the petition alleges facts that potentially fall within the policy's coverage. Because the allegations regarding failure to monitor could be construed as professional services, the insurer had a duty to defend until the facts were fully developed. The plaintiffs brought a negligence and wrongful death action against a nursing home facility. The defendant's liability insurer sought a declaratory judgment regarding its duty to defend and indemnify under the professional liability policy. The primary dispute centered on whether the claims fell within the policy's definition of 'professional services' or were instead excluded under general liability provisions. The policy contained a specific exclusion for services provided by unlicensed personnel, which the insurer argued applied to the conduct at issue. The trial court initially granted summary judgment in favor of the nursing home, concluding that the insurer had a broad duty to defend. The appellate court reviewed the insurance policy language and applicable case law concerning the scope of professional liability coverage versus general negligence. The case involved complex questions of whether the failure to monitor a resident constituted an error in professional medical services or a failure in general facility management. The court analyzed the exclusions in conjunction with the insuring agreement to determine if the insurer could disclaim coverage based on the specific qualifications of the staff members involved. This case highlights the necessity of precise policy language when defining professional acts.

## N.H. Ins. Co. v. D.L.C., Inc.

243 S.W.3d 492 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the pollution exclusion applied because the contamination was the result of a long-term, gradual seepage. The 'sudden and accidental' exception was not triggered because the release was not abrupt. The insurer brought this action to determine if it was required to indemnify its insured, a chemical company, for environmental cleanup costs associated with groundwater contamination. The central issue was the 'pollution exclusion' clause. The insurer maintained that the exclusion was broad enough to cover all environmental cleanup costs, while the insured argued that the 'sudden and accidental' exception to the pollution exclusion applied. The case turned on whether the release of the chemical was unexpected and abrupt or a gradual process of seepage that occurred over several years. The court reviewed the evidence regarding the timeline of the leaks and the maintenance history of the chemical storage tanks. This decision is a classic Missouri case on the interpretation of pollution exclusions in CGL policies and the narrow construction of the 'sudden and accidental' exception. The appellate court scrutinized the intent of the parties and the typical interpretation of the term 'sudden' within the industry, providing guidance for future environmental litigation in Missouri courts.

## N.H. Scheppers Distributing Co. v. Anheuser-Busch, Inc.

675 S.W.2d 387 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1984 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the manufacturer was within its contractual rights to terminate the agreement. It ruled that statutory protections for distributors did not apply because the agreement was a valid private contract. This litigation involved the termination of a beer distributorship agreement. The distributor argued that the manufacturer breached the contract by terminating the relationship without 'good cause,' as allegedly required by state franchise statutes and the parties' written agreement. The manufacturer argued that the contract provided for termination upon notice and that the statute was not applicable to their specific business arrangement. The court examined the interplay between statutory regulations for distributorships and private contract rights. The decision involved a detailed study of whether the contract's termination provisions were unconscionable or violated public policy regarding the protection of small businesses. The court had to determine if the distributor had a 'reasonable expectation' of a continuing relationship based on the conduct and the duration of the contract. The ruling provides significant insight into the regulation of manufacturer-distributor relationships in Missouri.

## N.H. v. Independence School District

439 S.W.3d 278 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: Sovereign immunity protects school districts from liability for negligence in supervision. An injury arising from the use of school equipment does not automatically trigger the dangerous condition of public property exception to sovereign immunity. The plaintiff, a student, sought damages for injuries sustained during a physical education class incident involving a school-provided trampoline. The plaintiff argued that the school district was negligent in its supervision and the maintenance of safety equipment, asserting that the district's sovereign immunity was waived under the dangerous condition of public property exception. The school district argued that it was immune from suit under the doctrine of sovereign immunity and that the equipment did not constitute a 'dangerous condition' as defined by statute. The court analyzed whether the trampoline was defective or inherently dangerous. The appellate court concluded that the mere presence of the trampoline did not constitute a dangerous condition of the property itself. Instead, the injury was caused by the student's activity and the instructor's supervision, which did not fall under the statutory exceptions to sovereign immunity. Consequently, the appellate court affirmed the dismissal of the claim, holding that sovereign immunity remained intact for the school district regarding the alleged negligence of its employees.

## N.H. v. Presbyterian Church of Kennett

641 S.W.3d 286 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: Missouri courts analyze the existence of a duty of care by balancing factors including the foreseeability of harm and the nature of the relationship. In this instance, the absence of a special relationship or foreseeable risk precluded a finding of negligence. The plaintiff sought damages for negligence related to a lack of supervision and protection from harm on church premises. The core of the legal dispute revolved around whether the defendant owed a duty of care to the plaintiff under the circumstances presented, given the nature of the relationship and the foreseeability of the harm. The trial court dismissed the action, ruling that as a matter of law, no

Second stored summary duty existed. On appeal, the court analyzed the 'special relationship' doctrine under Missouri tort law. The court looked at whether the harm was a foreseeable consequence of the defendant's actions or inaction. The appellate court examined existing precedents regarding the duty of care for volunteers and organizations. The decision focused on the balancing test used to determine if a duty should be recognized, considering the societal interest in the defendant's activities. The court ultimately concluded that the circumstances did not support the expansion of duty as requested by the plaintiff, affirming the trial court's dismissal based on the lack of a legal duty.

## N.M. v. Zurich American Insurance Co.

621 S.W.3d 479 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the sexual abuse constituted an 'occurrence' because, from the perspective of the corporate insured, the events were unexpected and unintended. The court ruled that the insurer was required to provide coverage under the terms of the commercial general liability policy. This high-profile case involved whether an insurer had a duty to indemnify a policyholder for a significant judgment arising from a sexual abuse claim. The insurer denied coverage based on the policy's 'expected or intended' injury exclusion and the argument that the abuse did not constitute an 'occurrence' under the policy. The victim argued that the abuse was accidental from the perspective of the corporate insured entity. The case required the Supreme Court of Missouri to determine the scope of coverage for acts of employees and the extent to which a corporation can be held liable under insurance law for intentional torts committed by its agents. The insurer relied heavily on the premise that the underlying acts were intentional and thus inherently excluded. The insured argued that the policy's definition of occurrence should be construed in favor of coverage to prevent the insurer from evading responsibility. The court engaged in an extensive analysis of the intent requirement, distinguishing between the perpetrator of the abuse and the corporate entity. The case explored the nuances of vicarious liability and how it interacts with standard policy exclusions related to intentional acts. The decision had significant implications for coverage in cases involving systemic abuse and corporate liability.

## N.S. v. Hyundai Motor America, Inc.

779 S.W.2d 747 (Mo. App. 1989) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1989 · Missouri

Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals reversed the grant of summary judgment, finding that the plaintiff presented sufficient evidence to create a genuine issue of material fact regarding a design defect in the vehicle's roof. The court held that the plaintiff's claim of a feasible alternative design was properly before the jury. Plaintiff brought a product liability action against the manufacturer of a vehicle after being injured in a rollover accident. The plaintiff alleged that the vehicle's design was defective, specifically concerning the roof's susceptibility to collapse, and that this defect rendered the vehicle unreasonably dangerous. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the defendant. On appeal, the plaintiff argued that the trial court erred by granting summary judgment and that genuine issues of material fact existed regarding the design defect and causation. The appellate court examined the evidence presented, including expert testimony on vehicle design and safety standards. The court considered whether the plaintiff had presented sufficient evidence to demonstrate that a feasible alternative design existed that would have prevented or mitigated the injuries. The appellate court reversed the summary judgment and remanded the case for trial.

## N.Y. Life Ins. Co. v. Griesedieck

128 S.W.3d 516 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that insurance companies are not liable for claims on lapsed policies if they provided proper notice of premium deadlines in accordance with the contract. Clear contractual language controls the rights and duties of parties. This case involved a dispute over the interpretation of a life insurance contract. The beneficiary argued that the insurer breached the contract by failing to pay the full proceeds upon the insured's death. The insurer contended that the policy had lapsed due to non-payment of premiums. The trial court examined whether the insurer provided proper notice of the premium deadline as required by the policy's terms and state law. The court analyzed the doctrine of substantial compliance in the context of insurance contracts, looking at whether the insurer's notices were sufficient to inform the insured of the potential lapse. The appellate court found that while insurance policies are interpreted in favor of the insured if ambiguous, the language regarding premium payment was clear. The court held that the insurer met its contractual obligations and the policy had indeed lapsed. The decision underscored the principle that insurance contracts are governed by their plain language, and courts cannot rewrite policies to provide coverage that was not paid for by the insured.

## Nahn v. The Heritage Hills Homeowners Association

81 S.W.3d 614 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: An easement expressly created in a recorded subdivision plat remains valid unless the owner of the dominant estate performs an intentional, affirmative act of abandonment. Non-use of an easement, even over a long period, is insufficient to extinguish the right of access granted by the plat. The plaintiffs challenged the Homeowners Association's (HOA) claim to an easement over their backyard, which the HOA intended to use as a pathway for common area access. The recorded plat showed the area as part of the plaintiffs' property, but the HOA claimed an easement existed based on a note on the development's master plat. The plaintiffs argued that the easement had been abandoned due to lack of use and that it was never properly dedicated to the public or the HOA. The dispute required the court to interpret the language on the subdivision plat and the HOA's bylaws. The HOA contended that the easement was essential for maintenance of common grounds. The court looked at the intent of the developer at the time of the plat filing. It found that the language in the plat created a valid, irrevocable easement for the HOA. Furthermore, the court held that an easement created by a recorded plat is not easily abandoned; non-use, regardless of duration, is insufficient to extinguish an express easement unless accompanied by an intentional act of abandonment by the owner of the dominant estate. The decision confirmed the validity of the HOA's easement and denied the plaintiffs' request to remove the access path.

## Nalley v. General Motors Corp.

147 S.W.3d 773 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a property owner is not liable for the negligence of an independent contractor unless the owner retains significant control over the work performed. The summary judgment for the premises owner was affirmed. This case was a product liability and negligence action following a vehicle accident on a commercial premises. The plaintiff, an employee of a contractor, sued the premises owner for failing to provide a safe place to work. The owner argued that it had no duty to monitor the work habits of the contractor's employees. The appeal examined the extent to which a property owner must supervise independent contractors to fulfill the duty of maintaining safe premises for business invitees. The court reviewed the contract between the owner and the contractor to determine the allocation of risk and responsibility. The decision focused on the balance between the

Second stored summary contractor's expertise and the property owner's obligation to maintain a reasonably safe workplace, specifically in an industrial context where heavy equipment and machinery are involved.

## Nasrallah v. Barr

590 U.S. 573 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2020 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that federal courts have jurisdiction to review the factual findings underlying a CAT claim, even when the alien is ineligible for other forms of relief due to criminal history. The Court ruled that the jurisdictional bar in the INA does not apply to the denial of CAT protection. This allowed the petitioner to challenge the agency's factual findings. The petitioner was a Lebanese citizen who was ordered removed from the United States. He sought relief under the Convention Against Torture (CAT), claiming that he would be tortured if deported. The immigration judge denied the CAT claim, and the Board of Immigration Appeals affirmed. The question before the Supreme Court was whether the federal courts have jurisdiction to review the factual findings underlying a CAT claim. The government argued that the INA's jurisdiction-stripping provisions, which bar review of orders of removal based on criminal offenses, also extend to CAT claims decided within the same proceedings. The petitioner argued that CAT relief is distinct from standard removal relief, as it is a non-discretionary form of humanitarian protection that serves to fulfill international obligations, thus falling outside the jurisdictional restrictions governing typical immigration appeals.

## National Collegiate Athletic Association v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma

468 U.S. 85 · Supreme Court · 1984 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the NCAA's television broadcasting plan violated Section 1 of the Sherman Act. It ruled that the agreement was an unreasonable restraint of trade that limited output and fixed prices. The decision established that even non-profit athletic associations are subject to antitrust scrutiny. The NCAA controlled the rights to televise college football games, restricting the number of games any individual university could broadcast. The University of Oklahoma and the University of Georgia challenged this policy, arguing that it violated Section 1 of the Sherman Act by fixing prices and limiting the output of broadcast games. The NCAA argued that the restrictions were necessary to maintain the amateur nature of college sports and to protect attendance at games. The Supreme Court rejected the NCAA's arguments, finding that the plan was an unreasonable restraint of trade that restricted the output of games and artificially inflated prices. While the Court recognized that college sports require some level of regulation to function properly, it determined that the NCAA's television plan went beyond what was necessary to achieve these goals and resulted in significant anticompetitive harm. The court applied an abbreviated 'rule of reason' analysis, noting that because the restraint was so obviously anticompetitive on its face, it required a substantial procompetitive justification that the NCAA failed to provide.

## National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan

536 U.S. 101 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2002 · Federal

Holding: Discrete discriminatory acts must be filed within the statute of limitations from the date they occurred. Hostile work environment claims are timely if at least one contributing act occurred within the filing period. Abner Morgan filed a charge of discrimination with the EEOC, alleging that he was subjected to discrete discriminatory and retaliatory acts and a racially hostile work environment throughout his employment. The employer argued that many of the events were time-barred under Title VII's statute of limitations. The Supreme Court clarified the rules for the statute of limitations in Title VII cases. The Court distinguished between 'discrete acts' of discrimination--such as firing, failure to promote, or denial of transfer--and 'hostile work environment' claims. For discrete acts, the filing period begins on the day the act occurred. However, for hostile work environment claims, the court held that as long as one act contributing to the hostile environment occurred within the filing period, the entire period of the hostile environment may be considered by the court. This ruling significantly impacted how employees file timely claims and how courts assess the scope of evidence in harassment cases.

## Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc.

572 U.S. 898 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2014 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that the 'insolubly ambiguous' standard for patent indefiniteness was improper. Instead, patent claims must provide reasonable certainty regarding the scope of the invention to a person skilled in the art in light of the specification and prosecution history. The case dealt with the requirement of 'definiteness' in patent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112. Biosig held a patent for a heart-rate monitor that included the claim term 'spaced relationship.' Nautilus challenged the patent, arguing that the term was indefinite because it did not clearly define the distance between the sensors on the monitor. The Federal Circuit had applied a standard where a claim was indefinite only if it was 'insolubly ambiguous' or 'amenable to construction.' The Supreme Court vacated this standard, finding it lacked sufficient guidance for competitors and the public. The Court articulated a new, stricter standard: a patent must 'inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.' This standard requires that the claims be read in light of the specification and the prosecution history. The Court emphasized that while absolute precision is not required, the patent must provide enough clarity to define the boundaries of the invention. This decision shifted the burden on patent applicants to draft clearer claims and provided a stronger defense for accused infringers to challenge patents based on vague or ambiguous terminology that prevents the public from knowing the scope of the monopoly.

## Navarette v. California

572 U.S. 393 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2014 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: An anonymous tip that provides specific details about reckless driving, when verified by officers who observe the vehicle in the reported area, provides sufficient reasonable suspicion for a traffic stop. The totality of the circumstances justified the intrusion. A 911 caller reported that a silver Toyota Tundra had run her off the road. The caller provided a license plate number and the general location of the vehicle. Officers located the truck shortly thereafter and initiated a traffic stop. During the stop, officers smelled marijuana and subsequently discovered 30 pounds of it in the truck bed. The defendants were arrested and challenged the stop, arguing that the officers lacked reasonable suspicion because the anonymous tip lacked sufficient 'indicia of reliability.' The Supreme Court had to decide whether an anonymous tip describing a traffic violation, without more, provides enough reasonable suspicion to justify an investigatory stop. The Court examined the reliability of the 911 system and the urgency of the situation regarding highway safety, focusing on whether the tip was sufficient to create a reasonable suspicion of criminal activity.

## NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma

468 U.S. 85 · U.S. Supreme Court · 1984 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the NCAA's television broadcasting restrictions constituted an unreasonable restraint of trade under Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The court ruled that the restrictions limited output and fixed prices without sufficient justification. This case involved a challenge to the NCAA's restrictions on the number of college football games that could be televised. The Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma sued, alleging that the NCAA's control over television rights violated the Sherman Act by fixing prices and limiting output. The NCAA argued that these restrictions were necessary to protect live attendance at games and to maintain the amateur nature of intercollegiate athletics. The Supreme Court applied a 'rule of reason' analysis, noting that while the NCAA's cooperative structure was essential to the sport, the specific restrictions on television broadcasts were not. The Court found that the rules restricted the market for college football television broadcasts, thereby artificially limiting output and preventing member institutions from selling their rights individually. The Court held that the NCAA failed to justify these restraints as necessary to protect the amateur character of the sport, concluding that the rules resulted in an unreasonable restraint of trade that harmed consumer interests.

## Near v. Minnesota

283 U.S. 697 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1931 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court struck down the Minnesota law. It held that the government cannot engage in prior restraint of the press, except under extremely narrow circumstances involving national security. A Minnesota statute allowed for the 'abatement' of any 'malicious, scandalous, and defamatory' newspaper or periodical as a public nuisance. Jay Near published a paper that attacked local officials, and the state sought an injunction to prevent future issues from being printed. Near challenged the law as an unconstitutional prior restraint. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Near, holding that the statute was an infringement of the liberty of the press as guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court established the fundamental doctrine against prior restraint, declaring that, while the press is not immune from subsequent punishment for libelous or obscene publications, the government cannot systematically censor content before it reaches the public. This decision stands as one of the most important precedents protecting the press from government efforts to stifle investigative or critical journalism through prior injunctions.

## Neff v. FDIC

979 S.W.2d 203 (Mo. App. E.D. 1998) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's decision. The court held that under federal law, the FDIC, as a receiver of a failed financial institution, was entitled to protection from state tax sales that did not provide it with adequate notice. Because the FDIC did not receive proper notice of the tax sale proceedings, its prior lien remained valid and was not extinguished. The court emphasized the supremacy of federal law in protecting federal interests. This case involved a dispute over title to real property and the validity of a tax deed. The Neffs purchased property at a tax sale. They subsequently discovered that the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) held a prior lien on the property, which they argued was not extinguished by the tax sale. The FDIC had a prior mortgage interest in the property that was not paid off by the tax sale proceeds. The Neffs sought to quiet title to the property, asserting that the tax deed conveyed full ownership free and clear of all prior encumbrances. The FDIC contested this, arguing its lien remained valid. The trial court ruled in favor of the Neffs, invalidating the FDIC's lien.

## Nesselrode v. Executive Beechcraft, Inc.

707 S.W.2d 371 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1986 · Missouri

5 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that the trial court's instructions regarding the design defect were improper. It reaffirmed the use of the consumer expectations test for strict liability, finding that the instructions effectively imposed a negligence standard instead of a strict liability standard. The Nesselrode case arose from a fatal plane crash involving an aircraft serviced by the defendant. The central issue revolved around whether the defendant, having performed maintenance and modification work on the aircraft, could be held liable under strict products liability for a design defect. The plaintiffs argued that the installation of the modification caused a control mechanism to jam, leading to the crash. The case required the court to interpret the scope of 'product' versus 'service' in the context of the Restatement (Second) of Torts. The jury found in favor of the defendant, and the plaintiffs appealed, arguing that the court provided erroneous jury instructions regarding the definition of a defective design. The court analyzed whether the distinction between design defects and manufacturing defects should be blurred or maintained. The appeal centered on whether the court correctly distinguished between a failure to warn and a design defect, and whether the jury was properly instructed on the risk-utility balancing test.

## Netco, Inc. v. Dunn

194 S.W.3d 353 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2006 · Missouri

Holding: The court held the non-solicitation agreement was enforceable. It affirmed that employers have a protectable interest in customer relationships developed through the employee's role. Netco, Inc. sued its former employee, Dunn, for breach of a non-compete and non-solicitation agreement. After leaving Netco, Dunn formed a competing business and contacted former clients, which Netco alleged was a direct violation of his employment contract. The trial court found the non-compete clause to be reasonable and granted an injunction against Dunn. On appeal, the Missouri Supreme Court considered whether the restrictive covenants were reasonably necessary to protect the employer's interests in customer relationships. The court scrutinized the breadth of the non-solicitation agreement, determining whether it prevented the employee from competing fairly or if it merely protected the employer's proprietary interest in its client base. The Court concluded that the non-solicitation clause was enforceable because it protected legitimate business interests without imposing an undue hardship on the employee. The decision reiterated the balance courts must strike between an employer's right to protect its business assets and an employee's right to pursue their livelihood, ultimately ruling in favor of the employer given the specific nature of the client relationships involved in the industry.

## Nettie v. St. Louis Cty.

271 S.W.3d 621 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2008 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the learned intermediary doctrine protects manufacturers of medical devices if they provide adequate warnings to the prescribing physician. It concluded that the manufacturer had sufficiently warned of the known risks associated with the device's use. The plaintiff brought a product liability suit against the manufacturer of a medical device following a complication during a surgical procedure. The litigation centered on whether the manufacturer provided adequate warnings about the potential risks associated with the device. The case examined the 'learned intermediary doctrine' in the context of prescription medical devices. Under this doctrine, a manufacturer's duty to warn is discharged if they provide adequate warnings to the physician, who then acts as the intermediary between the manufacturer and the patient. The court analyzed whether the warning provided to the medical professional was sufficient as a matter of law to trigger the doctrine's protection for the manufacturer. The decision involves a detailed review of the informational materials supplied with the device and whether any warnings were omitted that could have altered the physician's decision-making process. This ruling provides clear guidelines on how manufacturers can satisfy their duty to warn in the medical field by targeting the appropriate audience with necessary safety information.

## New Horizons Leasing, Inc. v. Haack

644 S.W.2d 672 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1982 · Missouri

Holding: A commercial landlord has a duty to mitigate damages by making reasonable efforts to re-let the premises after a tenant breaches the lease. Failure to attempt re-letting can limit the amount of damages the landlord is entitled to recover. The dispute involved the recovery of unpaid rent and property damages following a tenant's early termination of a commercial lease. The landlord attempted to hold the tenant liable for the entire remaining balance of the lease term. The tenant contended that the landlord had a duty to mitigate damages by attempting to re-let the premises once they were vacated. The court addressed the issue of whether the duty to mitigate applies to commercial leases in Missouri. The court analyzed the doctrine of mitigation, which requires a non-breaching party to take reasonable steps to minimize losses. The court held that the duty to mitigate is a standard requirement in contract law and should apply to commercial leases, rejecting the older, more rigid property law view that held a landlord could simply let a property sit idle and sue for rent. The decision was significant because it aligned commercial landlord-tenant law with broader principles of contract law, ensuring that property owners cannot recover losses that could have been reasonably avoided. The case

Second stored summary reinforced the requirement that landlords exercise good faith in attempting to secure a replacement tenant when a breach occurs.

## New Jersey v. T.L.O.

469 U.S. 325 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1985 · Federal

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: School officials do not need a warrant to search a student's property; they need only 'reasonable suspicion' that the search will uncover evidence of a violation of law or school rules. The search must also be reasonable in scope. A high school student was caught smoking in a school bathroom. When brought to the principal's office, she denied smoking. The principal demanded to see her purse. Upon opening it, he found cigarettes, marijuana, and evidence of drug dealing. T.L.O. argued that the search of her purse violated the Fourth Amendment, claiming it was conducted without a warrant or probable cause. The state argued that school officials need broad authority to maintain discipline and that the Fourth Amendment's stringent requirements were ill-suited for the school environment. The Court addressed the standard of 'reasonableness' for searches in schools. It sought to balance the student's expectation of privacy with the school's fundamental duty to provide a safe and orderly educational environment, leading to a new, lower standard than that required for law enforcement.

## New York Times Co. v. Sullivan

376 U.S. 254 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1964 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court reversed the judgment for the plaintiff. It established the 'actual malice' standard, requiring public officials to prove intentional or reckless falsehoods to win a libel suit. L.B. Sullivan, a public safety commissioner in Alabama, sued the New York Times for libel after the newspaper published an advertisement containing factual errors regarding the police handling of civil rights protests. The case arrived at the Supreme Court during the height of the Civil Rights Movement. The Court established the 'actual malice' standard for public officials suing for defamation. To recover damages, a public official must prove that a statement was made with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for whether it was true or false. The Court held that the First Amendment requires a 'breathing space' for debate on public issues, and that the fear of libel litigation could lead to 'self-censorship' that would undermine the core of the democratic process. This landmark decision provided significant protection for the press to report on public officials without fear of bankruptcy from retaliatory lawsuits.

## Newcomb v. Donald Duck Mfg. Co.

748 S.W.2d 742 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1988 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a consumer can maintain an action under the MPA for damages related to defective merchandise if the seller engaged in deceptive conduct. It affirmed that the MPA is a distinct and additive remedy for consumers. The plaintiff brought an action against a manufacturer of defective clothing, alleging that the product was not as represented and that the company had engaged in deceptive practices by concealing known defects in the product line. The manufacturer argued that the plaintiff's remedy was limited to the warranty and that the MPA could not be used to seek damages beyond the contract. The court addressed whether the MPA provides an alternative, non-contractual remedy for the sale of defective goods. The court determined that the MPA was designed to augment traditional remedies and that it allows for the recovery of actual damages and potentially punitive damages if the manufacturer's conduct was sufficiently deceptive. The court found that the manufacturer's knowledge of the defect coupled with the continued marketing of the product was sufficient to support an MPA claim. This case illustrates the utility of the MPA in providing a pathway to recovery when product warranties are insufficient to cover the totality of the consumer's loss due to bad-faith manufacturing.

## Newcomb v. Robb

116 S.W.3d 622 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the sale of a single-family home does not fall within the definition of 'merchandise' under the MPA. It concluded that the statute is aimed at consumer transactions involving goods and services, not private residential real estate sales. In a dispute involving the sale of a residential property, the plaintiffs alleged that the sellers intentionally concealed structural defects. The plaintiffs sued under the MPA, contending that the failure to disclose known material defects in the home constituted a deceptive practice in the 'sale' of merchandise. The defendants moved to dismiss, arguing that the sale of a single-family home does not constitute 'merchandise' under the MPA, which is primarily aimed at retail consumer goods. The appellate court examined the statutory definition of 'merchandise' and whether the legislative intent behind the MPA was to encompass real estate transactions. This case is significant because it explores the boundaries of the MPA and whether homeowners who are not professional real estate developers can be considered 'merchants' for purposes of the act, or if the statute applies to the nature of the transaction itself rather than the status of the seller.

## Newman v. Ford Motor Co.

975 S.W.2d 147 · Missouri Supreme Court · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a plaintiff in a design defect case must prove the existence of a safer alternative design that was economically and technologically feasible. Failure to provide such evidence renders the design defect claim insufficient as a matter of law. The plaintiff, an injured party, brought a strict liability claim against Ford Motor Company following an accident involving a vehicle's seatbelt restraint system. The central issue concerned the design of the seatbelt and whether an alternative design was feasible, practicable, and safer. The case centered on the 'risk-utility' test utilized in Missouri product liability law. The plaintiff presented evidence suggesting that a different restraint configuration could have prevented the injury, while Ford contended that the current design met all federal safety standards and was within the state-of-the-art parameters at the time of manufacture. The Missouri Supreme Court addressed the burden of proof required when a plaintiff alleges a design defect. The Court analyzed the necessity of providing evidence regarding the cost and feasibility of a safer alternative design. It reinforced that Missouri law requires a plaintiff to demonstrate that a safer alternative design existed and was reasonable. The court ruled that the plaintiff failed to establish that a viable alternative design existed, thereby failing to make a submissible case for strict liability design defect. The decision reaffirmed the importance of expert engineering testimony in establishing a prima facie case.

## Nichols v. American National Insurance Co.

154 F.3d 875 · United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (applying Missouri law) · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the Missouri Human Rights Act acts as the exclusive remedy for employment discrimination claims, preempting common law wrongful discharge actions based on the same public policy. Plaintiffs must utilize the statutory framework provided by the MHRA. Common law claims are therefore barred when a statutory remedy exists. Nichols, an insurance agent, alleged that she was subjected to a hostile work environment and was wrongfully terminated after reporting sexual harassment. While this case involved federal claims under Title VII, it also addressed Missouri state law claims for wrongful discharge in violation of public policy. The employer moved for summary judgment on the state claim, arguing the at-will doctrine. The court analyzed whether the Missouri Human Rights Act (MHRA) provides the exclusive remedy for discriminatory discharge. The court concluded that when the MHRA covers the discriminatory conduct, it preempts common law claims for wrongful discharge based on the same public policy. Since the plaintiff could pursue her claims under the MHRA, she could not simultaneously bring a common law wrongful discharge claim for the same conduct. The appellate court affirmed the dismissal of the common law claim, noting that the statutory framework provided the comprehensive remedy for her grievance. This established that statutory remedies for discrimination must be used rather than general public policy claims.

## Nichols v. Bubel

456 S.W.3d 897 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a property owner is liable for injuries caused by a pet if they are aware of the animal's aggressive tendencies and fail to take reasonable precautions. The trial court's judgment was reversed and remanded for trial. The plaintiff was injured by a dog while visiting a friend's property. The dog had a known history of aggressive behavior. The plaintiff sued the owner for premises liability and negligence, citing the failure to restrain a dangerous animal. The trial court entered judgment for the dog owner, suggesting that the plaintiff assumed the risk by visiting. The appellate court reversed, noting that the duty to keep premises safe includes preventing harm from animals the owner knows are dangerous. The court addressed whether the 'one-bite' rule applied or if the owner's knowledge of past behavior was sufficient. It determined that the owner had a duty of ordinary care to control the pet given the known risk. The case clarifies that residential property owners must ensure that domestic pets do not present an unreasonable hazard to invited guests, and that the duty extends beyond mere warnings to active control and containment of the animal.

## Nielsen v. Preap

586 U.S. 327 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2019 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the government's authority to detain aliens under 1226(c) is not limited to those arrested immediately upon release from criminal custody. The Court concluded that the statute does not require the government to perform an immediate arrest to trigger mandatory detention. Therefore, the respondents were not entitled to bond hearings based on the timing of their arrests. This case addressed the interpretation of the mandatory detention statute, 8 U.S.C. 1226(c), which requires the government to detain aliens who have committed certain crimes during the pendency of removal proceedings. The core dispute was whether the government's authority to detain such individuals without a bond hearing is time-limited. Specifically, the respondents, a group of lawful permanent residents, argued that because they were not detained immediately upon their release from criminal custody--some having been apprehended years later--the government could no longer invoke the mandatory detention provision. They contended that the 'when... released' clause acted as a temporal limitation on the authority to detain without bond. The government argued that the statute requires detention regardless of when the arrest occurs relative to the release from criminal incarceration. The case turned on statutory construction and whether the phrase 'when released' serves as a temporal condition or merely identifies the category of aliens subject to detention.

## Niewald v. American Family Insurance Co.

391 S.W.3d 918 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the earth movement exclusion was unambiguous and applied to all causes, including those instigated by human activity. Because the policy clearly stated it excluded earth movement 'regardless of any other cause,' the efficient proximate cause doctrine did not override the specific policy exclusion. The Niewalds sought recovery under their homeowner's insurance policy for structural damage caused by earth movement and subsidence. American Family denied the claim, relying on a policy exclusion that barred coverage for loss caused by earth movement, regardless of the cause. The Niewalds argued that the 'efficient proximate cause' doctrine should apply, asserting that human activity (a nearby construction project) triggered the earth movement, rather than natural geological processes. The dispute centered on whether the absolute earth movement exclusion in the policy could be circumvented by identifying an man-made cause as the primary catalyst. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the insurer. The appellate court reviewed whether the exclusion was unambiguous and whether the proximate cause doctrine required the insurer to cover losses where the initial cause was a covered peril but the resulting damage was specifically excluded by the policy's plain terms.

## Nijhawan v. Holder

557 U.S. 29 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2009 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that the monetary loss threshold in the aggravated felony definition is a circumstance-specific inquiry rather than a categorical element of the crime. Immigration judges are permitted to look beyond the elements of the statute to the record of conviction to determine if the specific harm exceeded the statutory threshold. This created an exception to the strict categorical approach. The petitioner, a lawful permanent resident, was charged with removability based on a conviction for an 'aggravated felony.' The specific statute involved fraud and deceit where the loss to the victim exceeded $10,000. Nijhawan argued that because the statute of conviction did not have a $10,000 loss threshold element, his conviction could not be categorically classified as an aggravated felony under the categorical approach. The government argued that the monetary loss threshold is a factual circumstance of the specific offense rather than a generic element of the crime, allowing for an examination of the record of conviction to determine if the loss amount was met.

## Niz-Chavez v. Garland

593 U.S. 155 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2021 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the INA requires the government to serve a single document containing all required information to trigger the stop-time rule. The Court reasoned that Congress clearly intended for an NTA to be a single, comprehensive notice. Therefore, the piecemeal notices provided to the petitioner were insufficient to trigger the stop-time rule. Following the Pereira decision, this case asked whether the government can satisfy its statutory obligation to provide a 'Notice to Appear' (NTA) by serving multiple documents over time, rather than a single document containing all required information. The petitioner was served with an NTA that lacked the time and place of his hearing, followed later by a separate document that provided those details. The government argued that the statute requires all information to be provided 'in' the proceedings but does not mandate that it all appear in one single document. The petitioner maintained that the INA explicitly defines an NTA as a specific document that must contain certain information to trigger legal consequences. The court evaluated the text of the INA to determine whether Congress intended for the notice to be a singular procedural instrument or a cumulative notice process.

## NLRB v. Noel Canning

573 U.S. 513 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2014 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that the Recess Appointments Clause allows the President to fill vacancies that occur during a recess, but the Senate is not in recess when it holds pro forma sessions. The decision clarified the scope of executive authority. This ensured that labor board panels adjudicating immigrant labor rights were properly constituted.

Second stored summary While primarily a constitutional case on the Recess Appointments Clause, this case directly impacted the composition of the National Labor Relations Board, which frequently adjudicates cases involving immigrant workers and immigration-related labor disputes. The petitioner challenged the validity of several Board appointments made by the President during a period where the Senate was arguably not in recess. The ruling established the extent of executive power to fill vacancies without Senate confirmation, affecting the consistency of administrative rulings in labor and immigration sectors.

## Nolting v. Missouri Department of Corrections

959 S.W.2d 483 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that public employees in positions affecting institutional security are held to high standards of conduct. The court will defer to the findings of administrative bodies when those findings are supported by competent and substantial evidence, provided due process was followed. The plaintiff, a corrections officer, challenged his termination, alleging it was retaliatory and violated his due process rights. The Department of Corrections maintained that the officer was terminated for inappropriate conduct and violation of facility security policies. The officer argued that the investigation into his actions was biased and designed to find a pretext for termination. The trial court focused on whether the officer received adequate notice and a fair hearing, which are requirements for a public employee with a property interest in their job. The appellate court reviewed the evidence presented to the Personnel Advisory Board and whether the findings were supported by competent and substantial evidence. The court noted that in the context of employment within a correctional facility, safety and order are of paramount importance, and employers are granted significant latitude to maintain these standards. The court ultimately concluded that the Department had provided a legitimate reason for termination and had afforded the employee all necessary due process protections, including an opportunity to be heard through administrative channels before reaching a decision on the merits of the case.

## Nooter Corp. v. Allianz Underwriters Ins. Co.

536 S.W.3d 251 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the policies at issue allowed for an 'all sums' allocation, permitting the insured to recover in full from any single triggered policy. The court rejected the pro-rata allocation method in the absence of clear contractual language requiring it. This complex insurance coverage case involved an insured party seeking coverage for massive asbestos-related liabilities spanning several decades. The insured held numerous primary and excess liability policies issued by various insurers over a period of thirty years. The dispute arose over the method of allocating liability among the multiple insurers whose policies were triggered by the progressive nature of the underlying injuries. The insurers advocated for a pro-rata allocation based on the time on the risk, while the insured argued for an 'all sums' allocation approach, which would allow the insured to seek full indemnity from any single triggered

Second stored summary policy up to its limit. The court examined the policy language, specifically the 'other insurance' clauses and the definition of 'occurrence' in the context of long-tail latent injuries. The lower court's decision regarding the allocation methodology was challenged by several parties. The appellate court provided an exhaustive analysis of Missouri law regarding continuous trigger theories and the interplay between excess and primary policies in multi-year environmental and toxic tort litigation. The decision significantly clarified how Missouri courts interpret 'all sums' language versus 'pro-rata' obligations in the absence of explicit contractual language directing a specific allocation method for long-term claims.

## Norris v. City of Sparks

This case involved claims of race discrimination and retaliation under Title VII. ## North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC

574 U.S. 494 · U.S. Supreme Court · 2015 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a state regulatory board controlled by market participants is only entitled to antitrust immunity if it is actively supervised by the state. The Court rejected claims of automatic state action immunity. The North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners, a state regulatory body composed mostly of practicing dentists, issued cease-and-desist orders to non-dentist teeth-whitening service providers. The FTC alleged that the board acted in violation of the Sherman Act by using its regulatory authority to protect its members from competition. The Board argued it was entitled to 'state action immunity,' a doctrine that shields state regulators from federal antitrust laws. The Supreme Court ruled against the Board, holding that because the board was controlled by active market participants, its anticompetitive actions were not immune unless they were actively supervised by the state. This case established a significant constraint on the ability of professional boards to use government authority for anticompetitive ends. It ensures that when state-authorized bodies are comprised of active market participants, their decisions must be subject to rigorous state oversight to prevent them from engaging in self-interested protectionism under the guise of regulation.

## North Central Missouri Production Credit Association v. Washington Sales Co.

665 S.W.2d 381 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1984 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the auctioneer was liable for conversion because it participated in the sale of collateral subject to a perfected security interest. The court affirmed that auctioneers must exercise due diligence regarding potential liens on items they sell.

Second stored summary This case dealt with the liability of an auctioneer for selling collateral covered by a security interest. A production credit association (PCA) held a perfected security interest in livestock owned by a farmer. The farmer delivered the livestock to an auction house, which sold them and remitted the proceeds to the farmer. The PCA subsequently sued the auction house for conversion. The auction house argued that it was merely an agent and did not hold title, and therefore, it should not be liable for the conversion of the secured property. The court evaluated the liability of auctioneers under the UCC, focusing on whether the auctioneer's involvement in the sale constituted an interference with the secured party's rights. The case addressed the tension between the auctioneer's role as a conduit for sales and the secured party's right to protect its interest in the collateral. It clarifies the scope of liability for third parties who facilitate the sale of collateral without verifying the status of potential security interests.

## North Georgia Finishing, Inc. v. Di-Chem, Inc.

419 U.S. 601 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1975 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that a statute authorizing the summary garnishment of bank accounts without notice or a prior hearing violates the Due Process Clause. The failure to provide a prompt post-seizure hearing is a fatal constitutional flaw. A corporation challenged a Georgia statute that allowed for the garnishment of corporate bank accounts based on an affidavit by a creditor without notice or a hearing. The statute permitted a judge to issue a writ of garnishment based solely on the creditor's conclusory allegations, and the debtor had no path to a prompt post-seizure hearing. The Supreme Court analyzed whether this process satisfied the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Building upon its prior rulings in Sniadach and Fuentes, the Court held the statute unconstitutional. The Court emphasized that even if the property is corporate in nature, the fundamental requirement of due process is notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard before property is taken by the state. The Court criticized the statute for lacking the procedural safeguards required to minimize the risk of erroneous deprivation, such as a requirement for judicial supervision or a provision for an immediate hearing. The ruling cemented the principle that procedural due process is a required shield against summary, unilateral seizures of property in commercial disputes.

## North Kansas City Hosp. Bd. of Trustees v. St. Luke's

984 S.W.2d 113 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1998 · Missouri

Also captioned North Kansas City Hospital Board of Trustees v. St. Luke's Northland Hospital

Holding: The court held that a public hospital board is subject to the Sunshine Law. Mere competitive market concerns do not provide a sufficient basis to close meetings concerning the disposition of public assets. This case involved a dispute over whether a board of trustees governing a city-owned hospital was required to open its meetings during merger negotiations. The hospital board argued that the competitive nature of the healthcare market justified keeping the merger discussions private under the Sunshine Law's 'negotiations' and 'trade secrets' exceptions. Opponents of the merger argued that the hospital, as a public entity, was obligated to maintain transparent operations regarding the potential transfer of public assets to a private entity. The court analyzed whether the competitive exception could be applied to a public hospital entity. It ruled that while certain specific financial data might be sensitive, the board could not exclude the public from the deliberative process regarding the future of a public asset. The court clarified that the Sunshine Law's exceptions are meant to be narrow and that competitive disadvantage must be specific rather than speculative. This decision served as a significant reminder that public entities cannot claim 'competitive' status as a blanket shield against the requirements of the Sunshine Law when making major organizational decisions.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that the hospital board, as a public entity, is subject to the Sunshine Law. It established that exceptions for competitive business practices must be narrowly construed and supported by evidence of tangible harm if disclosed. This litigation involved a dispute over whether the Board of Trustees of a public hospital was required to disclose records related to a strategic partnership or merger. St. Luke's argued that the Board, as a public body, must operate in the open, while the Board claimed that disclosing competitive information would harm its ability to compete in the private healthcare market. The court analyzed whether the 'business secrets' or 'competitive advantage' exceptions applied. The court reviewed whether the Board of Trustees operated under the Sunshine Law's definition of a public governmental body and if the hospital's internal deliberations qualified for the 'closed session' protection. This case explored the extent to which public entities competing with private entities can shield their financial and strategic records from public view. The court carefully balanced the hospital's need to maintain a competitive position against the public's right to oversee how public funds and assets are managed. The ruling reinforced the principle that public entities, even when functioning in a competitive business environment, are bound by the Sunshine Law unless they can strictly prove that disclosure would cause actual, specific harm to their competitive position.

## Norwin G. Gerhart v. Director of Revenue

776 S.W.2d 881 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 1989 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the Department of Revenue properly disallowed the deductions because the taxpayer failed to provide sufficient documentation to substantiate the business purpose and nature of the expenses claimed. The burden of proof remains with the taxpayer. The taxpayer, Norwin G. Gerhart, appealed a decision by the Administrative Hearing Commission regarding the assessment of income tax. The dispute involved the deductibility of certain business expenses. Gerhart claimed deductions for various travel, entertainment, and professional development expenses incurred in his business. The Director of Revenue disallowed these deductions, arguing that the taxpayer failed to provide adequate documentation to substantiate the business purpose of the expenses as required by law. The court reviewed the evidence presented to the Commission and the standards for substantiation of business expenses. The taxpayer argued that the expenses were ordinary and necessary for the conduct of his trade or business. The state asserted that the burden of proof is on the taxpayer to maintain and produce records that justify the tax deduction. The court evaluated whether the evidence presented was sufficient to meet the statutory requirements for deducting business expenses. This case emphasizes the importance of record-keeping in tax matters and the authority of the Department of Revenue to disallow deductions that lack proper verification.

## Norwin G. Heimos Greenhouse, Inc. v. Director of Revenue

724 S.W.2d 505 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1987 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the greenhouse operations constituted agricultural production and that the taxpayer was entitled to the relevant sales tax exemptions. The court adopted a broad interpretation of agricultural production consistent with the legislative purpose. The taxpayer, a commercial greenhouse operator, sought a refund for sales tax paid on items used in the production of plants. The argument was based on the 'agricultural exemption' within the Missouri tax code, which allows for exemptions on materials used in agricultural production. The Director of Revenue argued that the greenhouse operations were more akin to retail gardening supply than agricultural farming, and therefore the materials were subject to tax. The case turned on the interpretation of 'agricultural production' and whether the greenhouse's cultivation processes met the threshold of farming activities. The court analyzed the statutory language and the intent of the legislature in providing exemptions for agricultural businesses. The court had to determine if the greenhouse cultivation of flowers and plants was intended to be treated as a form of crop farming for tax purposes. This ruling was significant for the agricultural sector in Missouri, as it clarified what specific business activities qualified for farm-related tax breaks.
