## Nussbaum v. Schaffer

531 S.W.3d 612 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the buyers failed to comply with the strict notice requirements set forth in the real estate contract. Consequently, the sellers were entitled to retain the earnest money as liquidated damages. This case involved a dispute over an earnest money contract in a residential real estate transaction. The buyers sought to recover their earnest money deposit after they terminated the contract due to unsatisfactory inspection results. The sellers refused to return the funds, arguing that the buyers failed to provide proper notice of termination as required by the contract's terms. The court evaluated whether the notice provided by the buyers was sufficient to trigger the termination clause and whether the sellers' subsequent refusal constituted a breach of the agreement. The dispute centered on the technical requirements for notice in real estate contracts and the interpretation of the 'satisfaction' clause. The court analyzed the intent of the parties and whether the communication from the buyers clearly expressed their desire to cancel the contract within the permitted timeframe. The case provides guidance on the strict adherence

Second stored summary to contractual notice provisions and the legal consequences of failing to satisfy those requirements in a real estate context.

## Nuts, Inc. v. Great American Insurance Company

649 S.W.3d 282 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the temporary inability to use property due to governmental shutdown orders related to COVID-19 does not constitute 'direct physical loss or damage' under a commercial property insurance policy. Coverage is contingent upon a physical alteration to the property, which the presence of a virus does not satisfy. Nuts, Inc. brought an action against its insurer, Great American, following a denial of coverage for business losses resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent government-mandated shutdowns. The insured argued that the presence of the virus on surfaces constituted physical loss or damage to property, thereby triggering the 'Business Income' and 'Extra Expense' coverage provisions of its commercial property policy. Great American argued that the policy required actual tangible alteration to the property, which was absent in this case. The circuit court granted summary judgment in favor of the insurer, concluding that the mere presence of a virus did not constitute direct physical loss. On appeal, the court examined whether the temporary loss of use of the premises due to regulatory orders fell within the scope of the policy language. The court relied on a strict interpretation of the phrase 'direct physical loss or damage,' requiring a distinct, demonstrable, physical alteration of the property. Because the virus did not physically damage the structural integrity of the facility, the court determined that coverage was not triggered under the plain language of the policy.

## O'Brien v. City of St. Louis

454 S.W.3d 375 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that off-duty electronic communications can constitute compensable work time if they are mandatory and not trivial in the aggregate. The court rejected the trial court's conclusion that such work is inherently de minimis and required further factual findings. This dispute involved police officers who were denied overtime compensation for time spent responding to work-related emails and phone calls while off duty. The City of St. Louis argued that these activities were intermittent and did not reach the threshold of compensable work time. The trial court ruled that the activities were too infrequent to trigger an overtime obligation. The officers appealed, arguing that the aggregate time spent on these communications was substantial and that it was mandatory for them to respond. The appellate court analyzed whether the time spent was 'de minimis.' The court determined that while individual emails took only minutes, the consistent, daily nature of these tasks meant they were not de minimis in the aggregate. The court found that when an employer requires employees to be reachable and to respond, the time spent on those activities, if not trivial, must be compensated. The appellate court reversed the trial court's decision, noting that in the modern era, work-related electronic communications can easily constitute significant, compensable work, and that courts must be cautious about dismissing such claims as de minimis without examining the total impact.

## O'Brien v. City of St. Louis

355 S.W.3d 480 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the board of adjustment failed to provide sufficient evidence of unnecessary hardship. Consequently, the court vacated the board's decision to grant the zoning variance. This matter involved a challenge to a zoning variance granted by the city's board of adjustment. The appellants, neighboring property owners, contended that the variance allowed for commercial use in a residential zone that would negatively impact the neighborhood's character and property values. They argued that the applicant failed to meet the strict statutory requirements for a variance, specifically the showing of 'unnecessary hardship' unique to the property. The city and the applicant argued that the unique topography and existing structural limitations of the site made the residential use impracticable. The appellate court examined whether the board of adjustment's decision was supported by competent and substantial evidence. The court looked at whether the board correctly applied the hardship standard, which requires the applicant to demonstrate that the property cannot yield a reasonable return if restricted to the currently permitted use. The decision provides insight into the high burden placed on applicants seeking zoning deviations and the limited scope of judicial review over the quasi-judicial decisions made by municipal boards of adjustment.

## O'Brien v. Dailey

331 S.W.2d 121 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Kansas City · 1960 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that adverse possession requires possession that is continuous relative to the nature of the property, not necessarily constant. Paving and regular maintenance of a disputed driveway are strong indicators of adverse possession. The plaintiffs sought to quiet title to a strip of land that was historically used as part of their driveway. The defendant contended that the strip fell within their deeded boundary and that the plaintiffs' usage had only been permissive. The trial court found in favor of the plaintiffs on the grounds of adverse possession. Upon appeal, the court evaluated the nature of the plaintiffs' use. Evidence showed that the plaintiffs had paved the area, maintained it, and used it as their primary entrance for many years. The defendant argued that because the use was sporadic, it could not be considered 'continuous' for the purposes of adverse possession. The court rejected this

Second stored summary argument, noting that 'continuous' does not mean daily use but rather use that is consistent with the nature of the land and typical for the owner of such property. The court held that the plaintiffs' actions in paving and maintaining the driveway provided clear notice of an adverse claim to the entire world, including the defendant. Therefore, the requirements of open, notorious, exclusive, and hostile possession were fully met, entitling the plaintiffs to title via adverse possession.

## O'Brien v. Miller

605 S.W.3d 456 · Mo. App. W.D. · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that hazardous mold conditions can constitute a breach of the implied warranty of habitability if the landlord fails to remediate them after notice. The judgment was remanded for a re-evaluation of the habitability evidence. The landlord sought to evict the tenant based on the non-payment of rent, but the tenant raised an affirmative defense of breach of the implied warranty of habitability due to persistent mold issues. The tenant provided evidence that they had notified the landlord of the mold, but the landlord had failed to remediate the condition for several months. The trial court rejected the defense, finding the mold was not severe enough to render the unit legally uninhabitable. The appellate court reviewed the definition of 'habitability' in Missouri jurisprudence, focusing on whether a rental unit meets minimum standards for health and safety. The court found that the trial court applied an overly restrictive definition of habitability, excluding environmental hazards that are commonly recognized as health threats. The court remanded the case, holding that the presence of hazardous mold, if properly documented and notified to the landlord, constitutes a breach that can justify the withholding of rent or the termination of the lease by the tenant.

## O'Brien v. Missouri High School Activities Ass'n

395 S.W.3d 574 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while the conduct contract was a valid agreement, the association had substantially complied with its disciplinary procedures. It emphasized that courts will generally not interfere in the internal governance of such associations unless there is a clear violation of their own rules. This case arose from the decision of the Missouri High School Activities Association (MSHSAA) to suspend a student athlete for violating a student conduct contract. The athlete challenged the suspension, alleging that MSHSAA breached the contract by failing to follow the disciplinary procedures defined in its bylaws. The court evaluated whether the student-parent-school conduct agreement constituted a contract that was subject to judicial review. MSHSAA argued that its decisions regarding student eligibility and conduct were internal matters that should be afforded deference by the courts. The case involved an analysis of the association's governing documents and the extent to which they created contractual rights for student athletes. The court scrutinized the process afforded to the student and whether the association substantially complied with its own rules. This decision is an important precedent for the limits of judicial intervention in the disciplinary decisions of voluntary member organizations and athletic associations.

## O'Brien v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.

124 S.W.3d 24 · Mo. App. E.D. · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the insurance policy terms clearly allowed for the use of parts of 'like kind and quality' and therefore the insurer did not engage in deceptive practice. The court affirmed the summary judgment in favor of the insurer. Plaintiffs brought a class action lawsuit against an automobile insurer, alleging that the company violated the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA) and breached its contract by failing to disclose that it would be using aftermarket, non-OEM crash parts for repairs instead of original manufacturer parts. The plaintiffs argued that this practice was deceptive and that the resulting repairs were of inferior quality, thereby reducing the value of their vehicles. The insurer argued that its policies permitted the use of 'like kind and quality' parts and that there was no requirement to disclose the source of the parts as long as the repair met functional standards. The trial court granted summary judgment to the insurer. The appellate court reviewed the interpretation of the insurance contract and whether the insurer's failure to notify policyholders of the parts policy constituted an unfair practice. The case raised questions about the scope of the MPA regarding common business practices in the insurance industry and whether a lack of disclosure constitutes a 'deceptive act' when the contract allows for broad discretion in claim fulfillment.

## O'Connell v. Cindell

565 S.W.3d 244 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that short-term rental activity in a subdivision restricted to residential use violates covenants prohibiting commercial use. The court affirmed that such covenants are enforceable despite evolving rental platforms. This case involved a dispute between neighbors over the enforcement of restrictive covenants contained in a subdivision's indenture. The plaintiffs sought to enjoin the defendants from operating a short-term rental business, arguing that the neighborhood's residential-use-only covenant prohibited such commercial activity. The defendants countered that the covenant was ambiguous regarding short-term rentals and that the character of the neighborhood had changed sufficiently to render the covenant unenforceable. The trial court granted a permanent injunction, finding that the clear intent of the indenture was to preserve the residential nature of the subdivision and that short-term rentals constituted a commercial use. On appeal, the defendants challenged the interpretation of the term 'single-family residence.' The appellate court conducted a de novo review of the restrictive covenants, applying the principle that

Second stored summary covenants are strictly construed in favor of the free use of land, but must also give effect to the clear intent of the drafters. The court agreed with the trial court that the short-term rental model, characterized by high turnover and transient occupants, violated the restriction against commercial use. The ruling affirmed the injunction, underscoring that residential covenants remain enforceable even if technology or market trends change, provided the underlying purpose of the restriction remains valid and relevant to the neighborhood's character.

## O'Connor v. Acustar, Inc.

874 S.W.2d 426 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1994 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an employer does not breach a contract by modifying benefits if the plan documents contain an explicit reservation of the right to amend. Unambiguous clauses allowing modification prevail over general expectations of lifetime benefits. The plaintiffs were retired employees who sued their former employer, alleging that the employer breached a contract by failing to provide the level of retiree health benefits promised during their employment. The employer argued that the summary plan description allowed it to modify or terminate benefits at any time. The appellate court examined the contractual nature of employee benefits, focusing on whether the promise of lifetime benefits had vested. The court looked at the specific language of the plan documents and the communications provided to the employees. The appellate court held that the employer had reserved the right to amend the benefits in the plan summary, which was incorporated into the contract. Because the employer followed the amendment procedures outlined in the documents, the court found no breach of contract. The ruling emphasized the importance of reservation-of-rights clauses in benefit plans, noting that unless a specific promise of 'vested' or 'irrevocable' benefits is explicitly made, employers generally retain the flexibility to adjust benefits.

## O'Connor v. Donaldson

422 U.S. 563 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1975 · Federal

Holding: A state cannot constitutionally confine a non-dangerous individual who is capable of surviving safely in freedom. Mere status of mental illness is insufficient to justify long-term involuntary detention. Kenneth Donaldson was civilly committed to a state mental hospital for 15 years, despite the fact that he was not dangerous to himself or others and was capable of surviving safely in freedom. He sued the hospital director under Section 1983, claiming a violation of his constitutional right to liberty. The director argued he was immune from liability because he had acted in good faith based on state law. The Supreme Court held that a state cannot confine a non-dangerous individual who is capable of surviving safely in freedom by themselves or with the help of willing and responsible family members or friends. The Court ruled that simply possessing a mental illness is not a constitutional basis for state-sanctioned confinement. This case established a high constitutional threshold for the civil commitment of individuals, reinforcing the principle that government power over liberty is strictly limited and must be supported by a legitimate state interest, such as safety. The ruling also underscored that state officials are not shielded by good faith when they violate clearly understood and fundamental constitutional rights.

## O'Connor v. Quigley

526 S.W.3d 176 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: Restrictive covenants are strictly construed and unenforceable if ambiguous. A covenant limiting view obstruction must clearly define what constitutes an infringement to be valid. This case focused on the interpretation of a restrictive covenant prohibiting the construction of structures that block a neighbor's view. A property owner built an addition that significantly obscured their neighbor's view of a nearby lake. The neighbor sued, seeking an injunction to remove the addition, citing the restrictive covenant attached to the neighborhood deeds. The appellate court examined the covenant's language, specifically whether it was drafted with sufficient clarity to be enforceable as an equitable servitude. The court concluded that the covenant was too vague and ambiguous to be enforced, as it failed to define what constituted a 'view' or what degree of obstruction would be considered a violation. In Missouri, restrictive covenants are strictly construed and will not be enforced if they are ambiguous. Therefore, the court reversed the trial court's order requiring the addition to be dismantled, as the covenant did not clearly prohibit the structure in question. The case highlights the necessity of clear, precise drafting for restrictive covenants to be effective.

## O'Dell v. General Motors Corp.

122 S.W.3d 41 (Mo. App. W.D. 2003) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment for the defendant. The court found that the plaintiff failed to present sufficient evidence that the vehicle's design was unreasonably dangerous or that the alleged design defect caused the fire. The evidence did not satisfy the burden of proof under the risk-utility analysis.

Second stored summary This product liability action concerned a vehicle fire allegedly caused by a design defect in the engine compartment. The plaintiff alleged that the placement of certain components and materials made the vehicle unreasonably dangerous and prone to fire. The defendant manufacturer argued that the design was reasonable and safe, and that the plaintiff had not proven causation. The court applied the risk-utility test, requiring the plaintiff to show that the risks of the design outweighed its benefits. The feasibility and cost of alternative designs were considered.

## O'Donnell v. Delux Public Charter, LLC

537 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the state-law MPA claims were preempted by the federal Airline Deregulation Act because they directly addressed the carrier's services and refund policies. It affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the claims. The plaintiffs sought to bring a class action against an air charter company for allegedly deceptive practices related to the cancellation of flights and the refusal to issue refunds as promised in their promotional materials. The company argued that the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 preempted the plaintiffs' state-law MPA claims. The trial court dismissed the action based on preemption. The court of appeals engaged in a detailed analysis of whether the MPA claims related to 'rates, routes, or services' of an air carrier. The court noted that while the federal law is preemptive, it does not bar states from enforcing general consumer protection laws against deceptive marketing that does not touch upon the core economic deregulation policies of the airline industry. However, in this instance, the court determined that the plaintiffs' claims were too closely tied to the carrier's service delivery and refund policies. The case serves as an important limitation on the reach of the MPA when it encounters federal laws governing specific industries. It illustrates the ongoing tension between state-level consumer protections and federal regulatory frameworks that seek to unify standards for interstate or national commerce.

## O'Donnell v. Fidelity & General Insurance Co.

104 S.W.3d 426 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an insurer's duty to defend is limited to claims that potentially fall within the definition of 'advertising injury.' If the alleged actions do not constitute an advertising activity, the insurer is not obligated to defend. The insured sought coverage for legal fees incurred in a separate litigation, arguing that the insurer had a duty to defend under the 'advertising injury' clause of a commercial general liability (CGL) policy. The underlying claim involved allegations of trade libel and disparagement. The insurer denied coverage, claiming the allegations did not fall within the definition of 'advertising injury.' The trial court granted summary judgment for the insurer. On appeal, the court examined the definition of 'advertising injury' in the policy. It found that for an injury to be covered, there must be a causal connection between the advertising activity and the harm suffered. The court concluded that the underlying lawsuit's allegations did not sufficiently describe a form of advertising activity, as the conduct occurred in private negotiations rather than public marketing. Therefore, the insurer's duty to defend was not triggered. The court's analysis focused on whether the specific acts alleged in the petition were within the policy's defined scope of coverage. Finding that they were not, the court affirmed the denial of coverage, holding that the insurer's duty to defend is limited to claims that arguably fall within the policy's scope.

## O'Donnell v. Fidelity Gen. Ins. Co.

394 S.W.2d 459 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Kansas City · 1965 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the insurer failed to meet its burden of proving that the insured's lack of cooperation caused actual prejudice to the defense. The insurer remained liable to pay the judgment. This case involved a conflict between an insurer and a third-party claimant following a judgment against the insured for a car accident. The injured party sought to collect the judgment from the insurer, but the insurer denied coverage, arguing that the insured had failed to cooperate as required by the policy's 'cooperation clause.' The insurer contended that the insured had provided contradictory statements and had disappeared before the trial, making it impossible to prepare an adequate defense. The claimant argued that the insurer had not exercised sufficient diligence in attempting to locate the insured. The court analyzed the burden of proof required for an insurer to prove a breach of the cooperation clause and the necessity of showing actual prejudice to the insurer's defense. The decision established the high threshold an insurer must meet to avoid its obligations based on the non-cooperation of the insured, emphasizing that mere lack of communication is not sufficient without evidence that the insurer was substantially harmed.

## O'Donnell v. Fidelity General Ins. Co.

371 S.W.3d 810 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the policy was not ambiguous and that the insurer complied with necessary disclosure requirements. The 'claims-made' nature of the policy was clearly defined within the contract, and no reformation was required. This matter involved a medical malpractice policy and a dispute over the 'claims-made' versus 'occurrence' nature of the coverage. The physician insured had been sued for malpractice, but the suit was filed after the policy had expired. The insurer denied coverage, relying on the fact that the policy was a 'claims-made' policy and no claim had been made during the policy period or the extended reporting period. The plaintiff argued that the policy was ambiguous because the declaration page did not prominently display the 'claims-made' nature of the coverage, which allegedly led to a reasonable expectation of continuous coverage. The court reviewed the requirements for 'claims-made' policies in Missouri, particularly the disclosure requirements designed to ensure that insureds are fully aware of the limitations of their coverage. The appellate court assessed whether the policy's formatting complied with regulatory standards and whether the absence of a 'claims-made' notice on the declaration page warranted reformation of the contract to provide

Second stored summary occurrence-based coverage.

## O'Donnell v. Fidelity National Title Insurance Co.

430 S.W.3d 269 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that whether a bonus constitutes a wage depends on the specific terms of the employment contract and whether the employee has met all conditions precedent. A clear 'active employment' requirement is enforceable and prevents recovery of a bonus by an employee who leaves before the payment date. O'Donnell focused on whether a bonus payment plan created a binding wage obligation under Missouri law. The plaintiff was terminated before the bonus payout date and sued for a pro-rata portion of the bonus, arguing it was an earned wage. The employer argued that the bonus was discretionary and subject to an 'active employment' requirement at the time of payout. The court evaluated the contract language governing the bonus program to determine if it was a contractually guaranteed wage or a discretionary gift. The decision discusses the importance of clear, unambiguous language in bonus plans. The court emphasized that if the employer makes the bonus a condition of employment through a written policy, it may be treated as a wage that vests as the work is performed. This case provides guidance for employers on how to draft bonus agreements to retain discretion while also warning employees about the specific contractual hurdles they face when attempting to recover 'earned' bonuses after separation from their company.

## O'Donnell v. Kitchen Aid, Inc.

531 S.W.3d 591 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The existence of a limited warranty does not preclude a claim under the MPA for deceptive practices occurring at the time of purchase. Pre-purchase fraud is actionable regardless of the terms of a subsequent product warranty. The plaintiff purchased a high-end appliance manufactured by the defendant. Following repeated failures of the appliance to function as advertised, the plaintiff filed an action under the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA), alleging that the defendant knowingly made false claims regarding the quality and durability of the product. The defendant contended that the product came with a limited warranty, which was the exclusive remedy available to the consumer, and that the MPA claim was an attempt to circumvent the contractual limits of that warranty. The trial court granted summary judgment for the manufacturer. On appeal, the Court of Appeals considered whether an express warranty limits the ability to sue under the MPA. The court held that the existence of a warranty does not bar an MPA claim when the consumer alleges that the merchant engaged in deceptive practices before the purchase. The court explained that the MPA addresses the deception that induced the purchase, whereas the warranty addresses the performance of the product. Because the plaintiff presented evidence of deceptive advertising, the court reversed the summary judgment, finding that the consumer's right to pursue an MPA claim for pre-purchase deception is independent of the contractual remedies provided by a warranty.

## O'Donnell v. PNK (River City), LLC

619 S.W.3d 136 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The open and obvious doctrine does not provide a complete defense in Missouri premises liability cases. Comparative fault principles apply when both the landowner and the invitee potentially contributed to the hazardous situation. O'Donnell sought damages for injuries sustained while visiting a casino owned by PNK. The plaintiff fell while walking on a walkway that she claimed was improperly illuminated and lacked adequate warning signs regarding a elevation change. The trial court granted summary judgment for the casino, arguing that the condition was open and obvious and that the plaintiff was contributorily negligent for failing to look where she was stepping. The appellate court reviewed the application of the open and obvious doctrine in light of recent Missouri jurisprudence, which limits the doctrine's application in negligence cases. The court determined that even if a condition is open and obvious, it does not act as a total bar to recovery if the landowner should have anticipated the harm. The appellate court remanded the case, holding that the jury must weigh the defendant's failure to maintain safe premises against the plaintiff's own failure to observe the path, applying comparative fault principles rather than a complete bar to liability.

## O'Donnell v. St. Louis Public Service Co.

246 S.W.2d 777 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1952 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that common carriers owe the highest degree of care to their passengers. It found that the jury was correctly instructed to determine if the driver's actions met this heightened standard. The plaintiff was injured as a passenger on a public bus when the driver stopped suddenly, causing the plaintiff to be thrown from her seat. The case involved the 'common carrier' duty of care. The bus company argued that the stop was necessary to avoid a collision, thus excusing the driver's conduct under the 'emergency doctrine.' The plaintiff argued that the driver's speed and failure to maintain a safe distance made the stop foreseeable and negligent. The court examined the standard of care for common carriers, which is the 'highest degree of care.' This case illustrates the high threshold required of public transportation providers to avoid liability for passenger injuries, distinguishing between unavoidable accidents and those caused by the failure to operate vehicles with the necessary level of caution required of common carriers.

## O'Malley v. Kroll

947 S.W.2d 147 (Mo. App. E.D. 1997) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment for the O'Malleys. The court held that the evidence supported a finding that Kroll knew or should have known about the serious latent defects in the property and failed to disclose them to the buyers. The court applied the principle that sellers have a duty to disclose material defects that are not readily observable by the buyer. The court found sufficient evidence of intentional concealment or misrepresentation, justifying the award of damages. This case involved a dispute over an alleged fraudulent misrepresentation in the sale of a residential property. The O'Malleys purchased a home from Kroll. After the sale, the O'Malleys discovered significant foundation issues and water intrusion problems that they claimed were not disclosed by Kroll at the time of sale. They sued Kroll for fraudulent misrepresentation and concealment, seeking damages for the cost of repairs and diminution in property value. Kroll denied intentionally misleading the buyers, asserting that he was unaware of the full extent of the problems or that the issues were patent. The trial court found that Kroll had failed to disclose known latent defects.

## O'Neal v. St. Louis County

165 F.3d 625 · United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit · 1999 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a municipality is not liable under Section 1983 simply for failing to discipline officers unless that failure rises to the level of an official policy or custom that causes the violation. The evidence presented was insufficient to establish such a causal link. O'Neal filed a Section 1983 suit against St. Louis County and individual officers following an arrest where he was allegedly subjected to excessive force. The key issue was whether the county could be held liable under a theory of 'custom or practice' (Monell liability) for failing to discipline officers who had a history of excessive force complaints. The plaintiff argued that the county's inaction fostered an environment where officers felt empowered to use force unlawfully. The court analyzed whether there was evidence that the county's failure to discipline officers constituted a policy that directly caused the constitutional violation. The court found that while the plaintiff showed a history of prior complaints, there was no showing that the county's disciplinary review process was so deficient as to constitute a tacit endorsement of excessive force. Thus, the court affirmed the grant of summary judgment for the county, maintaining that Section 1983 liability for municipalities requires a direct link between an established, deliberate policy and the constitutional harm suffered.

## O'Neal v. Stifel, Nicolaus & Co.

996 S.W.2d 570 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1999 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the brokerage firm acted within the scope of its authority under the signed client agreement. The court ruled that the contract, which provided the firm with discretionary authority, precluded the investor's breach of contract claim regarding the specific trades in question. This case involved a dispute between an investor and a brokerage firm regarding the handling of a trading account. The investor alleged that the firm breached the client agreement by executing unauthorized trades and failing to manage the account in accordance with the investor's stated risk tolerance. The firm argued that the customer signed a standard brokerage agreement that granted them broad discretion and included a mandatory arbitration clause. The case centers on the interpretation of standard-form client agreements in the financial services industry. The court examined the scope of 'discretionary' accounts and the fiduciary duties owed by brokers, balanced against the explicit contractual terms that limited the firm's liability. This decision highlights the enforceability of standardized industry agreements and the challenges investors face in proving breach of contract when the underlying agreement grants the brokerage firm significant leeway. The court's analysis focuses on whether the broker's conduct exceeded the authority granted in the signed document, illustrating the importance of specific trading instructions over general verbal understandings.

## O'Neil v. Schnucks Markets

650 S.W.3d 390 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of benefits, holding that the claimant was not in the course of his employment. The court ruled that a personal errand during a lunch break constitutes a deviation that suspends workers' compensation coverage. The claimant was injured while using a company vehicle to run a personal errand during a lunch break. The employer contested the claim, arguing that the claimant was off the clock and on a 'frolic and detour' that removed him from the scope of his employment. The Commission denied benefits, agreeing that the lunch break, coupled with the personal nature of the errand, meant the injury did not arise out of and in the course of employment. The claimant appealed, arguing that he was on call during his lunch and that his use of the company vehicle was a benefit intended to facilitate work. The appellate court evaluated the 'arising out of' and 'in the course of' requirements. The court found that the injury occurred during a clear deviation for personal business that had no connection to the employer's interest. Therefore, the injury was not compensable under Missouri law.

## O'Reilly Automotive, Inc. v. Director of Revenue

992 S.W.2d 881 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1999 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the equipment used by the taxpayer did not meet the definition of manufacturing or processing machinery. The refund request was denied because the activities were purely distributive. O'Reilly Automotive, Inc. sought a refund of sales tax paid on equipment used in its distribution center. The central issue was whether the equipment qualified for the manufacturing and processing machinery exemption. The taxpayer argued that the automated sorting systems and conveyors performed a 'processing' function essential to their inventory management, thereby falling within the scope of the tax exemption for manufacturing machinery. The Director of Revenue argued that the taxpayer's activities were merely warehousing and distribution, which are not considered 'manufacturing' or 'processing' under Missouri law. The Administrative Hearing Commission agreed with the Director, finding that the taxpayer was not engaging in the production of tangible personal property. O'Reilly appealed to the Missouri Supreme Court, asking for a broader interpretation of the processing exemption to include modern logistics equipment. The court reviewed the legislative definition of 'processing' and its applicability to the business of wholesale distribution. The court examined whether the act of organizing and sorting goods constitutes a value-added service or a change in the form or substance of the product that would trigger the processing exemption. The case provides key guidance on the limits of manufacturing exemptions for logistics and distribution companies.

## O'Reilly Automotive, Inc. v. Director of Revenue

99 S.W.3d 468 · Missouri Supreme Court · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the taxpayer did not meet the criteria for the contractor exemption because it did not structure the purchase of materials as an agent of an exempt entity. Tax was properly assessed. O'Reilly Automotive appealed an assessment involving the applicability of use tax to materials used in the construction of its corporate facilities. The company argued that the materials were purchased by a contractor under a contract that should have been treated as an exempt transaction. The Director of Revenue contended that the taxpayer was the ultimate purchaser and that the exemption did not apply to the specific materials used in the construction project. The case focused on the 'contractor exemption' and the extent to which entities can structure construction contracts to minimize tax liability through the use of exempt entities. The court examined the requirements for contractors to act as agents of exempt organizations and the necessity of documenting these relationships to qualify for tax-free status. The decision provided clarity on how businesses can properly manage their tax obligations when undertaking large-scale construction projects using external contractors.

## Ohio v. American Express Co.

585 U.S. 529 · U.S. Supreme Court · 2018 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that credit card networks are two-sided platforms, and antitrust claims must account for both sides of the market. The plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the anti-steering provisions unreasonably restrained trade in the relevant market. This antitrust dispute centered on credit card 'anti-steering' provisions, which prevented merchants from incentivizing customers to use cards with lower transaction fees. The central issue was whether credit card networks should be treated as 'two-sided platforms' where competitive effects must be evaluated on both the merchant and the consumer side. The district court found that American Express's provisions restricted competition among credit card companies, but the Supreme Court disagreed, ruling that the market must be viewed as a single, two-sided transaction platform. The Court held that the plaintiffs failed to prove the anti-steering provisions caused net harm because they did not provide evidence of reduced output or increased prices across the entire platform. By focusing on the integrated nature of the two-sided market, the Court established a significant precedent that complicates antitrust claims against platforms that balance the interests of two distinct sets of users simultaneously, requiring a broader analysis of competitive effects across both sides of the market.

## Ohio v. American Express Co.

838 F.3d 179 · Second Circuit · 2016 · Federal

Holding: The court held that the anti-steering provisions did not violate Section 1 of the Sherman Act. It concluded that the plaintiffs failed to show competitive harm to the entire two-sided platform market. This case involved a challenge to American Express's 'anti-steering' provisions in its merchant contracts, which prevented merchants from encouraging customers to use other, lower-cost credit cards. The State of Ohio and several others argued these provisions violated Section 1 of the Sherman Act by restraining price competition among credit card networks. The district court initially ruled for the plaintiffs, finding that the anti-steering provisions caused anticompetitive harm in the market for network services. On appeal, the Second Circuit reversed, holding that the relevant market included both sides of the two-sided credit card platform--the cardholder side and the merchant side. The court reasoned that because American Express operates a two-sided transaction platform, one cannot determine the anticompetitive effect of its rules without analyzing the impact on both sides of the market simultaneously. Since the plaintiffs failed to prove net harm to the entire two-sided platform, they could not demonstrate an antitrust violation. The Supreme Court later affirmed this 'two-sided market' analysis, cementing the precedent that antitrust harm in platform markets must consider the interdependencies between distinct sets of users and the indirect network effects present in those business models.

## Ohio v. United States Dept. of the Interior

880 F.2d 432 · United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit · 1989 · Federal

Holding: The court held that the DOI's reliance on 'market value' to calculate damages for natural resources was inconsistent with CERCLA. The ruling required the inclusion of non-market valuation methodologies to better reflect the full value of the damaged resources. This case challenged the Department of the Interior's (DOI) regulations regarding the assessment of natural resource damages under CERCLA. The state of Ohio, along with several environmental groups, challenged the DOI's rule that prioritized 'market value' as the measure of damages for lost natural resources. The plaintiffs argued that market value often fails to capture the true ecological and recreational value of the environment. The D.C. Circuit agreed with the plaintiffs, striking down the regulation and holding that the DOI must allow for the use of 'contingent valuation' and other methodologies that account for non-market values. The court emphasized that the goal of CERCLA was to ensure that the environment is fully restored, not just compensated for at the lowest market price. This decision forced the government to revise its assessment procedures to include more comprehensive valuation methods for natural resource damages, which remains a cornerstone of federal environmental damage litigation.

## Oil States Energy Services, LLC v. Greene's Energy Group, LLC

584 U.S. 325 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2018 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that IPRs are constitutional and do not violate Article III or the Seventh Amendment. The adjudication of patent validity in administrative proceedings is a permissible exercise of congressional power regarding public rights. Oil States challenged the constitutionality of the Inter Partes Review (IPR) process, arguing that the cancellation of patent claims by an administrative agency (the PTAB) violated Article III of the Constitution and the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial. Oil States contended that patent validity is a private property right that can only be adjudicated by a court of law. The Supreme Court rejected this argument, ruling that the grant of a patent is a 'public franchise' and that the government has the authority to revisit the grant of a patent through administrative proceedings. The Court held that Congress has the power to assign the adjudication of patent validity to an administrative agency because it involves public rights. This decision confirmed the constitutionality of IPR proceedings, ensuring that the PTAB remains a legitimate mechanism for challenging patent validity outside of federal district courts, which helps to maintain the quality of the patent system by filtering out improperly granted patents.

## Olmstead v. L.C. ex rel. Zimring

527 U.S. 581 · United States Supreme Court · 1999 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the ADA's integration mandate requires states to provide community-based treatment for persons with disabilities when such placement is appropriate, the affected persons do not oppose such treatment, and the state's resources allow for it. Unjustified institutionalization constitutes discrimination under the ADA. Two women with mental disabilities were confined in a state-run psychiatric institution in Georgia, even though their treatment professionals determined that they could be appropriately cared for in a community-based program. The state continued to keep them in the institution, citing budget constraints and administrative concerns. The women filed suit under the Americans with Disabilities Act

Second stored summary (ADA), arguing that their continued confinement in the hospital rather than a community setting constituted unlawful discrimination based on their disabilities. Georgia contended that the ADA did not require the state to reorganize its service delivery system or allocate limited funding to provide community-based care, particularly when the state had its own interest in institutional management. The case forced the Supreme Court to interpret the integration mandate of the ADA in the context of state-provided healthcare and housing services for individuals with disabilities.

## Omnicare, Inc. v. Laborers District Council Construction Industry Pension Fund

575 U.S. 175 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2015 · Federal

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that a statement of opinion is not actionable simply because it turns out to be incorrect. Liability only arises if the speaker did not genuinely believe the opinion, or if the speaker omitted material facts about the basis for the opinion that would make it misleading to a reasonable investor. This case further refined the rules regarding statements of opinion in securities filings. Omnicare had included statements in a registration statement asserting that its legal arrangements were in compliance with federal and state law. When it turned out that the company was under investigation for violations, investors sued, claiming the statement of legal compliance was a material misrepresentation. The lower courts struggled with whether an opinion--such as an opinion about legal compliance--could be considered 'false' if it turned out to be legally incorrect. The Supreme Court clarified the standard for liability for statements of opinion, explaining that an issuer is not liable for an opinion that turns out to be wrong, provided the issuer genuinely believed the statement at the time and had a reasonable basis for it. However, the Court also established that an investor could potentially claim that a statement of opinion omitted material facts regarding the basis for that opinion, rendering the statement misleading.

## Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services, Inc.

523 U.S. 75 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1998 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: Same-sex sexual harassment is actionable under Title VII. The key factor is whether the harassment occurred because of the victim's sex, regardless of the genders involved. Joseph Oncale was subjected to sex-related humiliation and assault by his male coworkers and supervisors on an offshore oil rig. He sued under Title VII for sexual harassment. The lower courts dismissed the claim, reasoning that Title VII did not cover same-sex harassment. The Supreme Court unanimously reversed, ruling that Title VII's prohibition of discrimination 'because of... sex' applies to same-sex harassment. The Court reasoned that the statute does not discriminate based on the gender of the harasser or the victim, but focuses on whether the harassment occurred because of the victim's sex. The ruling established that as long as the harassment is sufficiently severe or pervasive, it violates the statute regardless of whether the perpetrator and victim are of the same or opposite sex. This case expanded the reach of Title VII to ensure that sexual harassment protection is not limited by gender dynamics, but rather by the nature of the misconduct and its impact on the work environment.

## Orchard Container Corp. v. Ford Motor Co.

107 S.W.3d 232 (Mo. App. E.D. 2003) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's judgment and remanded the case for a new trial. The court found that the trial court erred in excluding evidence of prior similar incidents involving fires in similar Ford trucks, as this evidence was relevant to establishing a design or manufacturing defect and Ford's notice of potential problems. The court determined that the excluded evidence was crucial for Orchard to prove its case against Ford. This case involved a commercial trucking company, Orchard Container Corp., that sued Ford Motor Company after one of its Ford trucks caught fire and was destroyed. Orchard alleged that the fire was caused by a defect in the truck's engine or electrical system, constituting a breach of warranty and strict product liability. They sought damages for the loss of the truck and lost profits. Ford argued that the fire was not caused by a manufacturing defect but by improper maintenance, misuse, or an unrelated external cause. The trial court excluded certain evidence related to prior similar incidents and ultimately entered judgment for Ford. Orchard appealed.

## Orf v. American Honda Motor Co.

365 S.W.3d 611 (Mo. App. W.D. 2012) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the plaintiff's claims. The court found that the plaintiff did not present sufficient evidence to establish that the motorcycle suffered from a manufacturing defect or that any such defect caused the accident. The evidence offered was considered too speculative to prove causation. This case involved injuries sustained when a motorcycle malfunctioned. The plaintiff alleged that the motorcycle contained a manufacturing defect that caused it to accelerate uncontrollably, leading to an accident. The defendant manufacturer argued that the plaintiff's evidence of the defect was speculative and insufficient to establish causation. The court reviewed the standard for proving a manufacturing defect, including the need for evidence that the specific product purchased deviated from the manufacturer's intended design. The burden of proof on the plaintiff to link the alleged defect to their injuries was a key focus.

## Overland v. City of St. Louis

569 S.W.3d 1 · Mo. Ct. App. E.D. · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the city was not required to pay overtime for the specific donning and doffing activities at issue, finding them to be non-compensable under the circumstances. The court emphasized the importance of collective bargaining agreements in defining the scope of work hours. This case involved a dispute over whether municipal employees were entitled to overtime compensation under the Missouri Minimum Wage Law (MMWL) for pre-shift and post-shift activities. The plaintiffs were city workers who claimed that the time spent donning and doffing mandatory safety equipment constituted compensable work hours. The City of St. Louis argued that such activities were preliminary and postliminary actions not subject to overtime pay under established municipal ordinances and collective bargaining agreements. The appellate court analyzed whether the state law provisions on wage payment preempted local ordinances or if the city had discretion in defining 'hours worked' for its employees. The legal discussion heavily leaned on federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) interpretations as guidance for state law applications, as the MMWL often mirrors federal statutes. The court examined whether the nature of the tasks performed by the employees was integral and indispensable to their primary job functions.

## Owen v. Gamble

234 S.W.3d 595 · Mo. App. E.D. · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the MPA does not apply to private residential real estate sales between individual parties. Consequently, the court reversed the portion of the judgment awarding damages under the MPA but affirmed the fraud-based claims. The dispute involved a contract for the purchase and sale of residential real estate. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants, who were the sellers, engaged in fraud and violated the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA) by failing to disclose significant structural defects in the home prior to the closing. The plaintiffs sought rescission of the contract and damages for the cost of repairs. The trial court found in favor of the plaintiffs, determining that the sellers' failure to disclose known water intrusion issues constituted a material omission. On appeal, the defendants challenged the application of the MPA to this specific real estate transaction, arguing that the statute was not intended to cover private residential sales between individuals. The court examined the definition of 'merchandise' under the MPA and whether the sale of a private residence constitutes a sale of 'goods or services' within the meaning of the act. The discussion also addressed the sufficiency of evidence regarding the defendants' knowledge of the defects at the time of the sale and whether their silence constituted a deceptive act intended to induce the sale.

## Owen v. General Motors Corp.

533 S.W.3d 213 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that a manufacturer may be liable under the MPA for the omission of a material fact, such as a known defect, if the omission was intended to induce the consumer to purchase the vehicle. It concluded that the evidence was sufficient to withstand summary judgment. The plaintiff purchased a vehicle that was allegedly subject to a secret defect known to the manufacturer but undisclosed to the public. When the vehicle experienced mechanical failure, the plaintiff brought an MPA claim, asserting that the manufacturer's failure to disclose the defect at the time of sale was an unfair practice. General Motors argued that the MPA does not impose a duty to disclose latent defects unless the manufacturer has a specific intent to deceive. The court examined the standard for 'unfairness' under the MPA and the duty of a manufacturer to warn consumers about potential safety or mechanical issues. The case is significant for its analysis of the 'duty to disclose' and whether the silence of a manufacturer regarding known product flaws constitutes an actionable deception under the MPA in the context of motor vehicle sales.

## Owen v. General Motors Corp.

533 F.3d 913 · United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit · 2008 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that to maintain a private action under the MPA, a plaintiff must demonstrate an ascertainable loss of money or property. It affirmed that the loss must be linked to the defendant's deceptive practice at the time of the transaction. A consumer filed an action alleging that General Motors violated the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA) by failing to disclose that certain vehicles were equipped with ignition switches prone to failure. The plaintiff claimed that had the defect been disclosed, they would not have purchased the vehicle. The defendant moved to dismiss, arguing that the plaintiff failed to show a causal connection between the alleged deceptive omission and their purchase decision, and that the defect did not manifest during the period of ownership. The appellate court examined the standard for establishing an 'ascertainable loss' under the MPA. It noted that the plaintiff must prove that they suffered a loss of money or property as a direct result of the defendant's unlawful practice. The court analyzed whether a 'benefit of the bargain' theory was sufficient to establish such a loss. The court concluded that the plaintiff must show that the actual value of the product was less than the value of the product as represented at the time of the sale, and that this difference in value constitutes the ascertainable loss required by the statute for a private cause of action.

## Owners Insurance Company v. Craig

514 S.W.3d 655 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that clear and unambiguous animal liability exclusions in a homeowner's insurance policy are fully enforceable. Courts will not create ambiguity where none exists to provide coverage for claims specifically excluded by the contract. The insurer, Owners Insurance, filed a declaratory judgment action to determine whether it owed coverage for a dog-bite incident occurring at a residential property. The homeowners policy included a liability section, but the insurer argued that an 'animal liability' exclusion barred recovery for injuries caused by the insured's dog. The insured argued that the exclusion was ambiguous or did not apply because the incident occurred in a specific context not contemplated by the policy's exclusionary language. The circuit court held that the exclusion was clear and unambiguous, granting summary judgment in favor of the insurer. On appeal, the court looked at the plain meaning of the policy text, which explicitly excluded bodily injury caused by animals. The insured's attempt to introduce extrinsic evidence to create ambiguity failed, as the court found the language of the exclusion to be standard and comprehensive. The court affirmed the lower court's ruling, emphasizing that when policy language is clear, the court must enforce it as written, even if the result is harsh for the insured party.

## P & K Invs., Inc. v. Mid-Am. Bank & Tr. Co.

491 S.W.3d 286 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a foreclosure sale conducted in accordance with statutory notice requirements cannot be set aside for price inadequacy alone. The plaintiff failed to establish fraud or significant procedural error. The dispute concerned the priority of liens on a commercial property. The plaintiff, a junior lienholder, sued to challenge the foreclosure sale conducted by the defendant, a senior lienholder. The plaintiff argued that the senior lender had failed to provide adequate notice of the foreclosure sale to junior interests, thereby invalidating the auction. Furthermore, the plaintiff contended that the sale price was grossly inadequate, which, when combined with procedural irregularities, should justify setting aside the foreclosure. The bank argued that it had followed all statutory notice requirements and that the low price was a result of the market conditions, not a defect in the sale process. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the bank. On appeal, the court examined whether the bank had strictly complied with the notice statutes. The appellate court found that while the bank complied with the literal requirements, the discrepancy in the sale price relative to the property value was indeed striking. However, the court ruled that without evidence of fraud or collusion, a court cannot set aside a foreclosure solely on the basis of a low purchase price, provided the statutory procedures were followed correctly.
