## Ports Petroleum Co. of Ohio v. Nixon

37 S.W.3d 237 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2001 · Missouri

Also captioned Ports Petroleum Co. v. Nixon

Holding: The Court held that the Attorney General has broad authority under the MPA to issue CIDs to investigate potential deceptive acts. It ruled that the statutory definition of trade or commerce encompasses the challenged pricing activities. This matter involved an investigation by the Missouri Attorney General into the pricing and supply practices of a gasoline retailer. The retailer challenged the Attorney General's civil investigative demand (CID), arguing that the MPA did not authorize the investigation of fuel pricing under the circumstances presented. The court had to determine the extent of the Attorney General's investigative power under the MPA. The court examined whether the act of price setting constituted an 'unfair practice' and whether the Attorney General could demand documents related to business practices that were not strictly 'sales.' The court concluded that the MPA grants the Attorney General broad authority to investigate potential violations in the interest of the public. The decision affirmed the expansive reach of the Attorney General's office, reinforcing that the statutory language of the MPA is intentionally broad to encompass evolving market behaviors that could harm Missouri consumers. This case is frequently cited for the authority of the state to scrutinize business practices that might seem legal on their face but function as deceptive, anticompetitive, or unfair conduct within the consumer market.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that the MPA does not authorize the state to regulate fuel pricing as a standalone economic practice. It clarified that an MPA claim requires evidence of a deceptive act, not merely evidence of aggressive or predatory pricing. The Attorney General initiated an investigation into the pricing practices of a fuel retailer, suspecting predatory pricing in violation of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA). The retailer filed for an injunction to stop the investigation, arguing that the MPA did not apply to fuel pricing and that the state lacked the authority to regulate prices under this statute. The court examined the legislative history and scope of the MPA. It determined that the Act was intended to address unfair practices that deceive consumers, but it was not intended to be a general price-control mechanism. The court held that predatory pricing does not constitute a 'deceptive' practice per se under the MPA unless there is an element of misrepresentation or trickery involved in the sale. The court drew a distinction between fair market competition involving aggressive pricing and the deceptive practices the MPA was designed to prevent. This ruling limited the state's power to use the MPA as a tool to regulate competitive pricing levels, requiring evidence of specific deceptive conduct.

## Pratt v. Vatterott

460 S.W.3d 435 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the denial of benefits. It held that the event was voluntary and not within the scope of employment, thus not subject to workers' compensation coverage.

Second stored summary The claimant sustained injuries during a company-sponsored event held after hours. The commission denied benefits, finding the event was voluntary and not within the scope of employment. The claimant argued that his attendance was effectively required and that he was performing a service that benefited the employer. The employer countered that the event was purely social and held outside the normal scope of work duties. The court analyzed the 'course and scope' test, focusing on whether the activity served the employer's interests or whether the employer exercised control over the employee during the event. The opinion discussed the 'dual purpose' doctrine and whether the activity fell under the 'recreational or social activities' exclusion in the Workers' Compensation Law. The court evaluated whether the claimant's presence provided a tangible benefit to the business or if it was merely a social gathering. The decision emphasized that when an activity is voluntary, the burden is on the claimant to prove that attendance was inherently linked to their work responsibilities or company advancement.

## Prewitt v. State of Missouri

399 S.W.3d 810 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the public policy exception is narrowly construed and requires a clear mandate of law. Public employees must demonstrate that their actions directly relate to a specific legal obligation to overcome at-will employment status. This case involved a former state employee who claimed he was wrongfully terminated in retaliation for his advocacy regarding state department policies. The state argued that as an at-will government employee, his termination was not subject to the same protections as private sector workers in certain contexts. The court addressed the intersection of the public policy exception and government employment. The plaintiff alleged that his actions served the public interest and that his termination was a violation of his constitutional rights, specifically citing free speech protections. The court examined whether the public policy exception applies to the state as an employer in the same way it applies to private entities. It determined that while public employees have some constitutional protections, they must still align their actions with clear legal mandates if they seek to utilize the public policy exception to avoid the consequences of at-will termination. The court found that the plaintiff's activities did not fall into the specific, narrow categories required for a public policy exception claim and that the termination was consistent with the employer's discretion in managing personnel. The case reaffirmed the narrow scope of wrongful termination claims in the public sector when clear statutory violations are not at issue.

## Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins

490 U.S. 228 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1989 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: In a mixed-motive case, an employer can avoid liability by proving they would have made the same employment decision absent the discriminatory motive. The burden of proof shifts to the employer once the plaintiff shows discrimination was a motivating factor. Ann Hopkins was a senior manager at Price Waterhouse who was denied partnership. Despite her record of billable hours, she was told she needed a 'course at charm school' and that she acted too masculine. She sued, claiming sex discrimination under Title VII. The case reached the Supreme Court, which examined the 'mixed-motive' framework. The Court held that when an employee proves that gender played a motivating part in an employment decision, the employer may avoid liability only by proving by a preponderance of the evidence that it would have made the same decision even if it had not taken the gender factor into account. This decision clarified how courts should handle cases where both legitimate and discriminatory motives exist. While the Civil Rights Act of 1991 later modified the remedial aspects of this ruling, the core legal principle regarding mixed motives remains a central component of Title VII litigation.

## Probasco v. Hubbell

538 S.W.3d 374 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the MPA applies to private sellers and that a failure to disclose a known latent defect can constitute a deceptive practice. The trial court's grant of summary judgment for the defendant was reversed. The plaintiffs purchased a used boat and later discovered that it had been significantly damaged and repaired in a manner that was not disclosed. They filed a claim under the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA), alleging that the seller engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by concealing the history of the boat. The seller argued that the sale was 'as-is' and that the disclosure of defects was not required by law, especially in a private transaction. The court examined whether the MPA applies to private sellers. The court clarified that the MPA applies to 'any person' who engages in deceptive acts in connection with the sale of merchandise. The court rejected the argument that the seller was exempt simply because they were not a professional dealer. The key issue was whether the silence or concealment of a material fact constituted an unfair practice. The court held that if a seller has superior knowledge of a latent defect and fails to disclose it, such silence can be deceptive under the MPA, regardless of the 'as-is' status of the contract.

## Progressive Northwestern Insurance Co. v. Brannan

632 S.W.3d 456 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that there was no evidence of implied permission, as the policyholder had explicitly forbidden the driver from operating the vehicle. Therefore, the insurer did not have a duty to defend. This case involved a dispute over the 'permissive user' clause in an automobile insurance policy. An accident occurred while the vehicle was being driven by an individual who did not have the explicit permission of the policyholder to operate the vehicle. The insurer sought a declaratory judgment that it had no duty to defend or indemnify the driver. The claimant argued that the driver had 'implied permission' based on the relationship between the driver and the policyholder. The insurer argued that the policy required 'express permission' and that the facts did not support such a finding. The court analyzed the doctrine of 'implied permission' in Missouri insurance law, looking at past behavior, relationship status, and the history of vehicle usage. The case required the court to balance the objective evidence of permission against the insurer's argument that the policy terms were strictly limited to express grants of permission. The court reviewed the evidentiary record to see if the trial court erred in finding that no implied permission existed. This case clarifies the standard for determining when an insurer must provide coverage to a non-named user of a vehicle.

## Pruett v. Anderson

395 S.W.3d 589 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: Actual possession for the purpose of adverse possession is determined by the nature and location of the land; where the land is residential, consistent maintenance, mowing, and landscaping can constitute sufficient possession to satisfy the elements of a claim. Such acts, when continuous for the statutory period, can ripen into legal title. This matter involved a dispute between neighbors over an old fence that had separated their properties for decades. The defendant removed the fence, claiming that a professional survey revealed the fence was encroaching upon their land. The plaintiffs brought a quiet title action, asserting title by adverse possession. The evidence showed that the plaintiffs had maintained the area, including mowing the grass and clearing debris, right up to the fence line for over twenty years. The defendants argued that this activity was not sufficient to show exclusive or hostile possession, as it was merely keeping the property tidy. The trial court determined that the plaintiffs had failed to demonstrate the level of hostility necessary for adverse possession, as they had not made any permanent improvements to the disputed strip. Upon appeal, the court held that the plaintiffs' consistent maintenance and treatment of the strip as their own constituted an actual, open, and notorious use of the property. The court reversed the trial court, ruling that the plaintiffs had met the elements of adverse possession, and the fence line, even though technically encroaching on the survey, had become the legal boundary. The case underscores how consistent maintenance can satisfy the requirement of hostile possession in boundary disputes.

## Pruett v. Elick

505 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an easement of necessity requires proof that the dominant and servient estates were once held in common title and that the easement is reasonably necessary for access upon severance. 'Necessity' in this context means a practical necessity rather than an absolute lack of any possible exit. The parties in this litigation were involved in a dispute over an easement of necessity. The plaintiffs, owners of a landlocked property, claimed they were entitled to an easement across the defendants' parcel, which was the only access point to a public road. The defendants argued that an alternative, though difficult, path existed through a different neighbor's land. The court examined the requirements for an easement by necessity, which requires a showing of unity of title followed by a severance, and that the necessity existed at the time of the severance. The court found that the plaintiffs established unity of title and that the necessity for the road was absolute at the time the parcels were divided. Rejecting the defendants' argument about the alternative route, the court clarified that 'necessity' does not mean the route must be absolutely impossible to circumvent, but rather that it must be reasonably necessary for the beneficial enjoyment of the property. The court affirmed the grant of the easement, noting that the defendants' path was the historical and only logical access point.

## Pruett v. Fed. Mogul Corp.

369 S.W.3d 783 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the judgment, holding that the plaintiff's internal complaints did not constitute a clear violation of a specific constitutional or statutory public policy. The court maintained the high threshold for the public policy exception in Missouri. Pruett initiated a lawsuit against Federal Mogul Corporation after his employment was terminated. Pruett alleged that the termination was retaliatory and violated public policy because he had expressed concerns about unsafe workplace practices that violated federal regulations. The company defended its actions by citing a restructuring of the department and poor performance reviews. The trial court entered judgment for the defendant, finding that Pruett failed to satisfy the requirements for the public policy exception. Pruett appealed, arguing that the court failed to properly weigh evidence of his adherence to federal safety protocols. The appellate court reviewed whether the safety violations cited by the employee were sufficient to create a clear mandate of public policy. The court explored whether the employee's internal complaints were protected activity or if the law required reports to be made to external regulatory bodies. This decision highlights the necessity for plaintiffs to align their wrongful discharge claims with specific, established statutes or constitutional provisions to bypass the at-will employment rule in Missouri, clarifying the evidentiary threshold for what constitutes protected whistleblowing activity within a private corporation context.

## Pruett v. General Motors Corp.

936 S.W.2d 866 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court erred in excluding certain expert testimony and reversed the directed verdict. It affirmed that federal safety standards provide a floor but not a ceiling for design liability. The case was sent back for a new trial. In this product liability case, the plaintiff alleged that a vehicle's seatbelt restraint system was defectively designed, causing catastrophic injuries during a rollover accident. The lawsuit focused on the failure of the restraint to properly lock during the crash sequence. General Motors contended that the vehicle met all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) and that the injuries were caused by the severity of the impact rather than a product defect. The appellate court examined the admissibility of evidence regarding the plaintiff's failure to wear a seatbelt, known as the 'seatbelt defense,' and whether such evidence is permissible in a strict liability action under Missouri law. The court also considered the sufficiency of the plaintiff's expert testimony, which used computer modeling to simulate the accident. The debate involved whether the plaintiff provided evidence of a 'feasible alternative design' that would have prevented or reduced the injuries sustained. The trial court had initially excluded some of the plaintiff's expert evidence, leading to a directed verdict for the defendant, which the plaintiff subsequently challenged on appeal. The case serves as a key precedent for the evidentiary requirements in automobile crashworthiness cases.

## Pruett v. Missouri Department of Transportation

528 S.W.3d 342 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the claimant did not meet the burden of proving that employment was the prevailing factor for his carpal tunnel. The denial of benefits was upheld based on the insufficiency of the medical evidence. The claimant alleged that his carpal tunnel syndrome was an occupational disease caused by repetitive keyboard usage at work. The employer argued that the condition was the result of the claimant's hobbies outside of work and was not primarily caused by employment duties. The Commission denied benefits, finding that the claimant failed to satisfy the 'prevailing factor' test. The appellate court analyzed the burden of proof required to link repetitive stress injuries to specific workplace tasks under the amended Missouri statutes. The court affirmed the Commission's decision, noting that the medical evidence provided by the claimant failed to clearly distinguish work-related causes from non-work-related causes. The case serves as an important illustration of the challenges claimants face when proving occupational disease for cumulative trauma injuries. The court emphasized that the mere possibility that work contributed to a condition is insufficient; there must be definitive medical evidence establishing that the workplace activity was the primary cause of the condition to satisfy the statutory requirements for compensability in Missouri workers' compensation law.

## Pruett v. Rinderman

276 S.W.3d 321 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: Easement by implication is established when there is evidence of common ownership followed by a severance, accompanied by a pre-existing use that is both apparent and reasonably necessary to the usage of the conveyed parcel. The plaintiffs in this case sought to establish an easement by implication across a neighbor's property to access their landlocked tract. The trial court dismissed the action, finding that the property was not strictly landlocked. On appeal, the court examined the evidence of the history of the tract. The court reaffirmed the Missouri rule that an easement by implication requires proof of: (1) common ownership; (2) separation of title; (3) the existence of a prior, apparent, and continuous use; and (4) that the easement is reasonably necessary. The court found that all elements were present, specifically noting that the prior owner had used the path for many years, which created an apparent use that existed when the title was severed. Because the original grantor did not reserve an express easement, the law of implication fills that gap to ensure the property remains functional. The appellate court reversed the trial court's judgment and ordered the creation of the easement.

## Pryor Properties, LLC v. K.C. Development Co.

558 S.W.3d 1 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District, affirmed the trial court's judgment. The court found that KCDC did not breach the development agreement. The court held that Pryor failed to demonstrate that KCDC wrongfully terminated the agreement or engaged in other breaches, and that KCDC's actions were consistent with the terms of their contract. This case involved a dispute over a real estate development agreement. Pryor Properties, LLC (Pryor) and K.C. Development Co. (KCDC) entered into an agreement for the joint development of a commercial property. Pryor alleged that KCDC breached the agreement by failing to secure necessary financing, by mismanaging the project, and by wrongfully terminating the agreement. KCDC denied the breach, asserting that Pryor failed to meet its obligations and that KCDC acted within its rights. The trial court found in favor of KCDC, dismissing Pryor's claims. Pryor appealed, arguing that the trial court erred in its interpretation of the development agreement and in its findings of fact. The appellate court reviewed the terms of the agreement, the parties' communications, and evidence related to project financing and management.

## Public Service Co. of Colorado v. Gates Rubber Co.

175 F.3d 1177 · United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit · 1999 · Federal

Holding: CERCLA Section 113(h) prohibits judicial review of EPA-selected remedial actions until the government commences an enforcement or cost recovery action. This jurisdictional bar is absolute and serves to prevent litigation-induced delays in environmental remediation. This case dealt with the scope of CERCLA's judicial review provision. The defendants were involved in a dispute over the cleanup of a site and sought judicial review of the EPA's cleanup plan before the plan was implemented. The government moved to dismiss, arguing that CERCLA Section 113(h) bars pre-enforcement review of EPA cleanup actions. The defendants argued that they were challenging the *process* of selection, not the cleanup itself. The Tenth Circuit reaffirmed the broad protection of Section 113(h), which is designed to prevent parties from delaying critical environmental remediation by filing litigation during the initial phases of a cleanup. The court held that the statute creates a clear jurisdictional bar, meaning that judicial review of EPA-selected remedial actions is generally not available until the government files a suit for cost recovery or enforcement, ensuring the expeditious cleanup of hazardous sites.

## Puckett v. Hughes

936 S.W.2d 232 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the plaintiffs failed to establish a prescriptive easement because their use of the driveway was permissive, as evidenced by the shared maintenance agreement. The plaintiffs filed a suit to quiet title to a strip of land used as a driveway. The defendants, the neighboring owners, had blocked access to the driveway, which the plaintiffs claimed they had used for years. The plaintiffs asserted a prescriptive easement, while the

Second stored summary defendants argued the use was permissive because they had shared maintenance costs. The court explored the legal criteria for a prescriptive easement, reiterating that the use must be adverse, which means used without the owner's permission and as a matter of right. The court examined whether the act of sharing maintenance costs for a driveway automatically negates the 'adverse' nature of the use. The court held that sharing maintenance can be seen as a cooperative act that implies permission. However, the court also found that if the user holds the path as his own and uses it regardless of the owner's consent, the easement can still be formed. Ultimately, the court found the usage had been permissive due to the mutual maintenance arrangement, precluding the existence of a prescriptive easement.

## Puckett v. Puckett

265 S.W.3d 873 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2008 · Missouri

Holding: Oral agreements to settle boundary lines are valid only when there is a genuine uncertainty or dispute regarding the true location of the boundary. If the boundary is clearly defined or discoverable via existing records, parties cannot use an oral agreement to relocate the legal property line in violation of the Statute of Frauds. In this family boundary dispute, two brothers disagreed on the location of the line separating their inherited lots. One brother had built a garage that crossed what the other brother claimed was the legal boundary line. The brother who built the garage filed a quiet title action, arguing that the parties had orally agreed to the line location before construction. The trial court heard conflicting testimony regarding whether such an agreement existed. The appellate court focused on the 'statute of frauds' requirement for land conveyances. It held that while parties can resolve boundary disputes through oral agreements, such agreements must be based on a genuine uncertainty regarding the true boundary line. If the parties are not uncertain, they cannot simply agree to change the property lines by oral contract. Because the evidence showed the parties had access to a survey that clearly defined the line, there was no 'genuine uncertainty' to justify an oral boundary agreement. The court ruled that the garage was an encroachment and ordered its removal or a legal conveyance of the land.

## Puckett v. Roser

208 S.W.3d 306 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2006 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an express easement is not abandoned simply due to the path becoming impassable or through disuse. A party claiming abandonment must prove a clear and affirmative intent to relinquish the property interest. The plaintiff appealed a summary judgment ruling regarding an easement dispute. The plaintiff held a deeded easement over the defendants' land, but the defendants argued that the easement was extinguished through abandonment. The defendants provided evidence that the plaintiff had failed to maintain the path and that it had become overgrown and impassable for several decades. The trial court agreed that the easement had been abandoned. On appeal, the plaintiff argued that the trial court ignored the principle that an express easement cannot be easily extinguished. The appellate court reversed the decision, stating that abandonment is a question of fact that requires evidence of the holder's intent to abandon. In this case, the fact that the path was overgrown did not necessarily prove the plaintiff intended to permanently give up their legal right to use it. The court reaffirmed that a deeded easement represents a vested property right that remains in effect unless there is a clear, affirmative action showing an intent to abandon or an act of estoppel. The court remanded the case, noting that the trial court failed to require a high enough burden of proof for the defendants to show the plaintiff's intent to abandon the easement.

## Pulitzer Pub. Co. v. Missouri State Employees' Retirement Sys.

927 S.W.2d 477 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1996 · Missouri

Also captioned Pulitzer Publishing Co. v. Missouri State Employees' Retirement System

Holding: The court held that retirement systems managing public funds are subject to the Sunshine Law. Investment records are generally public, and agencies must narrowly redact only specific, proprietary financial data rather than withholding entire documents. The Pulitzer Publishing Company requested access to the Missouri State Employees' Retirement System (MOSERS) investment records. MOSERS argued that the records were exempt from disclosure because they involved investment strategies and could potentially impact the system's financial performance if disclosed. The court evaluated whether the records were 'public records' and if the specific investment performance data fell under any of the listed exemptions in the Sunshine Law. The court noted that because MOSERS manages public pension funds, the accountability for those funds is a matter of significant public concern. The court rejected the argument that the investment strategies were immune from the sunshine requirements, finding that while some granular trade secret data might be redacted, the overall investment performance and allocations were public information. This case reaffirmed that public pension boards and similar agencies are fully subject to the Sunshine Law. It established that the public's right to monitor the management of public funds is paramount and that exemptions should not be used to shield the performance of public investment entities from public scrutiny.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that the records regarding the performance of investment managers for a public retirement system are public records. Trade secret exemptions do not apply to records related to the management of public funds. The plaintiffs sought access to records held by a public retirement system regarding the performance of its investment managers. The retirement system claimed that the records were proprietary and trade secrets of the investment firms, and therefore exempt from the Sunshine Law. The media organization argued that because the retirement system was a public entity using public funds for investments, the records were subject to public scrutiny. The court evaluated the intersection of trade secret protections and the public's right to information regarding the management of public funds. The decision analyzed whether the economic interests of third-party contractors can override the statutory requirement to disclose public records. The court concluded that the retirement system's fiduciary duty to manage funds transparently outweighed the contractors' claims of commercial confidentiality. The ruling clarified that when private entities contract with the government to manage public money, they must accept that their activities become subject to the Sunshine Law. This case provides significant guidance on the disclosure requirements for public-private financial partnerships and the limitations of trade secret claims when dealing with taxpayer-supported assets.

## R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul

505 U.S. 377 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1992 · Federal

Holding: The ordinance was struck down as unconstitutional. The Court held that the government cannot discriminate based on viewpoint, even when regulating categories of otherwise unprotected speech. A teenager and several others burned a crudely fashioned cross on a Black family's lawn in St. Paul, Minnesota. The teenager was charged under a local ordinance that prohibited the display of a symbol, such as a burning cross or Nazi swastika, which one knows or has reasonable grounds to know arouses anger, alarm, or resentment in others on the basis of race, color, creed, religion, or gender. The Supreme Court reviewed the constitutionality of this 'hate speech' ordinance. While the Court condemned the conduct, it found the ordinance facially unconstitutional. The Court held that the ordinance was content-based and viewpoint-discriminatory because it only prohibited speech that aroused anger based on specific disfavored topics. The decision underscored that even if speech falls into a category that the government could theoretically prohibit (like fighting words), it cannot regulate that speech based on the specific viewpoint it expresses.

## R.B. v. K.B.

379 S.W.3d 842 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's award of joint legal custody, primary physical custody to the mother, and the established visitation schedule. The court found these decisions to be in the children's best interests and supported by substantial evidence. This case involved a divorce decree that allocated parental responsibilities, including child custody and visitation. The father appealed the trial court's award of joint legal custody and primary physical custody to the mother, as well as the established visitation schedule. He argued that the custody and visitation orders were not in the children's best interests and that the court erred in its division of marital

Second stored summary property. The appellate court reviewed the evidence presented, including testimony concerning the parents' fitness and the children's relationships with each parent. The court applied the "best interests of the child" factors and examined the trial court's discretion. The court found that the trial court's findings were supported by substantial evidence and that the custody and visitation awards were in the children's best interests. The property division was also affirmed as equitable.

## R.D. v. Mercy Hospital

602 S.W.3d 287 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the 'lost chance of survival' doctrine is a viable theory in Missouri medical malpractice law. The evidence provided was sufficient to create a jury question on the causal link between the negligence and the harm. The appeal concerned a medical malpractice case involving a diagnostic error that allegedly led to a severe health decline. The primary issue on appeal was the trial court's application of the 'lost chance of survival' doctrine in Missouri. The appellate court examined whether a patient can recover damages when medical negligence significantly reduces their chances of recovery, even if the patient cannot prove that the outcome would have been better 'but for' the medical error. The court reviewed the legal requirements for establishing causation in cases where the injury involves the loss of an opportunity for a better medical outcome. This case serves as a critical reference for plaintiffs asserting claims where the injury is defined by a lost chance rather than a direct, easily attributable physical injury. The decision also discusses the role of expert testimony in quantifying the 'lost chance' and how it should be presented to the jury to support a claim for damages.

## R.H. Barnes, L.L.C. v. City of St. Louis

631 S.W.3d 654 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the City was not in breach of the redevelopment agreement. Economic downturns did not qualify as force majeure events, and the developer remained bound by the original performance schedule. The plaintiff, a real estate developer, entered into a redevelopment agreement with the City of St. Louis. The agreement stipulated that the developer would receive tax increment financing (TIF) based on specific performance milestones. When the developer failed to hit the milestones due to economic downturns, the City rescinded the agreement and denied the associated tax incentives. The developer sued, alleging that the City breached the agreement by failing to extend deadlines during an period of general economic hardship, arguing that a 'force majeure' clause should have applied. The court evaluated whether the city's refusal to modify the contract terms constituted a breach and whether economic conditions fell under the definition of force majeure provided in the contract. The analysis focused on the plain language of the contract and the lack of any express requirement for the city to renegotiate terms in the event of market volatility. The decision highlights the rigid application of contract terms in municipal redevelopment projects.

## R.H. Macy & Co. v. City of Kansas City

934 S.W.2d 589 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the lease language was not ambiguous and the tenant was responsible for the taxes as defined by the agreement. The decision affirmed the trial court's judgment, emphasizing that commercial parties are bound by the plain language of their drafted contracts. This case involved a dispute regarding the interpretation of a commercial lease agreement and the tax liability of the parties involved in a redevelopment project. The landlord and tenant had entered into a long-term commercial lease that included provisions for the payment of real estate taxes and assessments. When the City of Kansas City implemented a tax increment financing plan, a conflict arose over whether the tenant was obligated to pay additional charges characterized as assessments rather than traditional ad valorem taxes. The litigation centered on the specific language of the lease contract and whether the definitions of taxes and assessments included the new financial burdens imposed by the city. The court was asked to determine if the contractual language was ambiguous and how the parol evidence rule applied to the negotiations surrounding the lease drafting. The appellate court examined the historical context of the lease and the intent of the parties to ascertain whether the tenant's payment obligations encompassed the new tax structure created by the TIF district.

## R.H. Macy & Co. v. Springdale Shopping Center

691 S.W.2d 237 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1985 · Missouri

Holding: Exclusive use clauses in commercial leases are valid and enforceable. When such clauses are drafted in a way that creates ambiguity, the court will construe the language in a manner that protects the reasonable expectations of the parties as established during lease negotiations.

Second stored summary This case involved a dispute between an anchor tenant and a shopping center owner regarding the interpretation of restrictive covenants and exclusive use clauses in a commercial lease. The tenant alleged that the landlord violated the exclusive use agreement by allowing a competing business to operate in the same shopping center. The court engaged in an extensive analysis of the lease's 'exclusive use' provision, focusing on whether the ambiguity in the language should be construed to favor the tenant, who relied on that provision to justify its high rent. The court applied the principle that contract language is to be given its plain and ordinary meaning, but where the language is susceptible to two interpretations, it must be construed against the drafter. The court found that the landlord had indeed breached the exclusive use provision and that the tenant was entitled to damages, including a potential rent abatement. This decision was significant for commercial real estate law in Missouri, as it emphasized the sanctity of exclusive use clauses as essential components of commercial leases and provided guidance on how courts should resolve disputes involving restrictive business covenants in large-scale rental properties.

## R.H. v. M.H.

495 S.W.3d 211 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: Premarital property can become partially marital through the contribution of marital funds for mortgage payments or renovations. Courts apply the source of funds rule to divide equity equitably. This family law-related real estate case involved the distribution of property in a dissolution of marriage. The main asset was a residence owned by the husband prior to the marriage, which the wife claimed had become marital property through the commingling of assets, specifically through the use of marital funds to pay the mortgage and perform renovations. The court analyzed the source of funds rule, which tracks how the property's equity was acquired. It was determined that a portion of the equity was non-marital, but the portion acquired during the marriage via mortgage payments from marital earnings became marital property. The appellate court affirmed the trial court's division, which granted the husband the non-marital portion while awarding the wife a portion of the value reflecting the marital contributions. This case illustrates how property acquired before marriage can be partially converted to marital property through the application of marital income to debt reduction and property improvements during the marriage.

## R.H. v. Missouri Department of Social Services

590 S.W.3d 320 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the state did not breach the contract because the termination-for-convenience clause allowed the agency to terminate the agreement at will without showing cause. The court ruled that the notice requirements for termination for cause did not apply to a termination for convenience. This case involved a challenge to the termination of a contract for family support services. The service provider, a non-profit organization, alleged that the state's termination of the contract was a breach, as the state had not followed the notice and cure provisions stipulated in the contract. The state argued that it had the right to terminate the contract for convenience under the terms of the agreement. The court analyzed the standard 'termination for convenience' clause, common in government contracts, and the extent to which it limits the contractor's rights. This case explores the balance of power in public-sector service contracts and the enforceability of termination clauses against the state. The decision provides a clear interpretation of how these clauses operate and the requirement for public entities to act in good faith when utilizing such provisions. It also touches upon the procedural requirements for notice when a contract is being terminated for cause versus for convenience, providing a clear map for practitioners dealing with public procurement contracts.

## R.J. v. Dallas County R-1 Sch. Dist.

489 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that sovereign immunity is waived under the dangerous condition exception when a plaintiff alleges injuries resulting from a physical defect in public property. The case was remanded to address the factual allegations concerning the playground equipment. The plaintiff, a minor student, sued the school district for negligence after being injured on a playground during recess. The student alleged that the school failed to supervise the activity, which involved rough play, and that the playground equipment was poorly maintained. The school district raised the defense of sovereign immunity under Missouri law. The trial court dismissed the action, ruling that the district was immune from suit. The appellate court analyzed whether the 'dangerous condition of public property' exception to sovereign immunity applied. The court evaluated whether the injury was caused by the physical condition of the playground itself or merely by lack of supervision. Finding that the allegations regarding the physical state of the playground equipment were sufficient, the court reversed the dismissal. The ruling emphasizes the narrow but important scope of the waiver of sovereign immunity when public property is maintained in a dangerous state, distinguishing it from claims based solely on discretionary acts of supervision.

## R.J. v. Golden Valley Hospital

515 S.W.3d 773 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: Claims involving clinical judgments in a healthcare setting are categorized as professional negligence, necessitating expert testimony. Ordinary negligence standards do not apply when the alleged failure involves specialized professional medical practice. A patient filed a negligence claim against a hospital after a fall during a medical procedure. The plaintiff alleged that the medical staff failed to use appropriate restraints, causing the fall. The hospital argued that the decision regarding the level of restraint was a professional clinical judgment protected under the medical malpractice statute. The trial court granted a directed verdict for the defendant. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that the claim was one of ordinary negligence, not medical malpractice, and therefore did not require expert testimony. The appellate court analyzed the distinction between professional negligence and ordinary negligence in healthcare settings. The court concluded that the decision to restrain a patient is inherently a clinical decision that requires specialized medical training, thus classifying the claim as professional negligence. Because the plaintiff failed to provide expert testimony to establish the standard of care for restraint usage, the appellate court affirmed the trial court's decision, emphasizing that expert testimony is required for claims involving professional judgment.

## R.K. Matthews v. M.H.C.A.

545 S.W.3d 378 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the tenant's failure to pay rent and fees constituted a material breach of the lease. The judgment was affirmed because the landlord's maintenance failures were not sufficient to excuse the tenant's performance. The parties were involved in a dispute over a commercial lease agreement. The landlord claimed that the tenant breached the contract by failing to pay common area maintenance (CAM) fees correctly and by allowing unauthorized subleasing of the premises. The tenant counterclaimed, alleging that the landlord failed to maintain the building as required by the contract, thereby causing a constructive eviction. The trial court found for the landlord, determining that the tenant had materially breached the lease. On appeal, the tenant

Second stored summary argued that the trial court erred in its calculation of damages and in its interpretation of the 'repair and maintenance' clause. The appellate court examined the lease document's specific definitions of maintenance obligations and the process for disputing CAM charges. The court found that while the landlord had some maintenance failures, they did not reach the level of constructive eviction or excuse the tenant's payment obligations. The court clarified the standard for determining a material breach in commercial leases and upheld the damage award calculated by the trial court, noting that the court's interpretation of the contract was consistent with the plain meaning of the terms as understood by sophisticated parties.

## R.K. v. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Co.

592 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the period of restoration was defined by the time reasonably required to rebuild the property. The court found that the insurer correctly applied the definition based on the facts presented in the record. This case dealt with an insurance coverage issue arising from a commercial property policy. The policyholder submitted a claim for business interruption losses following a fire. The insurer denied coverage for a significant portion of the loss, arguing that the policy's 'period of restoration' definition limited the time for which lost income could be recovered. The insured contended that the insurer failed to account for delays caused by local building codes and supply chain issues. The court examined the policy language defining the 'period of restoration' and whether the insurer correctly calculated the time frame for coverage. The dispute focused on whether the insured's delay in reconstructing the property was excusable under the contract. The insurer argued that the period of restoration is fixed by the time it should have taken, with reasonable diligence, to rebuild, regardless of the insured's actual performance. The court analyzed the relevant provisions, looking for ambiguity that would require construction in favor of the insured. The decision centered on the standard of 'reasonable speed and quality' in the context of the period of restoration clause.

## R.K. v. R.K.

595 S.W.3d 505 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the implied warranty of habitability cannot be waived by a residential lease provision. It remanded the case for a factual determination on whether the landlord received sufficient notice of the specific defects. This case involved a dispute regarding residential lease obligations and the scope of implied warranties. The tenant alleged that the landlord failed to maintain the premises in a habitable condition, specifically citing issues with HVAC functionality and water intrusion. The landlord argued that the tenant had waived these claims through continued occupancy and failure to provide formal notice as required by the lease agreement. The trial court examined the extent to which Missouri law implies a warranty of habitability in residential leases and whether such a warranty can be waived by contractual provisions. The appellate court reviewed the evidence regarding notice, assessing whether the landlord had actual or constructive knowledge of the defects. The analysis focused on the tension between freedom of contract and statutory requirements protecting residential tenants from unsafe living conditions. Ultimately, the court had to determine if the trial court erred in its interpretation of the lease terms and the application of the implied warranty doctrine.

## R.L. v. T.S.

290 S.W.3d 115 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: Statutory notice requirements for the termination of a month-to-month tenancy are mandatory and must be strictly followed. Defective notice that fails to align with the rental period renders the termination attempt invalid. This case addressed the validity of a notice of termination in a month-to-month residential tenancy. The landlord provided notice to terminate the tenancy, but the tenant argued the notice was defective because it did not comply with the statutory requirement of a thirty-day notice period ending on a rental period date. The trial court found the notice sufficient despite the technical error, citing the landlord's intent. The appellate court reversed, holding that statutory notice requirements for the termination of a periodic tenancy are mandatory and must be strictly followed to be effective. Because the notice provided by the landlord did not align with the end of the rental period as required by Missouri statute, the termination was ineffective, and the tenancy was extended by operation of law. This decision reaffirms that compliance with statutory notice procedures is a condition precedent to a valid termination of a periodic lease, and failures in timing cannot be cured by equitable considerations.

## R.M. v. St. Louis County

283 S.W.3d 276 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the county's assessment was valid because the property owner failed to provide sufficient evidence to support an alternative valuation. Mass-appraisal techniques were found to be appropriate for tax assessment purposes. This property tax dispute arose after a county reassessment significantly increased the valuation of a commercial office building. The property owner challenged the reassessment, arguing that the county failed to account for a high vacancy rate and the resulting decline in the property's income-generating potential. The county argued that the appraisal followed standard mass-appraisal techniques and that the owner failed to provide sufficient financial documentation to justify a lower valuation. The court examined the evidentiary standard required to challenge a tax assessment and the weight given to the income approach to valuation. This case clarifies the responsibilities of commercial property owners to produce credible and verifiable evidence when contesting tax assessments. The appellate court evaluated whether the board of equalization's decision was supported by substantial evidence and if it properly accounted for economic factors affecting the value of the property at the time of the reassessment.

## R.P. v. K.P.

505 S.W.3d 382 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The trial court's judgment was affirmed. The court held that the trial court acted within its discretion to preserve joint custody while providing structured mechanisms for dispute resolution. This custody case centered on the issue of legal custody and decision-making authority. The parents, who shared joint legal custody, were unable to agree on major decisions regarding the children's education and medical treatment. The father sought a modification to grant him sole decision-making authority. The trial court maintained the joint legal custody arrangement but implemented a detailed protocol for resolving disputes. On appeal, the father argued that the lack of cooperation between the parents made joint custody unworkable and detrimental to the children. The appellate court examined whether the trial court's decision was consistent with the children's best interests. The discussion focuses on the requirements for joint legal custody under Missouri law and the circumstances under which a trial court might transition from joint to sole legal custody. The opinion highlights that the inability to communicate is a relevant factor but does not mandate a move to sole custody if the trial court believes the parents can be incentivized to collaborate.

## R.S. v. B.C. Property

630 S.W.3d 899 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a landlord must strictly follow statutory notice and storage requirements for abandoned property. Failure to do so constitutes conversion, and the landlord was liable for the value of the disposed items. The tenants sought damages for conversion after the landlord disposed of their personal property following an eviction. The landlord argued that the property was abandoned under the terms of the lease and that statutory procedures for notice of abandoned property were followed. The tenants claimed that they had attempted to retrieve their belongings and that the landlord had willfully ignored their requests, thereby violating the statutory requirements for the disposal of personal property. The court evaluated the specific procedures required by Missouri law for landlords dealing with abandoned personal property, emphasizing the notice periods and the duty of the

Second stored summary landlord to store the items safely. The case highlighted the tension between the landlord's need to clear the unit for the next tenant and the rights of the former tenant to recover their possessions. The court reviewed the evidence of the communication between the parties and whether the landlord's actions met the standard of 'willful or wanton' misconduct required for punitive damages.

## R.S. v. H.K.

823 S.W.2d 128 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1991 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that lease provisions prohibiting illegal activity are material terms, and a breach of such a provision may justify summary eviction without a cure period, provided the landlord can demonstrate the breach occurred on the premises. Evidence of the arrest and the nature of the criminal conduct were sufficient. The landlord sued for possession after the tenant was arrested for illegal drug activity on the leased premises, in violation of a 'criminal activity' clause in the lease. The tenant argued that they had no knowledge of the criminal activity and that the landlord failed to provide the required notice before filing the eviction action. The trial court ruled in favor of the landlord, finding that the criminal conduct was a material breach of the lease that did not require a specific cure period. The tenant appealed, challenging the interpretation of the lease clause and the procedural aspects of the eviction. The appellate court reviewed the standard for enforcing 'no-crime' clauses in residential leases, assessing whether the landlord had sufficient evidence to attribute the criminal activity to the tenant. The court also looked at the interplay between state drug-nuisance laws and private lease enforcement, determining whether the landlord's swift action was supported by Missouri law and the terms of the specific residential lease agreement.

## R.S. v. R.S.

615 S.W.3d 872 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the property division but reversed and remanded the child support award. The court held that the trial court erred in its Form 14 calculation regarding the father's existing support obligations. This case involved a dispute over the division of a military pension and the modification of child support. The father appealed the trial court's division of his military retirement benefits, asserting that the court erred by failing to account for his service years prior to the marriage. Additionally, the father challenged the calculation of his child support obligation, arguing that the court failed to account for his mandatory contributions to other support obligations. The appellate court reviewed the military pension division, noting that Missouri law allows for the equitable division of the portion of a pension earned during the marriage. The court found that the trial court had correctly utilized the 'time rule' formula to calculate the marital portion of the pension. Regarding child support, the court determined that the trial court failed to accurately account for the father's existing support orders in the Form 14 calculation. Consequently, the appellate court reversed and remanded the child support issue for recalculation, while affirming the remainder of the judgment regarding the property division. The decision highlighted the importance of strict adherence to the Form 14 child support guidelines to ensure accurate and equitable financial support for children.

## R.S. v. R.S.

377 S.W.3d 601 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of the modification, holding that the trial court's assessment of parental behavior was not an abuse of discretion. Claims of parental alienation require high standards of proof. This case involved a motion to modify custody based on allegations of parental alienation. The father alleged that the mother was engaging in behavior designed to poison his relationship with their children, including disparaging him in front of them and consistently interfering with scheduled calls. The trial court found that while there was friction, it did not rise to the level of systematic alienation and denied the motion. The appellate court reviewed the record to see if the trial court ignored evidence of behavior that would warrant a change in custody. The appellate court noted that alienation claims require high levels of proof and that courts must be careful not to mistake general conflict for targeted alienation. The appellate court found no abuse of discretion in the trial court's assessment, noting that the trial court was in the best position to observe the parents' testimony and determine credibility. The ruling confirms that courts are cautious about changing custody arrangements solely based on one parent's claims of alienation without robust, impartial evidence of harmful behavior.

## R.S.I. Industrial v. United States Steel Corp.

173 S.W.3d 375 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the lease agreement required the tenant to return the premises in a specific state of repair. The tenant was found liable for remediation costs as the damages exceeded reasonable wear and tear permitted by the contract. The parties were involved in a protracted dispute regarding a commercial lease for industrial property. A major component of the litigation involved the interpretation of a contamination clause and the tenant's duty to restore the premises to its original condition upon vacating the property. The landlord sought damages for remediation costs associated with environmental hazards discovered after the tenant surrendered possession. The tenant contended that the landlord had full knowledge of the industrial activities conducted on the site and had effectively waived the right to demand restoration for ordinary wear and tear consistent with the property's specialized use. The court analyzed the environmental regulations applicable at the time of the lease signing and the specific indemnification clauses included in the contract. The decision explores the standards of proof required to establish environmental damage and the extent to which commercial tenants are liable for long-term soil and water remediation under standard industrial lease forms.

## R.S.I. Prop. v. A.D.C. Corp.

936 S.W.2d 862 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1997 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that a commercial landlord has no implied right to enter leased premises without an express provision in the lease. The tenant was within their rights to change the locks.

Second stored summary This case dealt with the landlord's right to access the commercial premises. The tenant, a restaurant owner, had changed the locks to prevent the landlord from entering after hours to perform inspections, claiming that the landlord's frequent visits were disrupting business operations and threatening the confidentiality of the tenant's trade secrets. The landlord sued for breach of lease, claiming the right of entry was implied by the lease's maintenance provisions. The court reviewed the lease and found that it did not contain an express clause granting the landlord a right of reasonable access for inspection. The court ruled that in the absence of a specific 'right of entry' provision in a commercial lease, a landlord does not have the unilateral right to enter the premises, even for maintenance, without the tenant's permission or a showing of an emergency. This ruling highlights the importance of including explicit access clauses in commercial lease documents.

## RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank

566 U.S. 639 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2012 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a bankruptcy plan providing for the sale of collateral must allow the secured creditor to credit-bid its claim. The 'indubitable equivalent' provision cannot be used to bypass the specific credit-bidding requirement in a sale. The debtor, RadLAX, sought to confirm a Chapter 11 reorganization plan that involved selling collateral free and clear of liens, but without allowing the secured creditor to credit-bid its claim. The secured creditor argued that the Bankruptcy Code required the debtor to allow credit-bidding if the plan included a sale of the collateral. The debtor contended that it could provide the creditor the 'indubitable equivalent' of its claim through other means, circumventing the requirement to credit-bid. The Supreme Court examined the relevant statutory provisions regarding the sale of assets and plan confirmation. The Court applied the canon of construction that the specific provision (the rule requiring credit-bidding during sales) governs over the general provision (the rule regarding the 'indubitable equivalent'). The Court found that the Code provides two distinct paths for a cramdown, and when a sale is involved, the creditor's right to credit-bid is protected. The decision clarified the balance between a debtor's desire for a quick sale and a secured creditor's right to protect its interest.

## Ragsdale v. Furrow

651 S.W.2d 509 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the easement was not abandoned. Mere non-use, even for a long period, is insufficient to terminate an express easement granted by deed. This case involved a dispute between neighbors over an easement for a private road. The plaintiffs had an easement recorded in their deed, but the defendants claimed the easement had been extinguished by abandonment or non-use. The court reviewed the legal standard for proving the abandonment of a written easement. In Missouri, an easement created by a grant is not extinguished by mere non-use, regardless of how long the non-use lasts. There must be an affirmative act of abandonment by the dominant estate owner or clear evidence of an intent to relinquish the right. The court found that the plaintiffs had simply chosen not to use the road because they had another, more convenient route at the time. This did not demonstrate an intent to abandon their legal right to use the road in the future. The court affirmed that the plaintiffs retained their right to access the road whenever they deemed necessary, as the easement was a permanent property interest.

## Ragsdale v. Harris

965 S.W.2d 219 (Mo. App. S.D. 1998) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment. The court held that the Ragsdales failed to meet a material condition of the purchase agreement by not securing financing by the stipulated deadline. The court found that the contract was clear and unambiguous regarding the financing contingency and its timeframe. Therefore, the seller was within his rights to terminate the contract and retain the earnest money as liquidated damages. This case concerned a breach of contract claim arising from a real estate purchase agreement. The Ragsdales agreed to purchase a property from Harris. As part of the agreement, the Ragsdales paid earnest money and agreed to secure financing by a certain date. The Ragsdales were unable to obtain the necessary financing by the deadline specified in the contract. Harris subsequently terminated the contract and retained the earnest money. The Ragsdales sued to recover their earnest money, arguing that they had made good faith efforts to obtain financing and that the seller had interfered with their ability to do so. The trial court found in favor of Harris, concluding the Ragsdales had breached the contract.

## Ragsdale v. New Holland N. Am., Inc.

129 S.W.3d 434 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while manufacturers must anticipate some misuse, substantial modifications made by the user that remove safety features generally relieve the manufacturer of strict liability. It affirmed the trial court's decision in favor of the manufacturer. The plaintiff was injured while using a hay baler and sued the manufacturer, claiming a design defect because the machine lacked a safety guard or a cutoff switch. The manufacturer argued that the plaintiff's modifications to the machine over several years constituted a substantial alteration that relieved them of liability. The trial court's focus was on whether the alterations were foreseeable. The appellate

Second stored summary court addressed the concept of 'substantial change' in the context of product modification. It examined whether a manufacturer should be expected to design machines with the knowledge that owners might remove or bypass safety features. The legal analysis revolved around the manufacturer's duty to design products that remain safe despite foreseeable misuse or modifications, and the limitations of that duty in the face of significant product modifications by the owner.

## Raintree Court Apartments v. Stotts

339 S.W.3d 535 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a landlord's acceptance of rent payments from a holdover tenant does not automatically create a new tenancy if the landlord has already provided proper notice of termination. The mere receipt of funds after the lease expiration is insufficient to waive the landlord's right to pursue an unlawful detainer action. This matter involved an action for unlawful detainer brought by a landlord against a tenant after the expiration of a written lease. The tenant argued that the landlord had effectively accepted a holdover tenancy by accepting subsequent rent payments. The trial court initially ruled in favor of the tenant, concluding that the landlord's conduct created a month-to-month tenancy, thus requiring a proper thirty-day notice to terminate. The landlord appealed the decision, asserting that the acceptance of payment did not waive the prior notice to vacate provided to the tenant. The appellate court examined the statutory requirements for unlawful detainer actions and the specific terms of the expired lease agreement. The court focused on whether the landlord's continued acceptance of rent payments, absent a new written agreement, constituted a waiver of the previous termination notice or created an automatic renewal of the tenancy under Missouri statutes. The analysis required an interpretation of Section 441.060 RSMo regarding the termination of tenancies at will and the effect of holdover status on landlord-tenant obligations. Ultimately, the court had to determine if the landlord's actions were inconsistent with their intention to terminate the tenancy, thereby nullifying the unlawful detainer claim.

## Rall v. Schoggins

648 S.W.2d 173 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that when a fence is treated as a boundary by mutual acquiescence for a long period, it supersedes a contrary survey. The court affirmed the trial court's judgment regarding the boundary location. The parties were neighbors who disputed the location of a boundary fence that had stood for approximately 35 years. The plaintiff alleged the fence was the boundary and that he owned the land up to the fence. The defendant, after obtaining a professional survey, moved the fence to the surveyed line, which was several feet onto the plaintiff's claimed side. The plaintiff sued for damages and to quiet title. The trial court looked at the history of the boundary, finding that the fence was constructed by the parties' predecessors to mark the limit of their respective fields. The court concluded that a boundary by acquiescence had been established. The defendant appealed, arguing that the survey should be the controlling evidence. The appellate court affirmed, noting that when a boundary has been settled for such a long period of time by mutual understanding, it is against public policy to disturb it simply because a new survey differs from the accepted historical line. The court ruled that the historical fence line must remain the official boundary.

## Ransom v. FIA Card Services, N.A.

562 U.S. 61 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2011 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a Chapter 13 debtor who does not make car payments cannot claim the 'car ownership' deduction under the Bankruptcy Code's means test. The deduction is only applicable to debtors who have actual expenses related to the vehicle. In calculating his 'disposable income' for a Chapter 13 plan, the debtor deducted a 'car ownership allowance' despite the fact that he owned his vehicle outright and had no loan payments. The creditor challenged this deduction, arguing that the allowance is only applicable when a debtor has actual vehicle expenses. The Supreme Court had to interpret the 'means test' provisions of the Bankruptcy Code, which dictate how debtors calculate expenses for their repayment plans. The Court focused on the word 'applicable' in the statute. The debtor argued that 'applicable' meant that the allowance is available to any debtor in the appropriate state, regardless of whether they have a loan. The Court disagreed, finding that the purpose of the means test is to determine actual disposable income. It concluded that a debtor who does not make loan payments cannot claim the allowance because it is not 'applicable' to his financial situation. The ruling focused on the legislative intent to ensure that only true expenses reduce the amount paid to unsecured creditors.

## Rapanos v. United States

547 U.S. 715 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2006 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: Federal jurisdiction under the Clean Water Act over wetlands requires a significant nexus to navigable waters. The plurality demanded a continuous surface connection, while the controlling concurrence adopted the significant nexus test. The petitioner, John Rapanos, backfilled wetlands on his property without a permit, asserting that the wetlands were not 'waters of the United States' under the CWA. The government argued that the wetlands were adjacent to tributaries of navigable waters and therefore subject to federal regulation. The Supreme Court provided a fractured set of opinions. Justice Scalia's plurality opinion held that the CWA extends only to relatively permanent, standing, or continuously flowing bodies of water and wetlands that have a continuous surface connection to them. Justice Kennedy, in a concurring opinion, provided the 'significant nexus' test. He argued that the CWA covers wetlands that possess a significant nexus to waters that are or were navigable in fact or could reasonably be so made. This nexus exists if the wetlands, either alone or in combination with similarly situated lands, significantly affect the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of other covered waters. This case has been the subject of extensive litigation regarding the scope of federal jurisdiction over wetlands and intermittent streams.

## Rapp v. K.A.L.S.

406 S.W.3d 505 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that on-call time is compensable if the restrictions placed on the employee are so substantial that they effectively prevent the employee from using the time for personal pursuits. The analysis focuses on the degree of control the employer exerts over the employee's time. Rapp involved a wage dispute regarding the classification of 'on-call' time. The employee, who worked in a security-related field, was required to remain on-call but argued that the restrictions placed upon her during this time effectively meant she was 'working' for the purpose of the Missouri Minimum Wage Law. The employer maintained that the employee was not working while on-call, as she was free to engage in personal activities, provided she remained reachable. The court reviewed the federal standards adopted by Missouri regarding 'waiting to be engaged' versus 'engaged to wait.' The decision provides an extensive analysis of the factors courts consider when determining if on-call time is compensable, including geographic constraints, response time requirements, and the frequency of interruptions. This is a vital case for industries relying on on-call personnel, as it clarifies the threshold at which on-call constraints transform into compensable work hours, helping employers avoid inadvertent wage violations.

## Raskas v. Missouri Department of Social Services

322 S.W.3d 530 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that general claims of ethical disagreement, even by an attorney, do not rise to the level of a public policy exception to the at-will doctrine. A plaintiff must demonstrate a clear violation of a specific constitutional or statutory provision. The employer was entitled to judgment. Raskas, an attorney for the Missouri Department of Social Services, sued for wrongful discharge, claiming her termination was in retaliation for her refusal to participate in what she believed were unethical or illegal legal strategies. The department contended that she was an at-will employee and that her performance was unsatisfactory. The trial court entered judgment for the department. The Court of Appeals analyzed the scope of the public policy exception as applied to attorneys. The court noted that while attorneys have ethical obligations, those obligations alone do not necessarily create a public policy exception to at-will employment unless the discharge directly violates a specific statute or regulatory mandate. The court found that the plaintiff's assertions regarding ethical disagreements were insufficient to overcome the at-will doctrine, as they did not demonstrate a clear violation of public policy. The appellate court affirmed the decision, finding that the department's actions were justified and that the law did not support the plaintiff's claim under the circumstances of her professional employment.

## Ratliff v. City of Kansas City

393 S.W.3d 89 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the training was mandatory because the employees were led to believe that failure to attend would negatively impact their careers. It ruled that the city was required to compensate the firefighters for the time spent in training, regardless of the official policy label. The decision reinforced that courts will look behind nominal labels to determine the actual nature of work expectations. This case involved firefighters claiming they were entitled to compensation for time spent during mandatory training sessions occurring outside of their normal shifts. The city argued that such training was voluntary and therefore not compensable under the terms of the collective bargaining agreement. The court focused on whether the training was truly 'voluntary' or if the implicit pressure to attend meant it was essentially mandatory. The court reviewed the evidence regarding attendance requirements, the impact of attendance on promotion, and the city's stated policies regarding training. The litigation required balancing the needs of a municipal emergency service to maintain well-trained staff against the legal mandate to pay for compensable training time. The court also examined the 'Four Criteria' test under the FLSA, which Missouri courts have used to determine whether training time is compensable work. The analysis was highly factual, involving testimony from firefighters and city administrators regarding the culture and expectations surrounding training participation within the department.

## Rauscher v. Halverson

92 S.W.3d 286 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the doctrine of strict liability applies to commercial lessors of products. Lessors who regularly engage in the business of leasing are subject to the same strict liability standards as manufacturers and sellers. This case involved a dispute over the strict liability of a lessor of equipment. The plaintiff was injured while using a rental piece of equipment that allegedly had a defective safety feature. The court had to determine whether the doctrine of strict liability applies to commercial lessors in the same way it applies to sellers of products. The defendant argued that because they were a service-oriented rental business and not a manufacturer or seller, they should be exempt from the strict liability provisions. The court reviewed the public policy rationale behind strict liability, which is to protect the consumer from defective products. The analysis focused on whether the commercial lessor is part of the 'stream of commerce' and occupies a similar position to a seller in terms of the ability to detect defects and allocate the costs of risk. The court considered the expansion of the Restatement (Second) of Torts, Section 402A to cover commercial lessors who lease products to the public on a regular basis, thereby ensuring consistent safety expectations across different types of commercial transactions.
