## T.C. v. Garrett

590 S.W.3d 330 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: Under Missouri law, the duty of a landowner to a trespasser is limited to avoiding intentional harm. The attractive nuisance doctrine requires specific proof that the owner knew or should have known children were likely to trespass and encounter a dangerous condition. This case involved a premises liability claim brought by a minor against a property owner after the child sustained injuries on the defendant's land. The central legal issue was the status of the child at the time of the incident--whether they were a licensee or a trespasser--and the corresponding duty owed by the owner. The property owner argued that the child was a trespasser and that the owner had not breached any duty to warn of hidden dangers. The trial court granted summary judgment to the property owner, finding no evidence of 'willful or wanton' misconduct or that the landowner knew of the child's presence. The appellate court analyzed the 'attractive nuisance' doctrine in Missouri. The court concluded that the evidence failed to support the claim that the property was an attractive nuisance or that the owner had reason to know of the child's presence. The judgment was affirmed, reinforcing that landowners have limited duties to those who enter property without permission, unless specific exceptions apply.

## T.C. v. R.C.

632 S.W.3d 465 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's judgment on both the classification of marital property and the custody determination. The court held that the findings were within the discretion granted to the trial court. The parties appealed a dissolution decree focusing on the classification of property and the child custody plan. The husband argued that certain real estate purchased prior to the marriage was non-marital property. The wife contested the custody plan, which mandated a split physical custody schedule, arguing it was disruptive to the child's academic routine. The trial court found the real estate to be marital property due to commingling of funds and maintained the custody plan as ordered. The appellate court analyzed the transmutation of property and the trial court's discretion in custody arrangements. Regarding property, the court found the trial court correctly applied the source-of-funds rule to classify the asset. Regarding custody, the appellate court reiterated that trial courts have substantial discretion to craft custody plans that minimize conflict and prioritize the child's stability. The court held that while the mother's concerns about the schedule were valid, the trial court's plan was not an abuse of discretion and was supported by the evidence of the parents' work schedules. The court underscored that appellate courts do not reweigh evidence when the trial court's decision is supported by the record and reflects a considered attempt to balance the needs of the child with the realities of the parents' lifestyles.

## T.C.L. v. T.R.O.

912 S.W.2d 691 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that to successfully claim constructive eviction, a tenant must vacate the premises within a reasonable time after the landlord's wrongful conduct. A tenant cannot remain in possession while simultaneously claiming the premises are uninhabitable or unusable. This case involved a commercial tenant who vacated the premises following a disagreement over the landlord's renovation project that allegedly disrupted the tenant's business. The landlord sued for breach of the lease, seeking damages for lost rent and the cost of preparing the space for a new tenant. The tenant counterclaimed for constructive eviction and breach of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment. The trial court ruled that the landlord's renovation, while disruptive, did not constitute a constructive eviction because the tenant had not vacated the premises in a timely manner after the disruption occurred. The tenant appealed, arguing that the 'reasonable time' standard for vacating after a constructive eviction should be flexible depending on the nature of the business. The appellate court reviewed the legal requirements for constructive eviction, focusing on the requirement that a tenant must abandon the premises within a reasonable time after the landlord's wrongful act. The court examined whether the tenant's continued occupancy while searching for new space waived the right to claim constructive eviction.

## T.G. v. Missouri Baptist Medical Center

544 S.W.3d 287 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the case because the plaintiff failed to comply with the court-ordered discovery deadlines. Strict adherence to procedural deadlines is required in medical negligence cases.

Second stored summary The case involved a claim against a hospital for damages resulting from the alleged negligence of a staff nurse in administering medication. The main issue on appeal was the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the defendant due to the plaintiff's failure to timely provide an expert witness report as required by the scheduling order. The appellate court reviewed the trial court's discretion in managing the case and enforcing discovery deadlines. The decision addresses the importance of procedural compliance in medical malpractice cases and the harsh consequences of failing to meet deadlines set by the trial court. It underscores the difficulty of reviving a case once a critical procedural mistake has been made and highlights the necessity for diligent case management in high-stakes medical negligence litigation in Missouri. The court analyzed whether the trial court acted within its authority to dismiss the case for lack of expert evidence, which is essential to proving a medical malpractice claim.

## T.J.W. v. J.M.W.

511 S.W.3d 446 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court's decision to grant primary custody to the mother was supported by evidence of the parents' inability to collaborate. The court maintained that trial courts have broad discretion in these matters to ensure the best interests of the children are met. The father appealed a custody determination in a dissolution of marriage proceeding, asserting that the trial court erred by denying him joint physical custody. He argued that the court's reliance on the mother's assertion that they could not cooperate was misplaced and that he had shown he was capable of effective communication. The mother argued that the father had a history of being controlling and that joint custody would be detrimental to the children's development. The trial court granted sole legal and primary physical custody to the mother, with liberal visitation for the father. The trial court's judgment was guided by the findings of a court-appointed guardian ad litem who interviewed the children and observed the interactions between the parents. The appellate court reviewed whether the trial court had appropriately applied the factors in Section 452.375 and whether the court's decision was consistent with the goal of ensuring the children's well-being. The court focused on the necessity of a stable and consistent environment and the impact of parental discord on the minor children during the pendency of the divorce.

## T.L. v. A.L.

542 S.W.3d 375 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's ruling. It held that there was no abuse of discretion in finding that the parent's condition did not rise to the level of requiring a change in custody. The case involved a dispute over the modification of a child custody decree after one parent was diagnosed with a health condition that allegedly affected their ability to provide care. The other parent sought full custody, arguing that the change in circumstances created a risk to the children's health and safety. The trial court denied the motion to modify, concluding that the parent was still capable of parenting and that the existing arrangement remained in the children's best interests. The appellate court reviewed whether the trial court ignored evidence of endangerment. The legal analysis focused on the statutory factors for determining custody and the threshold for demonstrating a 'significant' change in circumstances. The court reiterated that parental health issues do not automatically trigger a change in custody unless they directly impact the parent's ability to provide a safe and nurturing environment. The opinion provides guidance on the evidence necessary to prove that a physical or mental health condition warrants a modification of custody.

## T.L. v. Mercy Hospital

639 S.W.3d 512 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the 'sudden emergency' doctrine is generally inappropriate in professional malpractice cases because the professional's training is designed to handle such emergencies. It affirmed the verdict against the hospital. The patient sued the hospital for negligence after sustaining a cardiac event during a routine procedure. The plaintiff alleged that the staff failed to monitor the patient's cardiac rhythm adequately during the administration of sedation, resulting in a delayed response to a life-threatening arrhythmia. The hospital defended its actions by claiming that the patient's cardiac event was an unexpected complication and that the nursing response was consistent with the guidelines for moderate sedation. The appeal examined the jury instruction on the 'sudden emergency' doctrine, which the defense had requested. The court evaluated whether the trial court's refusal

Second stored summary to grant the instruction was appropriate, focusing on whether a medical staff member can claim the defense of sudden emergency when the situation is one that they are professionally trained to handle as a routine part of their job, thereby questioning if the doctrine has any place in professional malpractice litigation.

## T.L.C. v. M.C.

578 S.W.3d 890 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a tenant cannot unilaterally withhold rent due to partial uninhabitability without following the formal legal procedures for rent abatement. The landlord was entitled to possession due to the undisputed non-payment of rent. A residential landlord initiated an eviction process following the tenant's failure to pay rent during a period when the premises were allegedly damaged by a third party. The tenant argued that the landlord's failure to repair the damage prevented the tenant from using the property as intended, thereby excusing the obligation to pay rent under a theory of partial constructive eviction. The court considered whether Missouri law allows for rent abatement when a rental unit is only partially unusable due to conditions outside of the landlord's direct control. The opinion reviewed the statutory definitions of rent and possession actions and the extent to which a tenant can counterclaim for damages in an eviction proceeding. The appellate court evaluated the trial court's decision, focusing on whether the judge had correctly weighed the competing interests of the landlord's right to collect rent against the tenant's right to a habitable environment throughout the term of the lease.

## T.L.C. v. T.G.C.

495 S.W.3d 211 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the custody arrangement but reversed and remanded the maintenance award. The court held that the trial court erred in its financial calculations, necessitating a redetermination of support obligations. The parties involved were engaged in a bitter dissolution proceeding focusing on child custody and maintenance. The trial court awarded joint legal and physical custody but established a specific residential schedule. The mother challenged the custody arrangement and the award of maintenance, asserting that the trial court misapplied the law regarding the calculation of the father's income and the need for support. The appellate court analyzed the trial court's application of the Form 14 child support guidelines and the statutory factors for maintenance under Section 452.335 RSMo. The evidence presented during the trial included testimony regarding both parties' financial status and their respective abilities to parent. The appellate court found that while the trial court's findings on custody were consistent with the evidence, there were errors in the mathematical calculation of the maintenance amount. Consequently, the court remanded the case back to the trial court to recalculate the maintenance award based on the corrected income figures. The court reiterated that while trial courts possess wide latitude in family law matters, mathematical accuracy in financial orders is mandatory to ensure fairness and compliance with statutory requirements.

## T.L.M. v. D.M.

324 S.W.3d 756 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's denial of the father's request to modify primary physical custody, finding no abuse of discretion. The child support modification was also affirmed. This case involved a post-divorce judgment modifying child custody and child support. The father sought to modify the custody arrangement, requesting primary physical custody, and a modification of child support. The trial court denied the father's request for a change in primary physical custody but modified child support based on a change in income. The father appealed, arguing that the trial court erred in denying his request for a change in custody and in its calculation of child support. The appellate court reviewed the evidence presented concerning a material change in circumstances and the "best interests of the child" factors. It also examined the child support calculation. The court found that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying the custody modification, as the father failed to demonstrate a sufficient change in circumstances warranting a change in primary physical custody. The court affirmed the child support modification.

## T.L.M. v. R.M.

505 S.W.3d 398 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The appeal regarding temporary child support was dismissed in part and otherwise affirmed. The trial court has the authority to base support on earning capacity in temporary orders. The court addressed an appeal concerning a temporary child support order entered during the pendency of a divorce. The husband appealed the order, claiming the amount was excessive and not supported by his actual income during the period of temporary unemployment. The appellate court noted that temporary support orders are interlocutory and generally not appealable; however, it reviewed the case to determine if the trial court had acted outside of its jurisdiction. The court found that the trial court possessed the authority to determine support based on the husband's earning potential rather than just his immediate income. This is a common practice in Missouri to prevent a parent from avoiding support obligations by voluntarily quitting their job. The appellate court found no error in the trial court's assessment and affirmed the temporary order, noting that final support could be adjusted once the dissolution was finalized and more permanent financial information was available.

## T.L.W. v. M.A.W.

642 S.W.3d 721 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the denial of the father's motion to terminate maintenance. The court held that the father failed to show that the cohabitation resulted in economic dependency. This appeal involved the denial of a father's petition to terminate his maintenance obligation following the ex-wife's cohabitation with another person. The father argued that the ex-wife's living situation created a financial interdependence equivalent to remarriage,

Second stored summary thereby triggering the termination provision in the separation agreement. The trial court disagreed, finding that the cohabitation did not rise to the level of economic dependency necessary to warrant termination under Missouri precedent. The appellate court examined the definition of 'cohabitation' in the context of maintenance termination. The court noted that simple shared housing is not enough; the movant must demonstrate that the ex-spouse is being supported by the new partner or is sharing living expenses in a manner that alleviates their need for maintenance. The appellate court found that the evidence presented by the father regarding shared household expenses was insufficient to prove economic dependency. Consequently, the appellate court affirmed the trial court's decision, emphasizing that the burden to prove a change in circumstances rests heavily on the party seeking to terminate the maintenance order.

## T.T.I. v. City of Jackson

28 S.W.3d 465 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2000 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a 'termination for convenience' clause in a commercial lease is generally valid and enforceable, even when the lessor is a municipal entity. Absent evidence of constitutional violations, the landlord may terminate according to the contractual terms without needing to prove 'good cause.' The case involved a dispute over a commercial lease involving an airport hangar. The tenant challenged the landlord's (a municipal entity) decision to terminate the lease, claiming that the termination was motivated by discrimination rather than a legitimate breach of the lease. The tenant alleged that the municipal landlord violated their due process rights and breached the covenant of good faith and fair dealing by terminating the lease without sufficient cause. The trial court granted summary judgment for the city, concluding that the lease contained a 'termination for convenience' clause that allowed the city to terminate the agreement for any reason. The tenant appealed, arguing that the clause was unconscionable and could not be used to justify discriminatory conduct. The appellate court examined the nature of public-private leasing agreements and the extent to which municipal landlords are bound by principles of fairness and transparency. The analysis focused on the enforceability of termination for convenience clauses in government-held property and whether the tenant had a legitimate expectation of continued possession that was protected by constitutional safeguards.

## Taggart v. Lorenzen

587 U.S. 554 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2019 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a bankruptcy court may hold a creditor in civil contempt for violating a discharge injunction only if there is no 'fair ground of doubt' as to whether the creditor's conduct was prohibited. This objective standard protects creditors from sanctions for good-faith misunderstandings. The debtor, Bradley Taggart, received a discharge in bankruptcy. Subsequently, a creditor sought attorney's fees from Taggart in a state court action related to the pre-bankruptcy dispute. Taggart argued that the creditor violated the discharge injunction and sought civil contempt sanctions. The trial court initially awarded sanctions, but the appellate court reversed, using a standard that asked whether the creditor had an 'objectively reasonable' belief that the discharge did not apply. Taggart appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that a more stringent standard should apply to hold creditors in contempt. The Court analyzed the bankruptcy court's power to enforce the discharge injunction through civil contempt. It rejected the 'strict liability' approach as too harsh, opting instead for a standard based on the common law of contempt. The Court held that a court may impose sanctions only if there is no 'fair ground of doubt' as to whether the discharge order applied to the creditor's conduct. This created a clear, objective standard for evaluating whether a creditor's pursuit of a debt constitutes a contempt of court.

## Taha v. Enganine

2018 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 20194 · U.S. District Court (Applying Missouri Law) · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that online subscription practices can constitute an unfair practice under the MPA. It found that design features intended to trick consumers into continued enrollment are potentially actionable. The plaintiff sued an online service provider, alleging that their subscription model was deceptive because it was difficult to cancel and included hidden fees. The plaintiff argued that the company's interface intentionally made the cancellation process obscure, which led to consumers paying for services they no longer wanted, constituting a violation of the MPA. The defendant argued that the terms of the subscription were clearly available and that the ease of cancellation is not a standard governed by the MPA. The court evaluated whether user interface design that hinders consumer choice can be classified as an 'unfair' practice. This case touched on the evolving nature of consumer protection in the digital age, where traditional business practices have shifted to online platforms. The inquiry centered on whether the company's digital business model was intentionally designed to exploit the 'inertia' of consumers to maximize revenue, thereby meeting the threshold for a deceptive act under Missouri law.

## Tallent v. Hance

923 S.W.2d 446 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the fence line was the legal boundary through the doctrine of boundary by acquiescence. The court found that the evidence of long-term mutual recognition was dispositive. In this boundary dispute, the parties contested the ownership of a narrow strip of land situated between their respective properties. A survey commissioned by the plaintiff indicated that the land belonged to him, while the defendant claimed the land based on the existence of a long-standing fence and a line of trees. The defendant argued that he and his predecessors had occupied the land up to the fence for decades. The trial court determined that the fence line was the boundary by acquiescence. The plaintiff appealed, contending that the defendant's use was not sufficient to meet the strict requirements of adverse possession. The appellate court examined the Missouri doctrine of 'agreed boundaries,' which provides that where parties treat a line as the boundary for a significant period, they are bound by that line even if it deviates from the legal description. The court concluded that the fence had served as a visible, permanent monument that both parties had accepted, creating a clear mutual understanding of the boundary.

## Tally v. City of Farmington

601 S.W.3d 528 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the injury arose out of and in the course of employment as it occurred during a mandatory training exercise. It concluded that such activities clearly qualify as work-related compensable events. An employee sustained injuries to her knees during a mandatory training exercise conducted by her employer. The claim for benefits was initially denied by the administrative law judge, but the Labor and Industrial Relations Commission reversed this decision, granting compensation. The employer appealed, arguing that the injury was not a 'compensable accident' under the amended Missouri statutes that require an accident to be an unexpected traumatic event or a 'usual strain' that exceeds the range of normal activities. The employer argued that the exercises were standard activities for the job. The court examined the language of the statute, focusing on whether the injury was 'clearly work-related.' The court noted that the recent legislative amendments have restricted the definition of compensability, aiming to limit claims that are purely degenerative in nature. However, because the injury occurred during a mandatory training event, the court found it was clearly work-related and arose out of the employment relationship. The decision reinforced that while the definition of 'accident' has been narrowed, the legislative intent remains to cover injuries sustained during specific work-mandated activities. The Commission's decision to award benefits was affirmed.

## Tandy Corp. v. Director of Revenue

970 S.W.2d 347 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the internal transfers were subject to sales tax because the subsidiaries involved were distinct legal entities. The court ruled that the common ownership did not exempt the transfer of property from the definition of a retail sale. Tandy Corporation, the parent company of RadioShack, challenged the sales tax assessment on items that were transferred between their various subsidiaries. The company argued that these were internal transfers and not retail sales subject to state tax. The Director of Revenue argued that the subsidiaries functioned as separate legal entities, and therefore the movement of goods between them constituted taxable transactions under the Missouri law governing 'sale at retail.' The court analyzed the corporate structure and the legal definitions of retail sales between affiliated entities. The central issue was whether the internal transfer of property could be shielded from the tax code when the transferor and transferee are technically separate but commonly owned. This case explored the relationship between corporate entity status and tax liability, highlighting the risks involved in internal business transactions if they are not carefully structured to avoid triggering sales tax assessments.

## Tarr v. St. Louis County

537 S.W.3d 922 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the decision, holding that the calculation of average weekly wage is limited to the earnings from the employer at the time of the injury. The court refused to judicially expand the definition to include outside employment. This case dealt with the calculation of 'average weekly wage' for a part-time employee who also held multiple other jobs. The issue was whether the employee's income from concurrent employment should be included in the calculation of his disability benefits. The employer argued that only wages earned while working for them should count toward the disability calculation. The claimant argued that the statute should be interpreted to reflect his actual earning capacity, which included income from a second, unrelated job. The Commission agreed with the employer, citing the plain language of the statute as limiting the calculation to wages from the employer where the injury occurred. On appeal, the court looked at the legislative intent behind the workers' compensation system, which is to compensate for the loss of ability to earn wages. The court ruled that the statute, as written, does not permit the inclusion of concurrent, non-related employment in the calculation of the average weekly wage. The decision confirms that the statutory definition is strictly applied, even if it results in a lower benefit amount for employees holding multiple jobs.

## Tart v. Hill Behan Lumber Co.

31 F.3d 668 · United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit · 1994 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the evidence was sufficient to create a jury question regarding the existence of a racially hostile work environment. It ruled that summary judgment for the employer was inappropriate when issues of management's prompt remedial action remained. In this Section 1981 and Missouri state law claim, the plaintiff alleged that he was subjected to a racially hostile work environment. The plaintiff argued that he was constantly subjected to racial slurs and derogatory comments from coworkers and supervisors. The employer contended that the conduct, while offensive, did not rise to the level of pervasive and severe harassment necessary to create a hostile work environment as a matter of law. The federal court applying Missouri law analyzed the totality of the circumstances to determine if the conduct was frequent, humiliating, and interfered with the plaintiff's work performance. The court reviewed the employer's response to the complaints, determining whether the employer took prompt and effective remedial action once they were aware of the harassment. The opinion emphasizes the standard of objective reasonableness in evaluating whether a reasonable person in the plaintiff's position would find the work environment hostile. The court also examined the role of management's knowledge in determining whether the employer was liable for the actions of non-supervisory employees.

## Tate v. Industrial Commission

488 S.W.3d 718 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the Commission's decision. It held that the claimant failed to satisfy the notice requirements to entitle him to reimbursement for self-procured medical expenses. This case involved a dispute over the reimbursement of medical expenses following a workplace injury. The employee had undergone unauthorized surgery after the employer denied the initial request for the procedure. The commission refused to order reimbursement, ruling that the claimant failed to follow statutory notice and pre-approval procedures. The claimant appealed, arguing that the employer's initial denial and refusal to provide adequate medical care waived the necessity of further authorization. The appellate court addressed the statutory requirement that an employer be given the opportunity to provide medical treatment before an employee seeks care on their own. The court interpreted Section 287.140 regarding the selection of physicians and the process for authorized medical treatment. The opinion clarified that while an employee has a right to necessary medical care, they must follow the specific procedures to trigger the employer's financial obligation. The court noted that 'self-procured' medical treatment requires a showing that the employer refused or neglected to provide reasonable and necessary medical aid after being properly notified of the injury.

## Tate v. Industrial Commission

545 S.W.3d 390 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The Court reversed the Commission's decision, holding that the claimant was an employee. The court found that the company's control over the essential aspects of the delivery service was sufficient to create an employer-employee relationship under Missouri law. The dispute involved the classification of a worker as an employee versus an independent contractor for the purpose of eligibility for unemployment benefits and wage protections. The claimant had worked as a delivery driver, using his own vehicle and operating with significant autonomy, but the company set delivery routes and required specific uniforms. The Labor and Industrial Relations Commission had initially determined the claimant was an independent contractor. The claimant appealed, citing the 'ABC' test and the degree of control the company exercised. The appellate court examined the evidence provided regarding the company's ability to discharge the worker, the payment methods, and the nature of the work performed relative to the company's main business operations. The court focused on whether the work performed was an integral part of the business, which is a significant factor in Missouri's determination of employment status for various labor law protections.

## Tate v. M & M Express, Inc.

658 S.W.3d 522 · Mo. Ct. App. · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that performance-based bonuses are included in the average weekly wage calculation. The court held that expense-related per diem payments are excluded from the calculation as they do not constitute income. The claimant, a long-haul truck driver, suffered injuries when his vehicle was involved in a collision while he was traveling for work. A significant dispute arose regarding the calculation of the claimant's average weekly wage because his compensation structure included per diem payments and irregular mileage bonuses. The employer argued that these non-salary payments should not be included in the calculation of the average weekly wage. The Commission included both the per diem and the bonuses in the calculation, reasoning that they constituted actual compensation for the claimant's services. On appeal, the employer challenged the inclusion of these items. The appellate court analyzed the statutory definition of wages in the Missouri Workers Compensation Law. The court looked at whether the payments provided an economic benefit to the employee that functioned as compensation. Finding that the per diem payments were designed to cover expenses rather than act as income, the court remanded the case with instructions to exclude the per diem payments from the calculation while upholding the inclusion of the mileage bonuses, which were directly tied to performance and volume of work.

## Tate v. Missouri Department of Transportation

641 S.W.3d 286 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the right-to-control test determines employee status, overriding contractual labels. It affirmed that the claimant was an employee entitled to workers' compensation benefits. The claimant, a road worker, sought benefits for an injury sustained while repairing a roadway. The employer argued that the claimant was an independent contractor rather than an employee, thereby disqualifying him from workers' compensation coverage. The Commission determined that the claimant met the criteria for an employee under the 'right to control' test, as the employer supervised his work and provided the necessary tools. The employer appealed, asserting that the contractual agreement explicitly labeled the worker as an independent contractor. The Western District reviewed the legal definition of an employee, emphasizing that the label provided in a contract is not dispositive if the actual relationship demonstrates control. The court upheld the Commission's decision, noting that the reality of the work relationship--specifically the employer's authority to direct the worker's tasks--controlled over the contractual language. The decision reaffirmed that employers cannot evade workers' compensation obligations simply by misclassifying employees as independent contractors in their agreements.

## Tate v. Total Air, Inc.

2018 WL 1506543 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that non-discretionary production bonuses, which are tied to an employee's performance or output, must be included in the regular rate of pay for calculating overtime premiums. Bonuses that are not truly discretionary are part of the base compensation. This wage dispute centered on whether bonuses should be included in an employee's regular rate of pay when calculating overtime. The employer paid the plaintiff a production bonus based on the number of units installed. When calculating the plaintiff's overtime, the employer calculated it at the base hourly rate, excluding the production bonuses. The trial court agreed with the employer, ruling that production bonuses were discretionary and thus excludable. On appeal, the Missouri Court of Appeals disagreed, distinguishing between discretionary bonuses and non-discretionary production bonuses. The court noted that because the bonus was tied to the number of units installed, it was directly related to the employee's performance and productivity, making it non-discretionary. Therefore, the bonus should have been included in the regular rate for calculating the overtime premium. The court reversed the trial court's ruling, emphasizing that employers cannot avoid overtime requirements by shifting a portion of the compensation into performance-based bonuses. This case provides clear guidance on the treatment of production bonuses under Missouri's wage calculation requirements.

## Tauchert v. Bernstein

964 S.W.2d 440 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a merger clause prevents the enforcement of oral warranties or promises not included in the contract but does not bar a claim for fraudulent inducement. Fraudulent misrepresentation remains an independent cause of action. The plaintiffs entered into a contract to purchase a business, including its assets and inventory. Following the closing, the plaintiffs alleged that the seller breached the contract by misrepresenting the value of the inventory and the profitability of the business. The seller argued that the plaintiffs had an opportunity to conduct due diligence and that the merger clause in the contract stated that no representations were made outside of the written document. The appellate court analyzed whether the merger clause precluded the plaintiffs' claims of fraudulent misrepresentation. The court held that while a merger clause is generally effective in defining the scope of the agreement, it cannot be used to shield a party from liability for intentional fraudulent inducement. The court distinguished between contract-based claims, which are barred by merger clauses, and tort-based claims of fraud, which are not. The ruling provided a clear distinction between these causes of action in the context of business acquisition contracts.

## Taylor v. B&B Properties

672 S.W.3d 105 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2023 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the landlord's consistent acceptance of late rent did not waive the requirement that the tenant be in good standing to exercise the option. The court denied the tenant's claim for specific performance. The dispute concerned an commercial lease option-to-purchase agreement. The tenant argued that they had timely exercised their option to purchase the property, but the landlord claimed the exercise was invalid because of an outstanding rent balance. The tenant contended that the landlord had previously accepted late payments, thereby waiving the 'time is of the essence' clause in the contract. The trial court examined the conduct of the parties and the language of the option agreement regarding the condition of 'being in good standing' to exercise the option. The appellate court reviewed whether the landlord's historical acceptance of late payments constituted a waiver of the strict performance requirement. The case addresses the principles of contract modification and the interpretation of option-to-purchase contracts in commercial settings, focusing on whether a party can suddenly enforce strict compliance after a pattern of informal behavior.

## Taylor v. Missouri State Treasurer

648 S.W.3d 104 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the Commission, holding that the claimant failed to demonstrate permanent total disability. The decision was based on evidence showing the claimant had retained residual functional capacity. The claimant sought Second Injury Fund benefits following an injury to his leg, arguing that his pre-existing back condition, when combined with the new injury, resulted in permanent total disability. ## Taylor v. O'Reilly Automotive

512 S.W.3d 840 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a claimant's refusal of surgery is not automatically unreasonable. The Commission acts within its discretion when determining if a refusal of surgery constitutes an unreasonable failure to mitigate damages. The claimant, a retail employee, suffered a knee injury while lifting heavy boxes. The employer requested that the Commission reduce the compensation amount, alleging that the claimant failed to mitigate her damages by refusing to undergo a recommended surgery. The employer provided evidence that the surgery had a high success rate and would have allowed the claimant to return to full-duty work. The Commission refused to reduce the award, finding that the claimant's fear of surgery and the associated risks were objectively reasonable under the circumstances. On appeal, the employer argued that the Commission ignored the 'refusal of treatment' provision of the Missouri Workers' Compensation Law, which permits a reduction in benefits if a claimant unreasonably refuses medical care. The appellate court reviewed the reasonableness of the refusal, holding that a claimant is not required to undergo major surgical procedures if there is a genuine concern for the outcome. The court found no error in the Commission's ruling.

## Taylor v. Phoenixville School District

184 F.3d 296 · 3d Cir. · 1999 · Federal

Holding: The court held that an employee does not need to use formal language to request a reasonable accommodation. If an employer has notice of a disability and a request for help, the duty to engage in the interactive process is triggered. Taylor, a school secretary, was terminated after she had been away on medical leave due to bipolar disorder. She claimed the school district failed to accommodate her. The school district argued that it did not know she needed an accommodation because the request was not specific enough. The Third Circuit reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment, stating that an employee does not need to use the phrase 'reasonable accommodation' to trigger the ADA protections. As long as the employer knows the employee has a disability and requests support related to that disability, the duty to interact is triggered. The court clarified that the employer's lack of knowledge about the specific nature of the bipolar condition did not excuse its failure to initiate the interactive process. The decision established a clear standard that employers must interpret requests for assistance in a flexible and responsive manner.

## Taylor v. Riojas

141 S. Ct. 52 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2020 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that qualified immunity is not a license to violate constitutional rights in ways that are 'obvious.' The court ruled that the conditions of the cell were a clear violation of the Eighth Amendment, regardless of the absence of a specific prior judicial precedent. Trent Taylor, an inmate, sued prison officials after they placed him in cells covered in feces for several days without providing him a way to clean himself or his clothing. He claimed this was a violation of the Eighth Amendment. The Fifth Circuit granted the officers qualified immunity, agreeing that the law was not clearly established. The Supreme Court vacated that decision, ruling that the conditions were so egregious that no reasonable officer could have believed them to be lawful. Even without a case featuring identical facts, the obviousness of the violation was enough to deny qualified immunity. This case serves as a rare exception to the requirement for a specific factual precedent, acknowledging that some conduct is so clearly unconstitutional that officials must know it is illegal regardless of whether it has been litigated previously in a similar manner.

## Taylor v. Riojas

592 U.S. 7 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2020 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment is violated by extreme conditions of confinement that deny basic human dignity, and that officials are not entitled to qualified immunity when their conduct is so obviously egregious that it violates clearly established law, even if no case with identical facts exists. Trent Taylor, an inmate, was placed in solitary confinement for six days. For four of those days, he was kept in a cell covered in human feces, and for the other two, he was kept in a cell with raw sewage on the floor, forcing him to sleep in it. He sued prison officials for cruel and unusual punishment. The lower courts acknowledged the extreme conditions but granted qualified immunity to the officers, reasoning that there was no 'clearly established' law stating that holding an inmate in such conditions for only six days was unconstitutional. The Supreme Court reversed, stating that no reasonable official could have believed that this treatment was lawful. The Court held that the outrageous nature of the conditions was so severe that it constituted a clear violation of the Eighth Amendment, even

## Taylor v. St. Louis County

563 S.W.3d 741 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that even if work is performed without explicit prior authorization, if the employer knows or should know that the work is being performed for their benefit, it must be compensated. A policy against unauthorized overtime does not waive the obligation to pay for actual work. This case dealt with police officers who sought back pay for time spent cleaning and maintaining their equipment and vehicles, arguing that such tasks were part of their required work duties. The county argued that the officers were not authorized to perform such work outside of their regular shift hours and that any such labor was voluntary. The case revolved around the scope of the MMWL's application to law enforcement personnel and whether the employer's lack of authorization could negate the duty to pay for work performed. The court looked at the 'suffer or permit to work' standard used in wage law. The legal debate centered on whether a policy forbidding unauthorized overtime effectively releases the employer from liability when the work is nonetheless performed and benefits the employer. The court considered the practical realities of the police department's operational requirements and whether the officers were realistically able to complete their duties within standard working hours.

## Taylor v. St. Louis County

580 S.W.3d 44 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the Commission's assessment of permanent partial disability was supported by evidence. The court declined to re-weigh the medical ratings. The claimant filed a claim for permanent partial disability (PPD) related to a knee injury. The Commission awarded benefits based on a specific percentage of disability. Both the claimant and the employer appealed--the claimant argued the percentage was too low, while the employer argued the injury was not work-related. The court conducted a thorough review of the medical testimony. The employer's expert contended the injury resulted from a non-work hobby, while the claimant's expert cited the work-related activity. The court reiterated that when evidence is conflicting, the Commission's resolution is binding unless it lacks a foundation in competent evidence. The court found that the Commission properly relied on the testimony of the primary surgeon who examined the claimant immediately following the injury. Furthermore, the court held that the determination of the PPD percentage is a factual finding within the discretion of the Commission. Since the evidence was substantial, the court affirmed the award, emphasizing that appellate courts should not interfere with the Commission's evaluation of the medical evidence in disability ratings.

## Taylor v. St. Louis County

639 S.W.3d 442 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of benefits, holding that the claimant failed to prove that his work was the prevailing factor in his cardiac event. The court upheld the Commission's finding that the medical evidence linked the heart attack to pre-existing conditions. The claimant, a police officer, suffered a cardiac event while on duty. He argued that the work-related stress was the prevailing factor in the heart attack. The employer argued that the cardiac event was entirely due to pre-existing hypertension and coronary artery disease, and that the workplace stress was minimal. The administrative law judge denied benefits, a decision the Commission upheld. The claimant appealed, arguing that the Commission failed to properly apply the 'prevailing factor' test as it pertains to internal body organ failure. Under Missouri law, heart attacks are subject to a specific burden of proof requiring that the work stress be a substantial factor. The appellate court reviewed the medical testimony and the Commission's application of the standard. The court found that the Commission properly identified the evidentiary requirements for cardiac claims and reasonably concluded that the medical record showed the heart attack was caused by long-standing natural disease processes rather than any specific, unusual exertion at work.

## Taylor v. St. Louis County

542 S.W.3d 411 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the psychological injury was compensable as it was a direct consequence of a work-related physical injury. The court affirmed the award as it met the prevailing factor requirements. The case involved a police officer who developed post-traumatic stress following a high-speed pursuit that resulted in a fatal accident. The officer filed for compensation for both physical injuries and the subsequent psychological trauma. The county argued that the psychological injury was not compensable because it lacked a corresponding permanent physical injury that was the primary factor in the distress. The Commission initially ruled in favor of the claimant. The county appealed, citing statutes that limit recovery for mental injuries. The appellate court analyzed the relationship between the physical impact of the accident and the onset of the psychological symptoms. This decision clarified how Missouri law treats 'physical-mental' claims versus 'mental-mental' claims. The court emphasized that when psychological injury flows directly from a work-related physical accident, it may be compensable, provided the physical harm remains the prevailing factor for the continued disability.

## Taylor v. St. Louis County Police Dep't

167 S.W.3d 735 (Mo. App. E.D. 2005) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment for the police department. The court held that the plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of racial discrimination or wrongful termination. The department provided substantial evidence of legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for the termination, supported by documented policy violations and insubordination. The court found no sufficient evidence that similarly situated white officers were treated more favorably or that the reasons for the plaintiff's termination were pretextual.

Second stored summary The plaintiff, a former police officer, alleged wrongful termination and racial discrimination, claiming she was fired due to her race. She argued that white officers who committed similar or more serious infractions were not terminated. The employer, the police department, maintained that the officer was terminated for legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons, including insubordination and failure to follow directives. The court reviewed the plaintiff's disciplinary record, the specific policy violations cited for termination, and compared her treatment to that of other officers. The central issue was whether the plaintiff could prove disparate treatment based on race or that the stated reasons were pretextual.

## Taylor v. St. Luke's Health System

661 S.W.3d 812 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2023 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of benefits, holding that the lack of an identifiable incident made the injury non-compensable under the new statutory criteria. A general claim of injury during a shift is insufficient to meet the strict evidentiary standards. Taylor, a nurse, sought workers' compensation for a musculoskeletal injury that occurred while assisting a patient. The health system argued that the claimant did not prove the injury resulted from an 'identifiable incident' during the work shift, as required by recent changes to the law that tightened the definition of a work-related accident. The Commission denied the claim, stating that the claimant had not met the burden of identifying the exact time and motion that caused the injury, as the pain was generalized and began after the shift. The appellate court reviewed the statutory requirement of a 'specific accident' versus a 'repetitive stress' injury. The court looked at the medical documentation to see if it established an identifiable occurrence, underscoring the shift in Missouri law toward requiring more granular documentation of workplace events.

## Taylor v. Taylor

598 S.W.3d 132 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court reversed the trial court's denial of the modification, holding that custody and visitation orders must be sufficiently definite to be enforceable and to protect the child's need for a stable and predictable schedule with both parents. The parties' dissolution decree granted the mother primary physical custody and the father visitation, with a provision that visitation would be determined by the mother's schedule. The father moved to modify, seeking a fixed visitation schedule, arguing that the vague provision led to constant conflict and denied him the right to frequent and meaningful contact. The trial court denied the modification, finding that the current arrangement was working despite the conflict. The appellate court reversed, finding that a visitation order must be sufficiently specific to be enforceable and to promote the child's stability. The court held that leaving visitation to the unilateral control of one parent is generally discouraged as it invites litigation and denies the child a predictable routine. The appellate court remanded with instructions for the trial court to establish a detailed, permanent visitation schedule that serves the best interests of the child. The decision underscores the necessity of clear, enforceable custody orders that do not rely on the ongoing cooperation of parents who are clearly in conflict, thereby ensuring the stability of the child's life.

## TC Heartland LLC v. Kraft Foods Group Brands LLC

581 U.S. 1 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2017 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that the patent-specific venue statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b), governs venue for patent infringement lawsuits. For a domestic corporation, the only proper venue is its state of incorporation. The litigation involved a dispute over venue in a patent infringement lawsuit. Kraft Foods sued TC Heartland for patent infringement in the District of Delaware. TC Heartland, a limited liability company organized under the laws of Indiana, argued that Delaware was an improper venue because it did not reside there and had not committed acts of infringement there. The case turned on the interpretation of 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b), the specific venue statute for patent litigation, and whether it was modified by the general venue statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1391. The lower courts had held that the broader definition of corporate residence in § 1391 applied to patent cases. The Supreme Court disagreed, affirming the long-standing precedent that for purposes of § 1400(b), a domestic corporation resides only in its state of incorporation. The Court held that the enactment of subsequent amendments to the general venue statute did not override the narrow venue provisions established for patent infringement actions. This decision significantly limited the ability of plaintiffs to engage in forum shopping by suing companies in jurisdictions like the Eastern District of Texas simply because they had a presence there, requiring plaintiffs to sue in a defendant's home state or where specific infringement and a regular established place of business exist.

## TC Heartland LLC v. Kraft Foods Group Brands LLC

581 U.S. 258 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2017 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the patent venue statute limits the definition of 'reside' to the state of incorporation. Consequently, patent infringement suits can only be brought where the defendant resides or has committed acts of infringement and has a regular place of business. Kraft Foods sued TC Heartland for patent infringement in the District of Delaware. TC Heartland, a company incorporated in Indiana with no meaningful presence in Delaware, argued that the venue was improper under 28 U.S.C. Section 1400(b). The lower courts applied a broader interpretation of 'reside' based on the general venue statute, which allows a corporation to be sued in any district where it is subject to personal jurisdiction. The Supreme Court overturned this approach, revisiting the Patent Act's specific venue statute. The Court clarified that for purposes of Section 1400(b), a domestic corporation 'resides' only in its state of incorporation. This decision drastically altered the landscape of patent litigation, particularly impacting the Eastern District of Texas, which had been a popular venue

Second stored summary for patent holders due to perceived plaintiff-friendly procedures. By restricting where companies could be sued, the ruling aimed to prevent forum shopping and ensure that patent litigation is tied to the defendant's actual business location or established place of business. It underscored that general corporate venue rules do not override the specific, narrower rules set forth for patent cases in the Judicial Code.

## Teague v. Lane

489 U.S. 288 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1989 · Federal

Holding: New rules of constitutional criminal procedure generally do not apply retroactively to cases on collateral review. Exceptions exist only for rules that decriminalize certain conduct or constitute bedrock, watershed procedural changes essential to the fairness of a criminal trial. Frank Teague was convicted of murder and robbery in an Illinois state court. He challenged the exclusion of black jurors by the prosecution, relying on a new rule that sought to expand the scope of constitutional protections for jury selection. The Supreme Court used this case to address whether constitutional rules should be applied retroactively to cases on collateral review. The Court held that new constitutional rules of criminal procedure do not generally apply retroactively to cases that have already become final on direct review, with two narrow exceptions: (1) rules that place certain kinds of primary, private individual conduct beyond the power of the criminal law to proscribe, and (2) 'watershed' rules of criminal procedure that are necessary to the fundamental fairness of the criminal proceeding. The decision sought to promote finality in state criminal judgments and respect for the state courts' ability to adjudicate federal constitutional issues without the threat of constant federal re-litigation. Teague remains one of the most influential precedents in the history of federal post-conviction jurisprudence.

## Tebbetts v. 1800-1802 Chouteau, LLC

319 S.W.3d 536 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the seller waived the strict enforcement of the time-of-the-essence clause. Specific performance was granted to the buyer because the seller's conduct implied an extension and prevented the buyer from closing on time. This litigation involved a complex commercial real estate transaction where the buyer sought specific performance of a purchase agreement after the seller attempted to back out. The agreement included a 'time is of the essence' clause, and the seller argued that the buyer failed to meet a crucial closing deadline, thereby terminating the contract. The buyer contended that they had requested a reasonable extension due to unforeseen delays in securing financing, which the seller had initially indicated was acceptable but later used as a pretext to cancel the sale because they found a higher offer. The court reviewed the principles of contract law regarding time-sensitive real estate performance. The case focused on whether the seller's actions constituted a waiver of the time-of-the-essence clause and whether the buyer's reliance on the seller's initial flexibility was reasonable. The court emphasized the need for clear communication in contractual extensions to avoid litigation over the validity of the purchase agreement in a competitive market.

## Tebbetts v. Suncorp

201 S.W.3d 596 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2006 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the anti-stacking provisions were clear and unambiguous. Consequently, the insurer was not required to permit the stacking of UIM benefits across multiple policies held by the insured. This case involved a dispute over the 'stacking' of underinsured motorist (UIM) benefits. The insured held multiple policies with the insurer, each providing UIM coverage. Following an accident, the insured sought to stack the UIM limits from each of the policies to cover the total damages sustained. The insurer relied on anti-stacking language in the policies, which stated that coverage could not be combined. The insured argued that the anti-stacking language was contradictory and that the policy's declarations page created an ambiguity that favored the insured. The appellate court examined the contractual provisions and the specific language used by the insurer to prohibit stacking. The court looked at whether the policies, when read together, were ambiguous and whether the insurer's failure to adequately highlight the anti-stacking provision constituted a violation of the insured's reasonable expectations of coverage. The decision highlights the strict scrutiny Missouri courts apply to anti-stacking provisions in automobile insurance contracts to protect the rights of consumers.

## Tebow v. Cont'l Cas. Co.

164 S.W.3d 548 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the policy's definition of total disability was unambiguous. It affirmed the judgment that the insured did not meet the criteria for disability benefits. Tebow filed a claim under his disability insurance policy following a medical diagnosis that he claimed rendered him unable to work. The insurer, Continental Casualty, denied the claim, asserting that the insured failed to provide sufficient proof of total disability as defined by the policy. The trial court ruled in favor of the insurer after a bench trial. Tebow appealed, challenging the trial court's interpretation of the policy's definition of 'total disability.' He argued that the court applied an overly restrictive definition that did not account for his inability to perform the 'material duties' of his specific occupation. The appellate court examined the policy language, which required the insured to be unable to perform 'each and every' material duty of his occupation to qualify for total disability benefits. The court found that the evidence presented supported the insurer's position that the insured could still perform several material duties. The court affirmed the judgment, stating that the plain language of the policy mandated a high threshold for total disability, which the insured had not met.

## Tebow v. Ellis

648 S.W.3d 911 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: Adverse possession requires possession that is hostile and under a claim of right. Where the use is permissive, it cannot satisfy the hostility element, and title by adverse possession is not established. This dispute arose from a claim of adverse possession concerning a strip of land between two neighboring properties. The plaintiffs claimed they had acquired the land through continuous, hostile, open, notorious, and exclusive possession for the statutory period of ten years. The defendants argued that the plaintiffs' use of the land was permissive, as it was based on a neighborly accommodation that had existed for decades. The appellate court reviewed the requirements for adverse possession, emphasizing that the claimant's possession must be hostile and under a claim of right, meaning it must be adverse to the interests of the true owner and not subject to the owner's permission. The trial court found that the plaintiffs failed to meet their burden of proof because they could not establish the requisite hostility, as the evidence supported a finding of permissive use. The appellate court affirmed, holding that when use is permissive, the period of possession cannot ripen into title via adverse possession, regardless of how long the use continued.

## Tebow v. Ellis

506 S.W.3d 378 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a long-standing fence line can establish a legal boundary under the doctrine of acquiescence if the parties recognized and treated it as such for a significant duration. The court affirmed the lower court's decision to maintain the status quo established by the fence. This matter involved a property line dispute between adjacent landowners concerning the location of a fence and an alleged easement. The plaintiffs sought to quiet title and establish a boundary based on an old fence line, while the defendants argued for a boundary based on a professional survey. The trial court determined the boundary based on the long-standing fence line under the doctrine of acquiescence. The defendants appealed, arguing that the survey should have controlled and that the evidence did not support a finding of acquiescence. The appellate court reviewed the principles of boundary by acquiescence, which requires that parties treat a line as the boundary for a long period of time, even if it does not strictly align with legal descriptions. The court found that the evidence of the fence standing for decades and being recognized by previous owners supported the trial court's decision. The appellate court affirmed, noting that equity supports the protection of long-standing boundaries relied upon by neighbors.

## Tebow v. Ellis

633 S.W.3d 483 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an easement by implication is established when there is common ownership, a pre-existing use of a path, and the necessity of that path for the reasonable use and enjoyment of the newly created landlocked parcel. This case dealt with an implied easement. When the owner of a large tract of land subdivided the parcel and sold sections, they failed to grant an explicit easement for access to the public road for one of the interior lots. The purchaser of the interior lot argued that an easement by implication was created based on the prior use of the road by the original owner. The defendant, who purchased the frontage lot, argued that no such easement existed because the initial division did not contemplate one. The court performed an analysis of the 'quasi-easement' theory, where a property owner uses one part of their land for the benefit of another part, and upon severance, that use becomes an easement by implication. The court determined that the essential elements for an easement by implication were present: the parcels were once owned by the same person, the use was established prior to the sale, and the access was reasonably necessary for the enjoyment of the landlocked parcel.

## Tebow v. U.S. Dental Corp.

478 S.W.3d 412 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a genuine issue of material fact existed regarding whether the defendant held itself out as the provider of care, establishing apparent agency. Summary judgment was reversed and the case remanded for trial. The plaintiff filed a medical malpractice action against a dental corporation, alleging that the staff's negligence during a routine procedure caused significant long-term facial nerve damage. The defendant corporate entity moved for summary judgment, arguing it could not be held vicariously liable for the actions of the independent contractor dentist. The appellate court addressed the concept of agency by estoppel in a medical setting, examining whether the hospital or corporation held itself out as the provider of services in a way that would lead a reasonable patient to believe the doctor was an employee. The court explored the evidence needed to establish ostensible agency, including hospital signage, billing procedures, and the patient's reasonable expectations regarding the employment status of their care providers. This decision is significant for understanding the scope of hospital or corporate liability for the conduct of medical providers who operate as contractors rather than direct employees, setting clear criteria for when such an entity may be held liable under the theory of apparent agency.

## Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd.

551 U.S. 308 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2007 · Federal

6 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that the 'strong inference' of scienter required by the PSLRA means the inference must be at least as compelling as any non-culpable explanation for the conduct. If an innocent explanation is more likely than the fraudulent one, the case must be dismissed. In a critical interpretation of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA), the Supreme Court set a high bar for pleading scienter. The case involved allegations that Tellabs misled investors about product demand. The PSLRA mandates that complaints

Second stored summary must plead facts giving rise to a 'strong inference' of scienter. Tellabs argued that the court must consider innocent explanations when evaluating this inference. The Supreme Court ruled that a complaint will survive a motion to dismiss only if a reasonable person would deem the inference of scienter 'cogent and at least as compelling' as any opposing inference of non-fraudulent intent. This 'holistic' test requires courts to weigh the plaintiff's allegations against all plausible alternative explanations for the conduct in question. This decision significantly increased the hurdle for plaintiffs to even get into the discovery phase of litigation, forcing them to provide high-quality evidence of fraudulent intent early in the case, thus curbing frivolous litigation against public companies.

## Tennessee v. Garner

471 U.S. 1 · U.S. Supreme Court · 1985 · Federal

4 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that the Fourth Amendment prohibits the use of deadly force to prevent the escape of a fleeing suspect unless it is necessary to prevent the escape and the officer has probable cause to believe that the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others. A Memphis police officer shot and killed Edward Garner, an unarmed 15-year-old burglary suspect, as he was attempting to flee over a fence. The officer acted in accordance with a Tennessee statute that authorized the use of 'all necessary means' to effect the arrest of a fleeing felon. Garner's father filed a § 1983 action against the police department and the city, arguing that the use of deadly force violated the Fourth Amendment because the suspect posed no threat of serious physical harm to the officer or others. The case presented a conflict between the common-law rule permitting deadly force against any fleeing felon and modern constitutional standards prohibiting unreasonable seizures. The Court reviewed whether the Fourth Amendment limits the use of deadly force to situations where the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury.

## Tension Envelope Corp. v. Director of Revenue

971 S.W.2d 314 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1998 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that the taxpayer was entitled to the manufacturing exemption as the printing process qualified as manufacturing. The conflicting statutes were resolved in favor of the taxpayer. Tension Envelope Corp. challenged the Director of Revenue's assessment of sales tax on the purchase of equipment used to print and manufacture envelopes. The taxpayer claimed the equipment was exempt under the manufacturing exemption for machinery used in the production of tangible personal property. The Director argued that printing envelopes was 'printing' and not 'manufacturing,' and thus the specific exemption for printing machinery was narrower than the general manufacturing exemption, which did not apply. The Administrative Hearing Commission sided with the Director, ruling that the specific statutes governing the printing industry took precedence over the general manufacturing exemption. Tension Envelope appealed to the Missouri Supreme Court, asking the court to reconcile conflicting sections of the tax code. The court reviewed the legislative history and the specific language of the exemptions to determine if they were mutually exclusive or if they could be applied concurrently. The decision clarifies how tax exemptions are interpreted when a taxpayer's activities fall under multiple descriptive categories in the tax code.

## Tepel v. Wimmer

574 S.W.2d 369 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1978 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that where adjoining owners have recognized a physical barrier, such as a fence, as the boundary line for a significant period, they are bound by that line under the doctrine of agreed boundaries. A formal survey cannot negate a boundary long settled by mutual acquiescence. The case involved a classic boundary dispute resolved by the doctrine of agreed boundaries. The parties disagreed on the exact location of the fence line separating their agricultural tracts. One party sought to have the boundary determined by a modern survey, while the other party argued that a long-standing fence had served as the recognized boundary for over forty years, effectively settling the line regardless of the original deed's description. The Supreme Court of Missouri analyzed the doctrine of acquiescence and agreed boundaries, noting that when adjoining landowners occupy to a line and treat it as the boundary for a long period, they are bound by that line even if it differs from the surveyed description. The court emphasized that the stability of land titles is paramount and that long-term recognition of a physical boundary creates a conclusive presumption of an agreement. The court affirmed the judgment favoring the fence line, upholding the established boundary over the conflicting modern survey.

Holding: The court held that the developer did not commit a material breach that excused the HOA from its financial obligations. This litigation involved a homeowner's association's (HOA) dispute with a developer over the maintenance of common areas and the transfer of control of these areas. The HOA alleged that the developer breached the original development contract by failing to complete infrastructure improvements and by charging excessive management fees before transferring control. The trial court ruled against the HOA, finding that the developer had complied with the substantial requirements of the agreement. The HOA appealed, asserting that the developer's failure to complete the project constituted a material breach that excused the HOA from paying the disputed fees. The court found that the developer's delays did not excuse the HOA from fulfilling its own obligations, as the two were not fully dependent. The opinion underscores the complexities of long-term development contracts and the necessity of clearly defined performance timelines for both developers and HOAs.

A police officer observed two men, including John Terry, pacing in front of a store window multiple times, suggesting they were planning a robbery. Second stored summary found pistols on Terry and another man. Terry was charged with carrying a concealed weapon. ## Terry v. United States

Holding: The decision clarifies the application of sentencing statutes related to prior convictions. It underscores the importance of adherence to clear procedural standards in cases where criminal outcomes depend on the historical validity of law enforcement encounters. This case dealt with the intersection of sentencing law and Fourth Amendment procedural issues. The analysis reaffirmed the importance of clear procedural standards in both the investigation and the resulting adjudication of criminal cases. Although primarily a statutory interpretation case, it reflects the ongoing judicial focus on the practical application of constitutional rules during the initial stages of a criminal encounter, ensuring that the standards established in earlier precedent remain coherent when applied to complex federal sentencing regimes that take into account the history of police stops and seizures in a defendant's record.

## Teson v. Vasquez

561 S.W.2d 119 · Missouri Court of Appeals, St. Louis District · 1977 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that a fence line does not automatically become a legal boundary merely through usage. To establish a boundary by acquiescence, there must be clear evidence of mutual recognition and agreement, which was absent in this case. This case involved a dispute over the location of a boundary line between two properties that were once part of a larger tract. The plaintiffs alleged that a fence line, which had been treated as the boundary for many years, was the correct legal boundary. The defendants, relying on a recent survey, claimed the boundary was located elsewhere, effectively encroaching on the plaintiffs' yard. The trial court ruled in favor of the defendants, finding the survey to be the definitive evidence of the boundary. The plaintiffs appealed, arguing that the doctrine of acquiescence should apply, as the previous owners had treated the fence as the true boundary for decades. The Missouri Court of Appeals examined the history of the property and the specific requirements for establishing a boundary by acquiescence. The court noted that mere usage is not enough; there must be an agreement or a long-standing mutual recognition that the fence line constitutes the boundary. Because the plaintiffs failed to present sufficient evidence of such a mutual agreement or recognition, the court held that the survey's deeded description must prevail over the informal fence line.
