## Todd v. Missouri United School Ins. Council

223 S.W.3d 156 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2007 · Missouri

Also captioned Todd v. Missouri United School Insurance Council

Holding: The court held that an insurance pool is not an 'insurance company' for the purposes of statutory sovereign immunity waiver. Therefore, the school district did not waive its immunity by participating in the risk-sharing council. In this matter, a student was injured in a school-related incident, and the question was whether the school district's membership in an insurance pool constituted an insurance policy for the purposes of sovereign immunity waiver. The school district argued that it was protected by sovereign immunity, while the injured party claimed that the insurance pool operated effectively as an insurer, waiving immunity up to the policy limits. The court had to determine the legal nature of the insurance council, which was formed by various school districts to share the risk of liability. The plaintiff argued that the council's governing documents contained provisions that mirrored standard insurance contracts. The lower courts struggled with whether a public risk-sharing entity qualifies as an 'insurer' under the statutes governing the waiver of sovereign immunity. The Supreme Court of Missouri reviewed the statutes governing municipal risk-sharing pools and analyzed whether the legislature intended to treat these pools identically to commercial insurance carriers for the purposes of immunity. This case is crucial for understanding how public entity risk management programs interact with insurance coverage laws and sovereign immunity protections in Missouri.

Second stored summary Holding: The Court held that a school district's participation in a self-insured risk pool constitutes the procurement of liability insurance. This procurement acts as a waiver of sovereign immunity to the extent of the policy limits. A student was injured in a school-sponsored activity and brought a negligence action against the school district. The school district was a member of a self-insured risk pool known as the Missouri United School Insurance Council (MUSIC). MUSIC denied coverage, arguing that the school district's sovereign immunity had not been waived because the risk pool was not an insurance company subject to the same requirements. The underlying issue was whether the school district was required to carry liability insurance and whether the risk pool functioned as such for the purpose of waiving sovereign immunity under the Missouri statutes. The district court determined

Second stored summary that the school district was covered. The case reached the Supreme Court of Missouri to resolve whether membership in MUSIC constituted procuring liability insurance. The Court looked at the enabling statutes that allowed school districts to form self-insured pools. It concluded that when a school district joins such a pool, it is essentially purchasing insurance for the purposes of the waiver of sovereign immunity under the law, specifically regarding bodily injury claims. The Court affirmed that the insurance provided through the risk pool acts as a waiver of immunity up to the limits of the coverage provided in the agreement.

## Tolan v. Cotton

572 U.S. 650 · United States Supreme Court · 2014 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that in ruling on a motion for summary judgment, courts must view the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party. The Fifth Circuit failed to properly credit evidence that would have supported a jury finding of excessive force, thereby violating the fundamental principles of summary judgment procedure. Robert Tolan was shot by a police officer, Jeffrey Cotton, in the driveway of his parents' home. Tolan filed a Section 1983 action, claiming the shooting was an unconstitutional use of excessive force. The district court granted summary judgment for the officer, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed, concluding that the officer was entitled to qualified immunity. The appellate court made several factual inferences in favor of the officer, specifically regarding whether Tolan posed an immediate threat. The Supreme Court reviewed the case to determine whether the lower courts had properly applied the standards for summary judgment in qualified immunity cases, particularly when there are disputed issues of material fact regarding the behavior of the victim and the officer during the encounter.

## Tolentino v. Starwood Hotels & Resorts Worldwide, Inc.

437 S.W.3d 754 · Missouri Supreme Court · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that class certification is appropriate when the plaintiffs allege a uniform policy of wage underpayment, even if damages must be calculated individually. It clarified that Missouri courts should favor class treatment when a common policy allegedly violates wage laws across a large workforce. The decision facilitated the pursuit of collective wage and hour litigation in the state. While technically a case concerning class certification, this decision fundamentally addressed the ability of employees to bring collective actions for wage violations under Missouri law. The plaintiffs sought to challenge the employer's practices regarding tipped employees and the application of tip credits toward the minimum wage. The defendants challenged the court's authority to certify a class for claims that involved individualized wage calculations. The Missouri Supreme Court examined the procedural requirements for class actions in the context of the Missouri Minimum Wage Law. This case is pivotal because it clarified how wage and hour claims, which are often fact-specific and dependent on individual hours worked, can be pursued collectively. The discussion included an analysis of whether the commonality of the employer's policy outweighed the individual differences in damages. The Court had to reconcile the need for judicial efficiency in wage enforcement with the rights of defendants to challenge the validity of each individual claim brought under a collective umbrella.

## Tolle v. St. Louis Public Service Co.

362 S.W.2d 674 (Mo. 1962) · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1962 · Missouri

Holding: The Supreme Court of Missouri reversed the trial court's judgment. The court found that the plaintiff failed to present substantial evidence that the bus driver was negligent. Furthermore, the court held that the evidence clearly showed the pedestrian was contributorily negligent as a matter of law, which barred recovery. The pedestrian's actions were deemed to be the direct and proximate cause of their own injuries. This action involved a pedestrian who was struck and injured by a bus operated by the St. Louis Public Service Company. The plaintiff claimed that the bus driver was negligent in operating the bus, specifically by failing to keep a proper lookout and by failing to yield the right-of-way to a pedestrian in a crosswalk. The bus company argued that the pedestrian was contributorily negligent by darting into the street unexpectedly and failing to exercise proper care for their own safety. The trial court entered a judgment for the plaintiff, and the defendant appealed, primarily challenging the sufficiency of the evidence to support the finding of negligence and the rejection of the contributory negligence defense.

## Topsy's Shoppes, Inc. v. Director of Revenue

558 S.W.2d 342 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1977 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the popping of corn by Topsy's Shoppes constituted manufacturing, thus making the equipment used in that process exempt from sales tax as machinery used in manufacturing. The court reasoned that the popping process transformed the raw kernels into a different product. Topsy's Shoppes, a chain of retail food stores, challenged the assessment of sales tax on its popcorn-making operations. The Director of Revenue argued that the process of popping corn and adding flavors constituted the production of a new product and was therefore a taxable manufacturing activity, or conversely, that the popcorn was a taxable prepared food. Topsy's argued that its operations were not manufacturing and that the sale of the popcorn should be treated under the same rules as other retail sales of food products. The court examined the definition of 'manufacturing' and 'processing' in the context of retail food preparation. The issue was whether the act of popping the corn constituted a change in the property sufficient to classify the store as a manufacturer. The court also analyzed whether the ingredients were exempt under the sale-for-resale rule. This case addressed the intersection of food industry practices and tax classification, specifically whether local food preparation for immediate sale to consumers constitutes manufacturing under the Missouri tax laws.

## Topsy's Shoppes, Inc. v. Director of Revenue

657 S.W.2d 465 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the popcorn popping equipment did not qualify for the manufacturing machinery exemption. The court reasoned that the legislative intent for the exemption focused on industrial manufacturing and not on equipment used for food preparation in a retail setting. Topsy's Shoppes challenged the Director of Revenue's decision to assess sales tax on the equipment used for popping popcorn in its retail locations. The Director characterized the process as a 'manufacturing' activity, which would normally exempt the equipment from taxation if the items produced were intended for sale. However, the Director argued that the specific nature of the business--retail sales--meant the equipment did not qualify for the manufacturing exemption under the governing statute. Topsy's Shoppes argued that

Second stored summary because they were creating a finished product from raw kernels, they were engaged in manufacturing, and therefore the equipment should be tax-exempt. The dispute touched upon the threshold between food preparation in a retail environment and industrial manufacturing. The Supreme Court of Missouri was tasked with determining whether the legislature intended to extend the tax exemption for manufacturing machinery to businesses that are primarily engaged in retail food service, a question that had significant implications for the tax obligations of similar businesses across the state.

## Topsy's Shoppes, Inc. v. State

676 S.W.2d 20 · Missouri Supreme Court · 1984 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the sales of popcorn and snacks at retail were taxable. The items sold constituted tangible personal property and did not qualify for food exemptions. Topsy's Shoppes, a popcorn and confectionery business, challenged the state's assessment of sales tax on its carry-out food items. The taxpayer argued that its sales were 'service' based and not 'retail sales' of tangible personal property, or alternatively, that they should be exempt as food items. The Director of Revenue argued that the popcorn and snacks sold by the shop constituted the sale of food at retail, which is clearly subject to sales tax under Missouri law. The case involved an analysis of the 'retail sale' definition and whether the prepared nature of the food brought it within the taxing authority. The court had to distinguish between food sold for immediate consumption and other types of grocery sales. The decision solidified the state's power to tax prepared foods sold through retail shops and clarified the scope of the food tax exemption.

## Torres v. Madrid

592 U.S. 306 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2021 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the application of physical force to the body of a person with the intent to restrain constitutes a seizure for purposes of the Fourth Amendment, regardless of whether the person is successfully stopped or submits to the officer's authority. Two officers approached a woman, Roxanne Torres, who was sitting in a parked car. Believing she was a suspect they were looking for, they approached the vehicle. Torres, fearing for her safety, drove away. The officers fired 13 shots at the car, hitting Torres twice. Torres survived and filed a Section 1983 lawsuit, arguing that the officers' shooting constituted an unreasonable seizure under the Fourth Amendment. The lower courts dismissed the claim, reasoning that because Torres had not been physically subdued or stopped by the shots, there was no 'seizure.' The Supreme Court reversed, holding that the application of physical force to the body of a person with the intent to restrain constitutes a seizure, even if the person does not immediately submit or stop. The ruling significantly expanded the definition of what constitutes a 'seizure' under the Fourth Amendment, allowing plaintiffs to pursue excessive force claims even if they escaped from the immediate encounter.

## Townsend v. E-Z Bail Bonds

2013 WL 5493019 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the services of a bail bond company constitute merchandise within the meaning of the MPA. The court affirmed that the MPA is applicable to the business practices of bail bond providers. Townsend brought a claim against a bail bond company under the MPA, alleging that the company failed to provide an itemized list of fees and misrepresented the refundable nature of the bond premium. The company argued that bail bond services are not 'merchandise' under the MPA and that the regulation of bail bonds is exclusively reserved for the courts and specific statutory bail bond regulations. The court examined the language of the MPA to see if the services provided by a bail bondsman fit the definition of a sale or advertisement of merchandise. The plaintiff contended that the bail bond premium is a payment for a service, thereby subjecting the company to the same consumer protection laws as any other commercial business.

## Traders Bank of Kansas City v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.

637 S.W.3d 456 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that Wells Fargo did not breach the participation agreement, as its actions fell within the scope of its discretionary authority as the agent. The exculpatory clauses were valid and protected the bank from claims of ordinary negligence. This commercial dispute centered on the interpretation of a participation agreement between two banks regarding a syndicated loan. Traders Bank alleged that Wells Fargo, acting as the lead agent, breached the agreement by failing to provide adequate notice regarding the status of the underlying collateral and by prematurely releasing certain security interests. The agreement contained specific provisions regarding the agent's duties to the participants, and Traders Bank claimed that Wells Fargo's actions fell below the standard of care required of a fiduciary or contractual agent. Wells Fargo argued that its actions were permitted under the broad discretionary authority granted to the lead agent by the terms of the agreement. The appellate court examined the interplay between the standard of care provisions and the exculpatory clauses contained within the contract. This case provides an analysis of the duties owed by lead lenders to participating lenders and the extent to which contractual liability can be mitigated through well-drafted discretionary language in complex financial instruments.

## Traders Insurance Co. v. Aetna Insurance Co.

38 S.W.3d 408 · Missouri Supreme Court · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that when two insurance policies have conflicting 'other insurance' clauses, they are mutually repugnant and must be ignored. In such instances, the loss should be prorated between the insurers based on their policy limits. This case involved an inter-insurer dispute regarding the interpretation of 'other insurance' clauses in two separate liability policies covering the same incident. One insurer paid the full claim and then sought contribution from the other insurer, claiming that the second insurer's policy was primary. The trial court found the language of both policies to be 'mutually repugnant' and ordered the losses to be prorated between the two companies. The appellate court examined the contractual language in each policy. Aetna argued that its policy was clearly excess, while Traders argued that the policies were contradictory. The Missouri Supreme Court, having accepted transfer of the case, analyzed the specific provisions for primary and excess coverage. The court held that when two insurance policies contain competing 'other insurance' clauses that attempt to limit liability in the same way, those clauses are indeed mutually repugnant and ineffective. Consequently, the court mandated that the loss be shared on a pro-rata basis, emphasizing that the court should not prioritize one policy over another based on slight differences in phrasing when the intent is to shift the burden entirely.

## Travelers Casualty & Surety Co. of America v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co.

549 U.S. 443 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2007 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the Bankruptcy Code does not disallow a claim for contractual attorney's fees solely because they were incurred during the post-petition period. Unsecured claims for such fees are enforceable provided they are permitted by state law. Travelers, a surety company, held an unsecured claim against PG&E based on a pre-petition contract that provided for the payment of attorney's fees incurred by the creditor. When PG&E filed for bankruptcy, the lower courts disallowed the claim for attorney's fees, applying a rule from the Ninth Circuit that prohibited the recovery of post-petition attorney's fees on unsecured claims. The Supreme Court reviewed this rule, known as the 'Fobian rule.' The Court noted that the Bankruptcy Code does not explicitly bar unsecured creditors from recovering contractual attorney's fees. Furthermore, the Court determined that the Bankruptcy Code generally defers to state law to determine the enforceability of claims. Because the contract was valid under state law, there was no basis in the Bankruptcy Code to disallow the attorney's fees simply because they were incurred after the bankruptcy petition was filed. This decision effectively abolished the Fobian rule and confirmed the importance of contract terms in bankruptcy claims.

## Treasurer of the State of Missouri v. Diana Penney

605 S.W.3d 536 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the Commission's award. It held that the interpretation of the statutory requirements for the Second Injury Fund was correct and that the medical evidence supported the finding of permanent total disability. This worker's compensation dispute focused on the Second Injury Fund and the eligibility criteria for benefits. Diana Penney sought benefits from the fund, alleging that a previous disability, combined with a recent work-related injury, left her permanently and totally disabled. The Treasurer, as the custodian of the fund, contested the claim, arguing that the prior disability was not sufficiently severe to meet the statutory threshold and that the recent injury alone did not cause the total disability. The case reached the appellate court after the Labor and Industrial Relations Commission found in favor of Penney. The Treasurer challenged the Commission's interpretation of the Second Injury Fund statutes, specifically regarding the methodology for calculating the degree of disability contribution from previous injuries.

## Treetop Village Apts. v. Mohammed

139 S.W.3d 581 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the landlord did not waive the right to enforce the lease terms. The presence of a non-waiver clause in the lease protected the landlord despite their prior acceptance of partial payments.

Second stored summary This dispute arose from a residential lease agreement. The landlord brought an action for unlawful detainer after the tenant allegedly violated the lease by keeping unauthorized guests and failing to pay late fees. The tenant argued that the landlord had waived the right to enforce the lease terms by accepting partial rent payments and failing to object to the guests in previous months. The trial court ruled in favor of the landlord. On appeal, the Western District examined the issue of waiver in the context of a lease agreement. The court explained that while a party can waive rights under a contract, such waiver must be intentional and clear. The court found that the landlord's acceptance of rent did not automatically constitute a waiver of the lease provisions regarding guests or fees, especially since the lease contained a 'non-waiver' clause. This case is important for its discussion of non-waiver clauses, which are designed to prevent a party from losing their contractual rights simply by acting reasonably in the day-to-day administration of a contract.

## Trevino v. Thaler

569 U.S. 413 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2013 · Federal

Holding: The Martinez v. Ryan exception for excusing procedural default of ineffective-assistance-of-trial-counsel claims applies even when state procedures differ from those in Arizona, provided the state's system effectively makes it impossible or highly impractical to raise such claims during direct appeal. Carlos Trevino was convicted of capital murder in Texas and sentenced to death. He sought state post-conviction relief, but his counsel failed to raise a claim of ineffective assistance of trial counsel regarding the failure to investigate mitigating evidence. Because Texas state law did not provide a procedural framework that allowed ineffective assistance claims to be raised on direct appeal, prisoners were forced to raise such claims during initial collateral review. Relying on the decision in Martinez v. Ryan, Trevino argued that his procedural default should be excused because he had no counsel during his initial collateral proceeding who was capable of raising the claim. The Fifth Circuit held that the Martinez exception did not apply to Texas because its procedures were more generous than the Arizona procedures at issue in Martinez. The Supreme Court reversed, holding that the Martinez exception applies in jurisdictions where, as in Texas, the state's procedural system makes it highly unlikely that a defendant can raise an ineffective assistance of trial counsel claim on direct appeal. The decision significantly broadened the applicability of the Martinez rule, ensuring that prisoners in states with similar restrictive procedural systems are not left without a remedy for meritorious Sixth Amendment claims.

## Tri-State Cent. v. City of St. Louis

633 S.W.3d 468 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the contractor failed to satisfy the contract's written change-order requirements, which were strictly enforceable in public works projects. The judgment in favor of the city was affirmed. This case originated from a dispute over a construction contract for municipal improvements. The contractor sued the City of St. Louis for breach of contract, claiming that the city failed to pay for additional work caused by unforeseen site conditions. The city argued that the contract contained an 'exculpatory clause' which shifted the risk of site conditions to the contractor, and that the contractor failed to follow the contract's strict change-order process. The trial court entered judgment for the city, noting that the contractor did not properly document the extra expenses as required by the contract. On appeal, the contractor contended that the city waived the formal change-order requirements through the conduct of its project managers who verbally directed the changes. The court analyzed the doctrine of waiver in the context of government construction contracts, specifically looking at whether local ordinances and contract provisions could be modified by verbal representations. The court concluded that strict compliance with change-order procedures is essential in public works contracts to protect taxpayer funds. Because the contractor did not provide written notice as required by the contract, the court held that the city was not liable for the additional costs, rejecting the waiver argument.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the non-compete agreement was unenforceable because it was overly broad in its geographic scope and lacked a reasonable time limitation. This case concerns the enforceability of a non-compete agreement within an employment contract. Triarch Industries sought to enjoin a former employee from working for a competitor, alleging that the employee breached a restrictive covenant. The trial court denied the request for a preliminary injunction, finding the non-compete clause to be overbroad and unreasonable. On appeal, the Missouri Supreme Court considered the standards for determining the reasonableness of restrictive covenants in employment contracts, focusing on temporal and geographic limitations. The court examined whether the employer had a legitimate protectable interest, such as trade secrets or customer contacts, that justified the restriction. The decision serves as a key precedent for assessing the validity of non-compete clauses in Missouri, emphasizing that such restraints are viewed with disfavor and must be strictly limited to what is necessary to protect the employer's interests. The analysis balanced the employer's need for protection against the employee's right to

Keep Trucking, LLC disputed the claim on the grounds of geographical jurisdiction, arguing that the contract of hire was not executed in Missouri and the injury occurred entirely in another state. The appellate court reviewed whether Missouri law could govern the claim when the employer was incorporated in another state but conducted business operations and maintained employment relationships within Missouri. The court scrutinized the specific requirements for jurisdiction when there is no clear nexus between the state and the location of the accident, focusing on where the employment contract was finalized and where the essential services were performed by the claimant.

## Trop v. Dulles

356 U.S. 86 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1958 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment's prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment must be interpreted in light of 'evolving standards of decency.' Denationalization as a punishment is constitutionally impermissible because it destroys the individual's status in society. Albert Trop, a native-born American, served in the U.S. Army during World War II. He deserted for a day and was court-martialed. Years later, he applied for a passport and was denied on the grounds that he had lost his citizenship by virtue of his desertion under a specific statute. Trop sued, arguing that denationalization as a penalty for wartime desertion was a violation of the Eighth Amendment's prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment. The Supreme Court, in a plurality opinion, agreed. The Court famously articulated that the Eighth Amendment must draw its meaning from the 'evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society.' By stripping a person of their citizenship, the government was imposing a punishment that is 'more primitive than torture,' as it essentially destroys the individual's status in organized society. The Court held that this form of punishment was beyond the power of the government, as it lacked a legitimate penological justification and was fundamentally inhumane.

## Truck Ins. Exch. v. Prairie Framing, LLC

162 S.W.3d 64 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2005 · Missouri

Also captioned Truck Insurance Exchange v. Prairie Framing, LLC

Holding: The court held that the 'care, custody, or control' exclusion was inapplicable because the insured did not have exclusive control over the entire job site at the time of the damage. The insurer was found obligated to indemnify the insured for the judgment. This case dealt with an insurer's declaratory judgment action regarding its duty to indemnify a framing company for a judgment entered against it in a construction litigation. The framing company had been sued for negligence and breach of contract. The insurer argued that the policy contained an exclusion for damage to 'property in the care, custody, or control of the insured,' and that the damage for which the framing company was held liable occurred while they were in possession of the building site. The trial court found the insurer had a duty to indemnify, based on its interpretation of the 'care, custody, or control' exclusion. On appeal, the court examined the specific facts of the construction project to determine the level of authority and control the insured exercised over the property. The appellate court addressed whether the exclusion applied to the entirety of the project or only to specific segments under the insured's direct control. The court reinforced the rule that policy exclusions are to be strictly construed against the insurer, and if the insurer wishes to exclude coverage, the burden of proving that the specific factual circumstances fall squarely within the exclusion rests on the insurer.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that the anti-subrogation rule bars an insurer from pursuing a subrogation claim against its own insured, including an additional insured under a commercial policy. The insurer cannot collect for a loss that it was contractually obligated to cover for the party in question. This case involved a subrogation action where an insurer attempted to recover costs from a subcontractor after a fire at a construction site. The subcontractor argued that it was an 'additional insured' under the general contractor's policy and that the insurer could not pursue a subrogation claim against its own insured. The insurer contended that the subcontractor was not an additional insured for the specific loss in question. The trial court entered judgment for the subcontractor, ruling that the anti-subrogation rule prohibits an insurer from suing its own insured to recover for a loss covered by the policy. On appeal, the court examined the scope of the additional insured endorsement and whether the subcontractor's potential liability fell within the contractual language. The court concluded that because the subcontractor was named as an additional insured on the policy at the time of the fire, the insurer's subrogation claim was barred by the principle that an insurer cannot seek reimbursement from a party it has insured against the very risk that led to the claim.

## Truck Insurance Exchange v. Prairie Framing, LLC

616 S.W.3d 479 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the 'your work' exclusion precluded coverage for the costs associated with repairing the framing itself. However, the court found that the insurer may have had a duty to defend if the complaint alleged damage to other property. This case involved a dispute between an insurer and a framing subcontractor over whether an insurer had a duty to defend the subcontractor in a construction defect lawsuit. The lawsuit alleged faulty framing that caused structural integrity issues. The insurer denied coverage, citing an 'impaired property' exclusion in the commercial general liability policy. The subcontractor argued that the policy provided coverage for property damage resulting from the subcontractor's faulty work. The court analyzed the 'your work' exclusion and the 'impaired property' exclusion, assessing whether they precluded coverage for the specific damages claimed. The focus of the case was on the intersection of standard policy language and the specific nature of construction defect claims. The court looked at whether the damage was limited to the insured's own work or extended to other property of the homeowner. The insurer argued that the costs to repair the faulty framing were not covered damages, as they constituted the 'business risk' of the contractor. The appellate court looked at the policy terms to determine if the specific allegations triggered the duty to defend, balancing the insurer's obligations against the specific exclusions written into the policy.

## Trump v. Hawaii

585 U.S. 667 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2018 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court upheld the travel ban, ruling that the President has broad statutory authority to suspend entry of aliens. The Court concluded that the policy was supported by a sufficient national security rationale and did not violate the Establishment Clause. The decision affirmed the principle of judicial deference to the executive in matters of national security. This case concerned Executive Order No. 13780, often referred to as a travel ban, which restricted entry into the United States for nationals of several countries. The State of Hawaii challenged the order, arguing that it exceeded the President's statutory authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment by specifically targeting Muslim-majority countries. The government contended that the President has broad plenary power under the INA to suspend the entry of aliens if he deems their entry detrimental to the interests of the United States. The lower courts had issued injunctions blocking parts of the order, focusing on the historical statements made by the executive branch regarding the intent of the policy. The litigation involved a complex balancing of executive power over foreign affairs and national security against the religious non-discrimination principles inherent in the Constitution.

## Trump v. Hawaii

138 S. Ct. 2392 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2018 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that the Proclamation was well within the President's delegated authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act to suspend the entry of noncitizens. The Court also determined that the Proclamation was supported by a sufficient neutral national security justification, thereby surviving the Establishment Clause challenge. The decision affirmed the breadth of executive authority over entry. The State of Hawaii challenged Presidential Proclamation 9645, which placed entry restrictions on nationals from several countries, most of which were Muslim-majority. Hawaii argued that the order exceeded the President's statutory authority under the Immigration and Nationality Act and violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The government argued that the President has broad plenary power to suspend the entry of aliens when it is in the interest of national security. The case involved intense litigation regarding the scope of judicial review over national security policy versus the protection of constitutional rights.

## TSC Industries, Inc. v. Northway, Inc.

426 U.S. 438 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1976 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court established the standard for materiality: an omitted fact is material if there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable shareholder would consider it important in deciding how to vote. The Court rejected the 'might' standard in favor of a 'substantial likelihood' test. This case dealt with the definition of 'materiality' in the context of proxy solicitations, a standard which has since been adopted for all securities fraud contexts, including Rule 10b-5. Northway sued TSC Industries, alleging that the proxy materials used to secure shareholder approval for a merger were misleading because they omitted certain material facts. The Seventh Circuit had adopted a relatively lenient standard for materiality, asking whether a reasonable shareholder might consider the information important. TSC appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the standard was too broad and would lead to the disclosure of unnecessary and potentially confusing information. The case provided the Court with an opportunity to define the exact threshold at which a misstatement or omission becomes 'material' enough to warrant a claim under federal securities law.

## Tull v. Boone

399 S.W.2d 635 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Kansas City District · 1966 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a landlord's acceptance of rent after the lease expiration creates a periodic tenancy. It affirmed that this conduct waives the right to immediate possession based on the expired lease. This case focused on the application of the 'tenant holdover' doctrine in a commercial context. Upon the expiration of a lease, the tenant remained in possession, and the landlord continued to accept rent payments. The landlord then sought to evict the tenant, claiming the holdover had not created a new lease term. The court examined whether the act of accepting rent after the lease expired effectively created a new, periodic tenancy by operation of law. The court looked at the intent of both parties, noting that if a landlord accepts rent without condition after the lease term expires, they generally waive the right to immediate possession and create a month-to-month tenancy. The decision explains the risks to landlords of accepting rent payments without reservation after a lease term concludes, as it essentially extends the tenancy indefinitely until proper notice is given. The ruling underscores the importance of clear communication and reservation of rights when a tenant holds over after their lease term ends.

## Tull v. City of Columbia

692 S.W.2d 840 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1985 · Missouri

Also captioned Tull v. Housing Authority of City of Columbia · Tull v. Housing Authority of City of Jefferson

Holding: The court held that a prescriptive easement for underground utilities existed, ruling that the presence of associated above-ground structures provided sufficient notice to the landowner, satisfying the 'open and notorious' element of a prescriptive easement. This case dealt with an easement for utilities and the right of the city to maintain the infrastructure on private property. The property owners challenged the city's assertion that it had an easement by prescription to install and maintain underground cables. The city argued that because the utility lines had been in place for more than twenty years, the prescriptive right had ripened. The owners contended that they were unaware of the underground lines and therefore could not have granted, nor should they be subject to, a prescriptive easement, as the use was not 'open and notorious.' The court analyzed the visibility and notoriety required for a prescriptive easement when the usage involves underground infrastructure. The court determined that the presence of above-ground utility poles and access boxes served as constructive notice to the landowners. The discussion centered on whether the subterranean nature of the wires made the use 'hidden' or if the surrounding infrastructure provided sufficient notice to satisfy the legal standard for adverse use and notice to the servient estate owner.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that open, notorious, and continuous use of a driveway for the statutory period creates a presumption of adverse use. The defendant failed to produce evidence that the usage was permissive, thereby confirming the existence of a prescriptive easement. The dispute involved the property owners' claim to a prescriptive easement over a driveway located on the defendant's land. The plaintiffs argued that they and their predecessors had used the driveway openly, notoriously, and continuously for over ten years to access their garage. The defendant argued that the use was permissive, based on a historical neighborly agreement between previous owners. At trial, testimony indicated that the use was established long before the defendant acquired the property and that no permission was ever sought or granted by any party involved during the prescriptive period. The appellate court examined whether the trial court correctly identified the elements of adverse use and the presumption of adversity that arises after the statutory period has elapsed. The court focused on whether the defendant presented sufficient evidence to rebut the presumption of adversity. ## Tull v. City of Ladue

## Tussey v. Missouri Dept. of Corrections

746 S.W.2d 110 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1988 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the plaintiff stated a valid claim under the Eighth Amendment because the prison officials' failure to act despite having knowledge of a specific threat constituted deliberate indifference. Summary judgment for the defendants was reversed. The plaintiff, an inmate, filed suit under Section 1983 alleging that the Department of Corrections violated his Eighth Amendment rights by failing to protect him from foreseeable physical violence by other inmates. The case focused on the 'deliberate indifference' standard as articulated by federal courts in cases involving prison safety. The court examined whether the prison administration had actual knowledge of the risk to the plaintiff and whether they acted with reckless disregard for that safety risk. The evidence showed that the plaintiff had informed prison officials of specific threats, yet officials failed to transfer him or implement sufficient protective measures. The court conducted a thorough review of the standard for 'cruel and unusual punishment' in the context of institutional prison management. This decision provides critical guidance for Missouri correctional facilities regarding their legal obligations to ensure prisoner safety and the potential for Section 1983 liability when they knowingly fail to act in the face of substantiated threats of violence.

## Tussey v. United Airlines, Inc.

756 F.3d 1074 · United States Court of Appeals, 8th Circuit · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the employer did not breach its fiduciary duty under ERISA, as the actions taken were within the scope of the plan's provisions and did not constitute intentional discrimination in the administration of benefits. Although a federal circuit case, it is frequently cited in Missouri civil rights litigation regarding ERISA and its impact on employee rights, which often parallel MHRA protections in terms of benefits administration. The plaintiffs alleged that the employer breached its fiduciary duty by mismanaging retirement plans, which effectively discriminated against certain classes of employees in terms of benefit distribution. The case involved extensive analysis of federal preemption and how state-level civil rights laws interact with federally governed employee benefit plans. The court examined the requirements for a breach of fiduciary duty claim and the necessity of demonstrating that the employer acted with specific intent to deny benefits. This case serves as a critical reference point for Missouri appellate courts when determining the scope of state-law claims versus federally governed retirement protections.

## Tussey v. United Airlines, Inc.

983 S.W.2d 163 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the reservation of rights clause was valid and enforceable. Consequently, the airline was permitted to modify its frequent flyer program rules without breaching the contract, as long as it adhered to the stated procedures. This case involved a dispute over an airline's frequent flyer program. The plaintiff argued that the airline breached the terms of the program contract by unilaterally changing the rules regarding the redemption of points, which resulted in a decrease in the value of the points the plaintiff had accumulated. The airline contended that the terms and conditions of the program explicitly reserved the right for

Second stored summary the company to change the rules at any time without notice. The central legal issue was whether such a broad reservation of rights clause in a contract allows for an absolute change that effectively cancels or fundamentally alters the value of the consideration already earned by the consumer. The court analyzed whether this clause rendered the contract illusory or whether the consumer's participation in the program constituted a valid acceptance of the airline's right to modify the terms. The case explores the boundaries of unilateral contract modification in consumer loyalty programs and whether such modifications violate the covenant of good faith and fair dealing.

## U.S. Bank v. State

488 S.W.3d 657 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the bank's previously perfected UCC security interest held priority over the state's subsequently filed tax lien. The tax lien did not contain explicit language to override established UCC priority rules. The bank sued for a declaratory judgment to determine the priority of its security interest versus a state-imposed tax lien on the debtor's business equipment. The state argued that its tax lien was superior to the bank's perfected UCC security interest because it was a statutory lien that arose upon the assessment of taxes. The bank argued that as a secured party who perfected its interest years before the tax assessment, its rights should be superior under the principle of 'first in time, first in right.' The court analyzed the interaction between Article 9 perfection and the specific state tax statutes. It had to decide whether the tax lien statute provided for automatic super-priority over previously perfected UCC security interests. The court reviewed the language of the tax statutes and the general principles of UCC commercial law. The case highlights the frequent conflict between private secured creditors and governmental entities attempting to recover tax liabilities through the seizure of property that is also subject to private debt obligations.

## Union Electric Co. v. Director of Revenue

75 S.W.3d 296 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the pollution control equipment met the functional definition of the exemption. The court ruled that the taxpayer's failure to strictly comply with the administrative filing procedures did not disqualify it from the substantive exemption given the purpose of the law. Union Electric Co., a major utility company, challenged the tax treatment of its pollution control equipment. The company argued that the equipment, required by environmental regulations to reduce emissions, should be exempt from sales and use tax under provisions designed to encourage environmental compliance. The Director of Revenue denied the exemption, arguing that the equipment did not meet the specific technical standards required by the statute for the environmental exemption and that the company had not filed the necessary declarations to trigger the status. Union Electric asserted that the statute should be interpreted liberally to promote environmental protection. The court reviewed the evidentiary requirements for environmental exemptions and the extent to which the Department of Revenue could impose procedural hurdles that effectively limited the scope of the incentive. The dispute centered on whether the functional purpose of the equipment alone was sufficient for the exemption or if strict adherence to the regulatory process was a mandatory prerequisite for the claim.

## Union Electric Co. v. Director of Revenue

732 S.W.2d 186 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1987 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the production of electricity constitutes a manufacturing process within the meaning of the tax code. Consequently, the utility company was entitled to the manufacturing exemption on equipment and materials directly used in the generation of power. Union Electric challenged the state's attempt to impose sales and use taxes on various inputs used in the production of electricity, including equipment and fuel. The utility company argued that these items were exempt under the manufacturing exemption because they were directly used in the generation of power, which they contended was a manufacturing process. The Director of Revenue denied the exemptions, maintaining that electricity generation did not qualify as manufacturing under the traditional definitions used in the tax statutes. The Supreme Court of Missouri conducted a comprehensive review of the historical definition of manufacturing and whether the process of generating electricity fit into this paradigm. The case involved extensive discussion on the nature of utility operations and whether the state intended for these large-scale operations to receive the same tax treatment as traditional industrial manufacturing. The ruling had significant fiscal implications for the state, as it clarified the applicability of industrial exemptions to the utility sector. The court focused on the language of the statute and whether the legislative intent was broad enough to encompass energy production facilities.

## Union Electric Co. v. Director of Revenue

425 S.W.3d 118 · Missouri Supreme Court · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the electricity generation process constitutes manufacturing. Therefore, the equipment used directly in that process qualifies for the sales tax exemption. Union Electric (Ameren) sought a refund for sales and use taxes paid on equipment and machinery purchased for the operation of its power plants. The dispute focused on the 'machinery and equipment' exemption, which allows for tax-free purchases of items used directly in manufacturing or processing. The Director of Revenue argued that the generation of electricity did not constitute 'manufacturing' under the plain language of the statute as it existed at the time of the purchases. Union Electric contended that the chemical and physical changes required to transform raw fuel into electrical energy fit the definition of manufacturing. The Court was tasked with determining whether the legislature intended to extend the manufacturing exemption to utility providers, a significant issue given the capital-intensive nature of power generation. This case underscored the strict construction rules applied to tax exemptions in Missouri and the importance of legislative definitions in tax litigation.

## Union Electric Co. v. Union Pacific Railroad Co.

309 S.W.3d 287 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the railroad breached the agreement by failing to provide the requisite documentation for the surcharges. It ruled that the utility was entitled to damages for the excessive amounts paid based on unsubstantiated costs. This dispute arose from a long-term rail transport contract between a utility company and a railroad. The contract contained a rate adjustment clause based on fuel surcharges. As fuel prices rose dramatically, the railroad increased the surcharges beyond the amount the utility believed was permitted by the contract. The utility alleged that the railroad breached the agreement by failing to provide adequate documentation to justify the surcharge increases. The railroad argued that the market-based pricing mechanism was intended to pass through the costs of fuel and that its documentation was sufficient under the business records exception to the hearsay rule. The court examined the contract's requirements for audit rights and the standards for reporting fuel costs. This case deals with the challenges of interpreting complex pricing mechanisms in long-term commercial contracts and the evidentiary standards necessary to enforce cost-shifting provisions in high-volume industrial service agreements.

## Union Planters Bank, N.A. v. Henderson

229 S.W.3d 155 (Mo. App. W.D. 2007) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that Union Planters Bank had a valid and perfected security interest in Henderson's cattle. Henderson had granted the security interest, value was given, and the bank filed a proper financing statement. The buyer did not qualify as a buyer in the ordinary course of business under the relevant UCC exceptions. The bank's security interest was enforceable against the buyer. This case concerns the attachment and perfection of a security interest in cattle. Union Planters Bank (UPB) loaned money to Henderson, taking a security interest in Henderson's cattle. UPB filed a UCC-1 financing statement. A dispute arose when Henderson sold some of the cattle to a third party who claimed to be a buyer in the ordinary course of business. The bank sought to enforce its security interest against the buyer. The appellate court examined whether UPB's security interest had attached and been properly perfected. Key issues included the adequacy of the description of collateral in the security agreement and financing statement, and whether the buyer qualified as a "buyer in the ordinary course of business" free from UPB's security interest. The court analyzed the requirements for attachment under UCC § 9-203 and perfection under UCC § 9-303, including the need for value, rights in collateral, and a security agreement. The case also touched upon the rules governing the rights of buyers of farm products.
