## Wooley v. Maynard

430 U.S. 705 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1977 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that the state could not force the driver to display its motto. It ruled that the right to avoid being forced to display a government message is protected by the First Amendment. George Maynard, a Jehovah's Witness, was prosecuted for covering the state motto 'Live Free or Die' on his New Hampshire license plate, finding the slogan morally, ethically, and religiously objectionable. Maynard argued that the state's requirement to display the motto on his private vehicle constituted compelled speech. The Supreme Court analyzed whether the state could force an individual to serve as a mobile billboard for the state's ideological message. The Court ruled in favor of Maynard, noting that the First Amendment protects the right to speak as well as the right not to speak. The state's interest in promoting its motto did not outweigh the individual's right to avoid being forced to express beliefs with which they disagreed. This case reinforced the principle that the government cannot force individuals to communicate a message that violates their personal convictions.

## Wooten v. Arakaki

388 S.W.3d 552 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the tenant failed to validly exercise the option because they did not strictly comply with the notice and payment terms. The court ruled in favor of the landlord, denying the request for specific performance. The parties entered into a lease-option agreement for a residential property, which later resulted in a dispute over whether the option to purchase had been validly exercised. The tenant claimed that they had sent written notice of their intent to purchase, but the landlord claimed the notice was insufficient and untimely under the terms of the agreement. Additionally, the landlord argued that the tenant had defaulted on lease payments, which invalidated the option. The court had to interpret the specific terms of the lease-option contract to determine the conditions precedent for the exercise of the option. The legal analysis centered on whether the tenant had met the financial prerequisites and the formal notice requirements. The court also examined the role of the doctrine of part performance, as the tenant had invested significant money into improvements on the property, which they argued should estop the landlord from denying the exercise of the option based on minor technicalities regarding the notice.

## Wooten v. Quiktrip Corp.

439 S.W.3d 252 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an employer cannot rely on a written policy against off-the-clock work if it creates an environment where such work is practically required to meet performance goals. Constructive knowledge is established when management ignores the reality of the hours needed for the work. The plaintiff, a retail employee, alleged that her employer maintained an 'off-the-clock' culture where managers pressured employees to finish closing tasks after they had clocked out to keep labor costs within targets. The defendant denied the existence of any such policy and claimed that any work performed off-the-clock was in violation of express company policy. The court scrutinized the adequacy of the company's anti-off-the-clock policies and whether those policies were effectively enforced. The litigation centered on the evidence required to prove that an employer had 'constructive knowledge' of unrecorded work. The appellate court looked at the testimony of store managers and whether the pressures of labor hour budgets created a foreseeable situation where employees would be forced to work without pay. This case provided significant clarity on the evidentiary burdens for establishing employer knowledge in off-the-clock wage cases within a high-volume retail setting, highlighting the discrepancy between written policies and actual store-level practices.

## Workman v. P.C.S. Co.

75 S.W.3d 741 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the distributor is subject to strict liability even if it did not participate in the manufacturing process or have the opportunity to inspect the product. Strict liability is intended to hold all entities in the chain of commerce accountable. The plaintiff was injured by a drill bit that shattered, leading to a personal injury suit against the distributor. The distributor argued that it was merely an intermediary and should not be held liable under strict liability because it did not manufacture the component and had no way of knowing about the internal metallurgical defect. The case revisited the application of Section 402A of the Restatement regarding whether the passive distributor or the retail seller could be held liable. The plaintiff emphasized that the policy behind strict liability is to place the burden of loss on those who benefit from the sale of the product, regardless of their lack of physical control over the manufacturing process. The court analyzed whether there should be exceptions for distributors who do not have the opportunity to inspect or modify the product before it reaches the end user.

## Workman v. State

184 S.W.3d 158 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2006 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the failure to investigate a known potential alibi witness constitutes ineffective assistance of counsel. When the witness's testimony is critical to the defense theory, failure to present such testimony satisfies the prejudice requirement. The petitioner filed a post-conviction relief motion alleging ineffective assistance of counsel in a criminal trial. He argued that his defense attorney failed to investigate a key alibi witness who could have refuted the prosecution's timeline. The state argued that the trial counsel's strategic decision not to call the witness was reasonable under the circumstances. The appellate court was asked to evaluate whether the counsel's failure to interview the witness met the 'deficient performance' prong of the Strickland v. Washington test, and whether that deficiency prejudiced the outcome of the case. This case reinforces the standards for criminal defense counsel performance under Missouri procedural rules.

## Wright v. Barr

62 S.W.3d 509 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the jury instructions were adequate and fairly represented the law. It upheld the defense verdict, finding that the plaintiff failed to convince the jury that the injury resulted from a breach of the standard of care. The plaintiff filed a medical malpractice lawsuit against a surgeon alleging negligence in the performance of a gallbladder operation. During the procedure, the surgeon allegedly nicked a bile duct, resulting in severe complications that required multiple follow-up surgeries and extensive recovery. The surgeon maintained that the injury was a known, non-negligent complication of the procedure and that all surgical steps were performed according to the standard of care. The plaintiff introduced expert testimony to argue that the injury occurred due to poor visualization and surgical technique. The appeal centered on whether the jury instructions were properly framed to prevent juror confusion regarding the difference between a bad outcome and actual negligence. The court reviewed the instructions for potential bias and whether they correctly reflected the burden of proof that the plaintiff must meet to show that the physician's actions, rather than the natural risks of the procedure, caused the injury.

## Wright v. City of Clinton

934 S.W.2d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the hiring process for high-level public officials must be conducted with maximum transparency. It ruled that the personnel exemption is not a blanket authorization to conduct the entire hiring process in secret. The decision clarified the balance between individual privacy and public oversight. A city council's process for selecting a new city manager was challenged as a violation of the Sunshine Law. The plaintiff argued that the screening and interview process for candidates was done in secret, which inhibited public participation and accountability. The city council argued that discussing personnel and candidates' sensitive information required a closed meeting. The court examined the personnel exemption of the Sunshine Law, specifically looking at whether it covers the process of hiring high-level public officials. The court held that while some personnel information regarding private individuals is protected, the public has a significant interest in the process of choosing the chief administrative official of the city. The court ruled that the city must conduct as much of the selection process as possible in public, reserving only specific sensitive discussions for closed session. This case balances individual privacy interests of applicants with the public's right to see how their municipal leadership is selected.

## Wright v. City of Salisbury

456 S.W.3d 898 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that meetings where public business is discussed, regardless of whether a final vote is taken, are subject to the Sunshine Law's open meeting requirements. It further ruled that financial ledgers of a municipality are public records subject to disclosure.

Second stored summary In this Sunshine Law case, the plaintiffs alleged that the City of Salisbury conducted closed meetings without proper notice and without a required vote, and improperly withheld financial records. The City defended its actions, claiming that the meetings were not 'meetings' as defined by the statute because no final action was taken. The court analyzed the definition of 'public governmental body' and 'meeting' to determine if the informal gathering constituted a violation. The discussion focused on whether a quorum of a public body discussing public business in an informal setting triggers the requirements of the Sunshine Law. The court looked at the legislative intent to prevent public bodies from conducting 'walking quorums' or serial meetings to avoid the scrutiny of the public. Furthermore, the court examined the City's failure to provide detailed minutes for the closed meetings that did occur. The decision emphasizes that the Sunshine Law's reach extends to informal gatherings where public business is transacted and that the definition of 'meeting' is not limited to formal voting sessions. The court also addressed the financial records request, finding that the City's refusal to provide ledger entries was unjustified as those documents are public records under Section 610.010.

## Wright v. City of Salisbury

656 S.W.3d 286 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the negotiations exception is limited. A city must demonstrate a specific, concrete threat to its bargaining position to justify closing a meeting for economic development negotiations. The plaintiff challenged the city's practice of closing meetings to discuss economic development incentives. The city argued that the discussions were protected by the 'negotiations' exception under the Sunshine Law. The plaintiff contended that the city was using the exception to prevent public debate on controversial projects and that the details of the negotiations were a matter of significant public interest. The court analyzed the scope of the negotiations exception, which allows public bodies to close meetings for discussions regarding potential contract terms. The court had to determine if the exception covers the entirety of the decision-making process or only specific bargaining points. The decision reinforced that the Sunshine Law requires transparency even in economic development matters. The court held that the governmental body must justify the closure by showing that public discussion would adversely affect the city's bargaining position. This ruling emphasizes that the city cannot use a broad interpretation of 'negotiation' to shield all aspects of economic development from public view, requiring the city to provide a detailed explanation for why disclosure of the meeting details would harm the public interest.

## Wyrick v. Pellerin

538 S.W.3d 383 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that a supervisor has a qualified privilege to make personnel decisions regarding subordinates. To sustain a claim of tortious interference, the plaintiff must show that the supervisor acted with malice or employed improper means to interfere with the contract. Wyrick, an employee, filed a wrongful termination suit against his former supervisor, alleging that the supervisor tortiously interfered with his employment contract. The trial court dismissed the action, ruling that as a supervisor acting within the scope of his employment, the defendant was entitled to qualified privilege. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that the supervisor's actions were motivated by personal malice rather than the interest of the company. The appellate court addressed the doctrine of tortious interference with a business expectancy in the employment context. It noted that to defeat the supervisor's qualified privilege, the plaintiff must show that the defendant used improper means or acted without justification. The court analyzed whether 'malice' alone was sufficient to remove the privilege. The court affirmed the dismissal, holding that the plaintiff failed to show that the supervisor acted outside the scope of his professional duties. The decision reinforces that internal personnel decisions made by management are generally protected from individual liability claims, provided the supervisor is acting within their role and not for purely personal reasons unrelated to the business.

## Wyrick v. T.G.I. Friday's

242 S.W.3d 330 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that tip-pooling arrangements that include non-tipped employees invalidate the employer's use of the tip credit under Missouri law. It ruled that the employer was required to pay the full minimum wage without the credit for the periods when the improper pool was in effect. The decision reinforced the protection of gratuities for traditionally tipped workers. The plaintiff, a restaurant server, challenged the employer's tip-pooling policy, which included non-tipped employees in the pool, thereby allegedly reducing the server's effective pay below the minimum wage after accounting for the tip credit. The restaurant argued that its tip-pooling arrangement was consistent with industry practice and allowed under federal FLSA regulations. The case required the court to interpret whether Missouri's wage statutes impose stricter limitations on tip pools than the federal FLSA. The appellate court examined the legislative history of Missouri's tip credit regulations and whether they were intended to be identical to federal standards. The case is a classic example of the legal challenges raised by service industry employees regarding the sharing of gratuities. The court assessed whether the inclusion of employees who do not customarily receive tips, such as cooks or dishwashers, in a tip pool violates the specific protections granted to tipped employees under Missouri law.

## Young v. American Airlines, Inc.

182 S.W.3d 647 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2005 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that the trial court properly entered a directed verdict for the employer on some counts but erred on others, as there was sufficient evidence to support a claim of disparate discipline. The case was remanded to address the specific evidence of differential treatment. The plaintiff, an African American flight attendant, alleged that she was subjected to a hostile work environment due to her race and gender in violation of the MHRA. She claimed that she was subjected to derogatory remarks and was disciplined more harshly than her white or male counterparts. The employer argued that the disciplinary actions were based on legitimate performance issues and that the alleged comments were not sufficiently pervasive to constitute a hostile environment. The appellate court examined the standard for a hostile work environment claim, which requires showing that the workplace is permeated with discriminatory intimidation, ridicule, and insult. The court scrutinized the evidence of 'comparable' employees to see if there was disparate treatment. The analysis focused on whether the plaintiff had established a prima facie case under the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework and whether the employer provided a non-discriminatory reason for the disparate treatment. The case highlights the importance of evidence regarding whether the employer's disciplinary policies were enforced neutrally and consistently across different racial and gender demographics.

## Young v. Boeing Co.

625 S.W.3d 745 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of benefits, holding that the claimant failed to satisfy the prevailing factor test for hearing loss. The court ruled that the Commission's reliance on age-related causation was supported by evidence. The claimant alleged a hearing loss injury due to years of exposure to loud machinery at a manufacturing facility. The employer argued that the hearing loss was age-related (presbycusis) and not work-related. The Commission found that the claimant failed to prove that the work noise was the prevailing factor in his hearing loss. The claimant appealed, arguing that the Commission ignored his audiologist's testimony which concluded that his hearing loss was 'consistent with' industrial noise exposure. The appellate court reviewed the Commission's decision and found that while the evidence was consistent with the claimant's argument, it did not satisfy the 'prevailing factor' standard, which requires that the employment be the primary cause of the condition. The court noted that age-related hearing loss is a common condition that can often be the primary factor. The Commission's determination that the employer's evidence regarding age-related causes was more compelling was upheld as a valid exercise of its fact-finding power.

## Young v. Boone Electric Cooperative

462 S.W.3d 783 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of benefits. It held that the claimant failed to prove that the stroke was caused by an 'unusual strain' as required by the statutory definition of an accident. The claimant alleged that his stroke was caused by job stress. The commission denied the claim because the claimant did not prove that the stroke was an 'accident' under the 2005 law, which excludes purely internal causes unless there is an abnormal physical strain. The appellate court reviewed the evidence regarding whether the work duties of the employee during the days leading up to the stroke met the standard of 'extraordinary' or 'unusual' strain. The claimant argued that his long hours and high-pressure duties constituted such a strain. The employer argued that a stroke is a biological event that occurs due to individual health factors and that there was no specific incident that could be labeled an accident. The court examined the definition of 'accident' and whether the legislative shift was intended to make these types of internal injuries non-compensable. The court concluded that the Commission correctly applied the law, emphasizing that there must be an identifiable physical event that is distinct from the employee's routine, even if that routine is high-stress.

## Young v. City of St. Louis

479 S.W.3d 675 (Mo. App. E.D. 2015) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment in part, holding that the employees were entitled to compensation for certain uncompensated work hours and overtime. However, the court reversed the trial court's denial of the meal and rest break claims, finding that the evidence presented raised genuine issues of material fact regarding the city's compliance with its own ordinances. The city was found liable for unpaid wages and overtime, with the break issue remanded for further proceedings. This case involved a class action lawsuit by former city employees alleging that the City of St. Louis failed to compensate them for all hours worked, including overtime, and failed to provide required meal and rest breaks. The plaintiffs argued that their workdays often extended beyond paid time, and that breaks were frequently interrupted or denied, thereby violating city ordinances and potentially the FLSA. The City maintained that employees were paid for all hours worked and that break policies were compliant. The trial court granted partial summary judgment to the employees on some claims and denied others, leading to an appeal. The appellate court reviewed the evidence of uncompensated time, the city's timekeeping practices, and the specific requirements of the city's break ordinances. The court assessed whether the plaintiffs had presented sufficient evidence to proceed on their claims.

## Young v. UPS

575 U.S. 206 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2015 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that employers may need to provide reasonable accommodations to pregnant workers, similar to those provided for disabled employees, unless doing so would impose an undue hardship. A policy that does not accommodate pregnant workers, while accommodating other temporarily disabled workers, may be discriminatory. This case addressed the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), which seeks to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnant workers, similar to disability accommodations. Young, a pregnant delivery driver, was unable to perform her job duties due to her pregnancy but was denied an accommodation by UPS, which offered her unpaid leave. She sued, alleging discrimination. The Court held that an employer's policy that seems neutral but has a disparate impact on pregnant workers may be discriminatory, and employers should provide accommodations similar to those provided for other temporary disabilities, absent undue hardship.

## Young v. Young

395 S.W.3d 588 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The judgment was reversed and remanded for findings on the nature of the debt. The court held that the trial court failed to determine whether the debt was marital or personal in nature before assigning it. The parties appealed the judgment of divorce regarding the allocation of debt. The trial court had assigned a significant amount of credit card debt, incurred by the wife for personal items during the marriage, entirely to the wife. The wife challenged this, arguing that the debt was marital and should be shared equally. The husband argued that the debt was 'separate' because it was used for non-essential personal expenses without his knowledge. The appellate court analyzed the law on marital debt, stating that debt incurred during the marriage is generally presumed to be marital debt unless the spouse incurring it was acting in bad faith or for non-marital purposes. The court found that the trial court failed to properly determine whether the debt was incurred for marital purposes or personal pleasure. It remanded the case for the trial court to make specific findings on the nature of the debt and to reallocate the debts if it determined they were indeed marital in nature. The court reiterated that the presumption of marital property extends to debts as well.

## Zadvydas v. Davis

533 U.S. 678 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2001 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the statute does not authorize indefinite detention. It established a 'presumptively reasonable' period of six months for detention following a final order of removal. After this period, if there is no significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future, the government must release the alien. The petitioner was a resident alien ordered deported, but no country would accept him. He remained in detention for an indefinite period following his removal order. He filed a habeas corpus petition, arguing that his continued detention violated the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause. The government argued that its authority to detain an alien after a final removal order is essentially unlimited, provided the government is working toward the eventual removal. The Supreme Court faced the challenge of interpreting the INA's language regarding post-removal-order detention. It had to reconcile the government's need to secure the border and ensure compliance with removal orders with the constitutional prohibition against indefinite administrative detention without judicial oversight or a clear end point.

## Zafft v. Eli Lilly & Co.

676 S.W.2d 241 (Mo. App. W.D. 1984) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1984 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment. The court held that a manufacturer has a duty to warn of known or reasonably discoverable dangers associated with its product. The court found sufficient evidence that Eli Lilly knew or should have known of the potential risks associated with DES and failed to provide adequate warnings, thus breaching its duty and causing the plaintiff's injury. This was a products liability case where the plaintiff alleged injury from the use of the drug DES (diethylstilbestrol), a synthetic estrogen. The plaintiff claimed that Eli Lilly and Company manufactured and marketed DES without adequate warnings about its potential dangers, particularly to the offspring of women who took the drug during pregnancy. The plaintiff, who suffered from vaginal adenosis, alleged this condition was caused by her mother's prenatal exposure to DES. Eli Lilly argued that at the time of manufacture and sale, the dangers were not known or scientifically established, and therefore, they had no duty to warn. The trial court entered judgment for the plaintiff, and Eli Lilly appealed.

## Zahner v. City of Perryville

551 S.W.3d 608 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the judgment. It held that the zoning ordinance was a valid exercise of legislative power and was supported by a rational basis, rendering it immune to the plaintiffs' challenge. The plaintiffs, residential property owners, challenged a municipal ordinance that rezoned their property from residential to commercial, arguing it was an 'arbitrary and capricious' exercise of the City's police power. They claimed that the rezoning negatively impacted their property values and violated the comprehensive plan. The City argued that the rezoning was necessary for orderly urban development and that it acted within its legislative discretion. The trial court granted summary judgment for the City, finding that zoning decisions are entitled to a high level of deference under the rational basis standard. The appellate court reviewed the standard of judicial review for municipal zoning ordinances, confirming that courts will not substitute their judgment for that of the local legislative body unless the ordinance is clearly unreasonable. The case discusses the scope of the 'fairly debatable' rule in Missouri zoning law and the balance between private property rights and the municipality's interest in regulating land use for the public good.

## Zahner v. N. Kansas City Hosp.

625 S.W.3d 520 · Mo. Ct. App. · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of benefits, holding that the claimant failed to establish a causal connection to her employment. The court held that speculative claims for occupational illness do not meet the burden of proof required for compensation. The claimant, a registered nurse, alleged she contracted a viral illness due to exposure to patients in the hospital where she worked. She sought medical expenses and temporary total disability benefits. The employer denied the claim, arguing that the claimant failed to prove that the exposure occurred at work rather than in the general community. The Commission denied the claim, finding that the medical evidence was insufficient to establish a causal nexus between the hospital environment and the specific illness. The nurse appealed, challenging the Commission's reliance on the employer's expert witness. The court reviewed the record and determined that the Commission's decision was based on a reasonable assessment of the evidence. It noted that the burden of proving that the illness arose out of and in the course of employment rests with the claimant. Because the claimant could not conclusively trace the illness to a work-related exposure, the court upheld the Commission's decision to deny benefits, emphasizing that speculative causation is insufficient for a workers compensation award.

## Ziglar v. Abbasi

582 U.S. 120 · U.S. Supreme Court · 2017 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the plaintiffs could not maintain a Bivens action. The Court significantly restricted the scope of Bivens, establishing that if a case presents a 'new context,' a court must conduct a rigorous analysis of whether any alternative remedy exists and whether special factors counsel against expanding the judicial remedy. Following the September 11 terrorist attacks, several aliens were arrested and detained in federal facilities. These individuals sued high-level government officials, including former Attorney General John Ashcroft and FBI Director Robert Mueller, alleging that the detention policies violated their constitutional rights, specifically due process and the Fourth Amendment. The plaintiffs sought damages under a Bivens theory. The government officials argued that the detainees were attempting to expand the reach of Bivens to a new context--challenging executive policy regarding national security. The case reached the Supreme Court to address the limitations of the Bivens remedy. The Court evaluated whether the courts should create new remedies for constitutional violations when the judiciary is asked to weigh in on high-level executive branch policies and security decisions made in the immediate aftermath of a national crisis.

## Zimmerman v. St. Louis Cnty.

567 S.W.3d 654 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: Zoning ordinances are presumed valid. A property owner challenging the denial of a variance must demonstrate that the board acted arbitrarily and without supporting evidence. This case concerned a property owner's challenge to a local zoning ordinance that prohibited certain types of accessory structures on their lot. The owner sought a variance from the zoning board, which was denied. The owner then sought judicial review, claiming the ordinance was arbitrary and unreasonable as applied to their specific property. The court reiterated that zoning decisions are entitled to a presumption of validity, and the burden is on the property owner to show that the zoning restriction is unreasonable. The appellate court examined the evidence presented to the board and found that there was substantial evidence to support the board's decision that granting the variance would be inconsistent with the neighborhood's overall zoning plan. The court concluded that the board did not abuse its discretion in denying the variance, as the ordinance served a legitimate public interest in regulating aesthetics and property usage density. The decision reinforces the deference courts afford to local planning bodies in zoning matters.

## Zip Express of Kansas City, Inc. v. Director of Revenue

88 S.W.3d 445 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the courier services provided by the taxpayer were not subject to sales tax because the statute did not explicitly encompass the services rendered by the company. The court ruled that tax statutes are to be construed strictly against the taxing authority. Zip Express, a courier company, contested the Director of Revenue's decision to assess sales tax on its delivery services. The Department of Revenue argued that the services provided by the courier were subject to sales tax because they fell within the classification of transportation or logistics services enumerated in the tax statutes. The taxpayer asserted that its business activities did not meet the definition of the services that were meant to be taxed and that the assessment was an overreach of the state's taxing authority. The case required a detailed statutory interpretation of the Missouri tax code regarding the taxation of service-based businesses. The court evaluated the scope of the state's authority to impose sales tax on specific services and whether Zip Express was providing the exact service subject to tax. The court looked at the legislative intent behind the tax provisions and whether the inclusion of such courier services was clearly authorized. This case provided important guidance on the taxation of the modern service economy and limited the ability of the Department of Revenue to interpret ambiguous service statutes broadly without explicit legislative support.

## Zipper v. Health Midwest

978 S.W.2d 398 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that although a 'termination for convenience' clause allows for termination without cause, it is still subject to the implied duty of good faith and fair dealing. The court concluded that such clauses cannot be used to exercise bad faith or fraudulent conduct. Dr. Zipper entered into a contract with a hospital entity, Health Midwest, to provide medical services. The contract was terminated by the hospital, leading Dr. Zipper to file a lawsuit alleging breach of contract and tortious interference with business expectancies. The hospital argued that it had the right to terminate the contract under a 'termination for convenience' clause contained within the professional services agreement. Dr. Zipper countered that the termination was motivated by bad faith and was an attempt to stifle his practice and eliminate a competitor. The case focused on the interpretation of the 'termination for convenience' clause and whether it implies an obligation of good faith and fair dealing. The court analyzed whether such clauses are absolute or if they are subject to an implied covenant of good faith that prohibits opportunistic or malicious termination. This dispute highlighted the tension between the freedom to contract, which allows parties to define their own exit strategies, and the judicial requirement that contractual powers must not be exercised in a manner that defeats the purpose of the agreement or violates fundamental fairness in a professional relationship.

## Zipper v. Sun Drop Bottling Co.

651 S.W.2d 163 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while puffery is permissible, advertising that makes objectively false health claims can violate the MPA. It emphasized the importance of the reasonable consumer standard. This early case involved a dispute regarding the marketing and sale of a soft drink. The plaintiff alleged that the company's advertising misled consumers about the nutritional benefits of the drink. The bottling company argued that its advertisements were clearly puffery and not intended to be taken as factual health claims by the average consumer. The court evaluated whether the MPA covers advertising claims that might be considered exaggerated but are not objectively false in a way that would defraud a consumer. The case

Second stored summary highlighted the tension between allowing companies creative marketing freedom and protecting consumers from misleading health claims. The court had to define the threshold for 'unfair' and 'deceptive' practices in the context of food and beverage marketing, considering whether a reasonable consumer would rely on such statements when making a purchasing decision, and whether such reliance could result in a legally cognizable injury under the act.

## Zukerman v. Landmark Savings Association

4 S.W.3d 566 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1999 · Missouri

Holding: A landlord who has transferred full possession and control of premises to a tenant is not liable for injuries occurring on the property, provided the landlord did not know of a dangerous condition at the time of the transfer. Liability is tied directly to the retention of control. This case dealt with the liability of a property owner for injuries sustained by a visitor to the premises, analyzing the status of the visitor as either an invitee or a licensee. The landlord, a financial institution, held title to the property but had leased it to an operator. The plaintiff was injured due to a defect on the premises and sued the landlord. The key question was whether the landlord retained sufficient possession or control to be held liable for the dangerous condition. The court reviewed the terms of the lease, noting that the tenant had complete control over the maintenance of the interior of the premises. Under Missouri law, a landlord who relinquishes possession and control to a tenant is generally not liable for injuries resulting from dangerous conditions on the property, unless the condition existed at the time of the transfer and the landlord failed to disclose it. The court concluded that because the landlord had no role in the day-to-day operations or maintenance of the specific area where the injury occurred, it could not be held liable. This decision reaffirmed the importance of the 'control' test in determining landlord liability for injuries to third parties on leased property.

## Zurich American Insurance Co. v. Insurance Co. of North America

619 S.W.3d 215 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the insurance carrier on the risk at the time of the last exposure is responsible for the entire claim. It applied the 'last exposure' rule to avoid the inequitable and complex apportionment of disability among insurers. This was an inter-insurer dispute over the apportionment of liability for a permanent partial disability claim involving cumulative trauma. One insurance company argued that the other was liable for a portion of the disability because they held the policy during the years the cumulative trauma began to manifest. The case required the court to interpret the 'last exposure' rule in the context of successive insurers. The appellate court examined which insurance carrier is responsible for claims arising from long-term occupational conditions that span multiple policy periods. This case is crucial for resolving liability between insurance companies that cover different parts of a company's long-term exposure history in the workers' compensation field.

About This Guide & Data Quality
Notes
About this guide
This is an offline reference compiled on September 3, 2026 from the legal reference library inside the LawMind AI
application (Base44 app 6a53429210c1ce40398a53a8). It was produced read-only: nothing in the live library was
altered, merged, or deleted.
What is included
Legal dictionary terms: 39,681 entries. Latin terms: 219. Encyclopedia articles: 1,458. Statutes and regulations:
10,284. Case summaries: 15,021.
Records excluded for suspected OCR corruption
The dictionary source includes a bulk import of Black's Law Dictionary from scanned page images, and a meaningful
share of it is structurally corrupted. 7,107 dictionary records were excluded from the main body: 604 confirmed by an
earlier sampled audit, and the remainder flagged by the same conservative test applied across the whole set.
Records were flagged for scan artefacts such as letters split by spaces ("A DM I N I C ULAR EVI D ENCE"),
definitions that begin mid-sentence, and fragments with no vowels. Nothing was repaired or reconstructed guessing at a legal definition would be worse than omitting it. Every excluded record is listed with its Base44 record
ID in the companion file lawmind_excluded_ocr_records.csv, so each one can be checked by hand against the
source.
Duplicate entries merged for readability
The library contains substantial duplication. In the statute set, 12,011 records were duplicates of another record and
are shown once here: the Missouri statutes are the worst affected, with 9,422 stored records covering only 1,030
distinct citations, and some individual sections stored as many as 257 times. The UCC set holds 3,442 records for
433 distinct citations. In the dictionary, 1,658 duplicates were merged, and where the same authority was stored
under different citation formats the variants are shown together on one entry. Case summaries: 979 merged.
Encyclopedia articles: 699 merged. This merging affects this document only - the duplicates still exist in the live
library.
How complete the case summaries are
Two thirds of the case records are citation stubs rather than real summaries. Of 15,021 case entries, 9,665 (64 per
cent) carry no summary text at all - the stored summary is just a placeholder naming the reporter volume - and 9,922
have no holding. Those entries are kept because the citation, court and year are still worth having offline, but each
one is marked "Citation record only" so it is never mistaken for a real summary. The 5,356 entries that do carry a
genuine holding and summary are the substantive part of Volumes 9 and 10.
Known limits of this snapshot
Three limits are worth stating plainly. First, coverage: the dictionary, Latin terms and encyclopedia were read to
exhaustion, but the statute and case-summary sets are larger than the export interface can page through in one
pass, so those two are substantially but not provably complete - Missouri case summaries in particular hit the
interface's 10,000-record paging ceiling. Second, residual corruption: the exclusion test is deliberately conservative,
so some corrupted dictionary entries remain in the main body; treat an entry that reads oddly as suspect and check
the original. Third, currency: this is a snapshot of one moment and statutes and case law change. Verify anything
load-bearing against the official source before relying on it in a filing.
Recommended next step (not yet done)
A dedicated data-cleanup pass on the live library is recommended and has not been carried out. It should
de-duplicate the statute set - the Missouri import in particular appears to have run repeatedly - and quarantine the
OCR-corrupted dictionary records for re-import from a clean source. This guide is a faithful picture of the library as it
stands, including its defects.
